en: (GBr_0.0.0a) Oṃ! Salutation to the Atharvaveda; salutation!
(GBr 1.1.1a) Om. In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman, the Self-existent, alone. (GBr 1.1.1b) It thought: "Verily, I am a great being, since I am alone."
"Come now, let me create from myself alone a second deity who is my very measure. He exerted himself, he heated himself, he brooded intensely.
From him, thus exerted, heated, and brooding intensely, a moisture arose on his forehead—something moist that was produced.
He rejoiced because of that. He said:
"Truly, a great Yakṣa! Well-found, I have found it!"
Because he said,
"Great indeed is this Yakṣa; well-found have I found it," therefore he became Suveda.
Although this is "Suveda" (easy to know), they call it "Sveda" (sweat) by means of a cryptic term;
(GBr 1.1.2ab) He labored further, he heated himself further, he tormented himself further.
From all the pores of his skin, as he was thus weary, heated, and tormented, streams of sweat flowed forth separately.
By means of them, he rejoiced.
He said:
"By these indeed shall I uphold all this, whatever exists here; by these indeed shall I generate all this, whatever exists here."
"By means of these, indeed, I shall attain all this, whatever exists here"— this is what he said. "By means of these, indeed, I shall sustain all this, whatever exists here"— this is what he said.
From that, the streams came into being; that is the "stream-nature" (*dhārātva*) of the streams, because they flow (*dhriyate*).
As for what he said:
"By means of these, indeed, I shall generate all this, whatever exists here.
Therefore they became wives (*jāyā*). That is the "wifeness" (*jāyātva*) of wives: that a man is born from them, and that a son is born.
Furthermore, there is a hell named Anekaśatatāra; one who rescues from that is a *putra* (son),
and that is the sonship of a son.
Because he said,
"By means of these, indeed, I shall obtain all this, whatever there is," therefore they became the waters.
That is the essence of the waters;
indeed, he attains all desires whatsoever that he may desire. // 2 //
Having created those waters, he gazed upon them; in them he saw his own reflection. As he was gazing at it, his semen fell of its own accord.
That established itself in the waters;
he exerted himself over them there, brooded over them, and heated them.
Exhausted, brooded upon, and thoroughly heated, they became divided into two parts along with the semen.

(GBr_1,1.3h) Of these, one was excessively salty, undrinkable, and unpalatable; (GBr_1,1.3i) those were restless and remained having covered the ocean with their seed. (GBr_1,1.3j) But the others were drinkable, palatable, and tranquil.
He exerted himself over them, he brooded over them, he heated them.
From them, when they were thus exerted, brooded upon, and heated, that which was their seed became parched.
From that, Bhṛgu came into being.
That is the origin of Bhṛgu’s name as Bhṛgu.
Indeed, he who knows this shines like Bhṛgu in all the worlds. 3.
Having created Bhr̥gu, he disappeared.
That Bhr̥gu, once created, moved toward the east.
Speech spoke after him.
"O Vāyu! O Vāyu! he said, and he turned back; he went toward the southern direction, and Speech spoke after him.
"Mātariśvan! Mātariśvan! he said, and he turned back; he went toward the western direction.
Speech spoke after him.
"Pavamāna, Pavamāna! he cried; he turned back and went toward the northern direction.
Vāk followed after him.
"O Wind, O Wind!
he said to him; he replied, "Did I not know?"
"No," he said.
"Then seek him further within these very waters. Because he said, "Then seek him further within these very waters," he became Atharvan.
(GBr_1,1.4t) That is why Atharvan is called "Atharvan.
(GBr_1,1.4u) Indeed, for this venerable seer Atharvan, his entire self came into being just as the hairs, the limbs, and the vital breaths of Brahmā had come into being.
(GBr_1,1.4v) Having created the offspring of Prajāpati, Brahmā said to that Atharvan: "Protect these creatures!"
Because he said to him, "Having created the creatures of Prajāpati, protect them," therefore he became Prajāpati;
that is the nature of Prajāpati. Atharvan indeed is Prajāpati.
He who knows this shines in all worlds like Prajāpati. 4.
He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated that seer Atharvan.
From him—exhausted, brooded upon, and intensely heated—he fashioned forth the ten-fold Atharvan seers:
those consisting of one verse, two verses, three verses, four verses, five verses, six verses, seven verses, eight verses, nine verses, and ten verses.
Thus, he exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those seers of the Atharvans;
from them, thus exerted, brooded over, and intensely heated, [he drew forth] the ten-fold Atharvanic ancestral lineages.
He fashioned eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen,
eighteen, nineteen, and twenty [verses].
He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those seers of the Atharvans and the Atharvanic lineages.
From them—exhausted, brooded upon, and intensely heated—the mantras which he beheld became the Atharva Veda.
He then exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated that Atharva Veda.
From him, when he was weary, heated, and thoroughly exhausted, the syllable *om*—the upward-moving imperishable—emerged from his mind.

Whoever should desire, "May I perform [this rite] with all these Atharvans and Atharvaṇas," let him perform it with this very Great Utterance (*mahāvyāhṛti*). Verily, for one who knows thus, and who, knowing thus, performs it with this Great Utterance, it becomes performed by all these Atharvans and Atharvaṇas.
He labored further, he heated himself further, he disciplined himself further.
From his very self-discipline, he fashioned forth the three worlds: the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky.
Indeed, from his two feet alone, he fashioned forth the earth.
From his belly [he fashioned] the intermediate space, and from his head the sky.
He exerted himself toward, brooded over, and intensely heated those three worlds.
From them—exhausted, brooded upon, and intensely heated—he brought forth the three gods.
"Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya"—
thus he indeed fashioned Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Āditya from the sky.
He exerted himself for, brooded over, and intensely heated those three deities.
From them—exhausted, heated, and thoroughly scorched—he fashioned forth the three Vedas: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda.
From Agni he drew out the Ṛgveda, from Vāyu the Yajurveda, and from Āditya the Sāmaveda. He then exerted himself with regard to those three Vedas; he brooded over them and thoroughly heated them.
When they were exhausted, distressed, and deeply afflicted, he fashioned from them the three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*): *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
*Bhūḥ* was drawn from the *Ṛgveda*, *bhuvaḥ* from the *Yajurveda*, and *svar* from the *Sāmaveda*.
If one should desire to perform [a rite] with all these three Vedas, one should do so by means of these very great utterances.

(GBr_1.1.6q) Indeed, for one who knows this, and for one who, knowing thus, performs [the rites] with these Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), everything has been accomplished by means of all three Vedas.
Those waters which, having encompassed the ocean as their seed, stood there, rushed together toward the east, the south, the west, and the north.
Because they rushed together (*samavadravanta*), it is therefore called the ocean (*samudra*).
Terrified, they said:
"We choose the Blessed One himself as our king," they said;
and because they chose him and stood [by him], he became Varuṇa. Although he is this very Varuṇa, they call him Varuṇa cryptically.
(GBr_1,1.7h) For the gods are fond of what is hidden and hate what is manifest.
(GBr_1,1.7i) He was released from the ocean; (GBr_1,1.7j) he became Mucyu.
Although he is indeed Mucyu, they call him "Death" cryptically;
for the gods, as it were, prefer the cryptic and dislike the manifest.
He exerted himself toward, brooded over, and intensely heated that Varuṇa, Death.
From him, being weary, heated, and thoroughly scorched, essence flowed from all his limbs; that became the *aṅgarasa* (limb-essence).
Because he was that *aṅgarasa*, they call him "Aṅgiras" cryptically.
(GBr_1,1.7q) For the gods, as it were, love what is hidden and hate what is manifest. // 7 //
He exerted himself, heated, and brooded over that seer Aṅgiras.
From him—exerted, heated, and thoroughly brooded upon—he fashioned the twenty Aṅgiras seers.
He then exerted himself, heated, and brooded over those twenty Aṅgiras seers.
For them, when they were exhausted, heated, and thoroughly scorched by austerity, he fashioned the ten-fold *āṅgirasa* lineages as ancestral seers:
those consisting of sixteen verses, eighteen verses, twelve verses; those of one verse, two verses, three verses, four verses, five verses, six verses, and seven verses.
He exerted himself over those seers, the Aṅgirases, and the ancestral lineages of the Aṅgirases; he brooded over them and heated them thoroughly.
From them—exhausted, brooded over, and thoroughly heated—the mantras which he beheld became the Veda of the Aṅgirases.
He then exerted himself over that Veda of the Aṅgirases; he brooded over it and heated it thoroughly.
From him, when he was weary, heated, and thoroughly scorched, the syllable *janat* emerged as a duality.
If one should desire, "May I perform [this rite] with all these Aṅgirases and descendants of Aṅgiras," he should perform it with this very Great Utterance (*mahāvyāhṛti*).
Verily, for one who knows thus, and who, knowing thus, performs it with this Great Utterance, it becomes performed by all these Aṅgirases and descendants of Aṅgiras.
He stood upright;
he propped apart these worlds.
Therefore, an Aṅgiras who is studying stands upright.
(GBr 1.1.9d) He should meditate with his mind on that vow: "Whatever I shall meditate upon with my mind, even so shall it come to be. (GBr 1.1.9f) And indeed, it came to be exactly so.
(GBr 1.1.9g) This has also been stated in a Rigvedic verse:
(GBr 1.1.9h) The most excellent Veda was born from ascetic heat; it came into being for the protection of those who have lost their Brahmanic power.
(GBr 1.1.9i) That which was created as the straight-moving reality—this dwelling place—is free from debt and far-reaching for him.
[Ed: *ṛcy ṛgbhūtam*—see Patyal’s note.]
These *menī* bricks are indeed the sisters of the Aṅgirases;
he who knows this performs heroic power by means of the *menīs*. 9.

He looked toward the quarters: the east, the south, the west, the north, the fixed direction, and the upward direction. He exerted himself over them, brooded over them, and intensely heated them. From them—exhausted, brooded upon, and intensely heated—he fashioned forth the five Vedas.
The Serpent Veda, the Piśāca Veda, the Asura Veda, the Itihāsa Veda, and the Purāṇa Veda.
He indeed fashioned the Serpent Veda from the eastern direction,
and the Piśāca Veda from the southern direction.
From the western direction, the Asuraveda;
from the northern direction, the Itihāsaveda; and from the fixed and upward directions, the Purāṇaveda.
He exerted himself over those five Vedas, brooded over them, and intensely meditated upon them.
From them—exhausted, brooded over, and intensely meditated upon—he fashioned the five great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*):
"vṛdhat," "karat," "ruhat," "mahat," and "tat."
"Vṛdhat" from the Sarpaveda;
"karat" from the Piśācaveda; "ruhat" from the Asuraveda.
"Mahat" is from the Itihāsa-Veda;
"tat" is from the Purāṇa-Veda.
If one should desire to perform [the sacrifice] with all these five Vedas, he should do so by means of these very Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).

(GBr_1,1.10t) Indeed, for one who knows this, and for one who, knowing thus, performs [rites] with these great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), everything is accomplished by means of all five of these Vedas.
10 (GBr_1,1.11a) He looked toward both the near shore and the far shore;
(GBr_1,1.11b) there he exerted himself, brooded, and concentrated intensely.
From those [vows], when they were weary, heated, and thoroughly distressed, the syllable *śam* rose upward.

He who should desire, "May I perform [the rites] with all these, both the near (*āvad*) and the distant (*parāvad*)," should perform them with this very Great Utterance (*mahāvyāhṛti*). For him who knows thus, and who, knowing thus, performs [the rites] with this Great Utterance, everything is indeed performed for him with all these, both the near and the distant.
He labored further, he heated himself further, he disciplined himself further.
From his mind alone, he fashioned the moon;
from his nails, the stars.
From his body hairs [he created] the plants and trees;
from his minor vital breaths, the many other gods.
He labored further, he heated himself further, he disciplined himself further.
He beheld this sacrifice, which is threefold, seven-threaded, and culminates in twenty-one parts.
Regarding this, it is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Agni [beholds] the sacrifice, threefold and seven-threaded."
Moreover, this playful verse also confirms it:
"There are seven Soma-pressings and seven Pākayajñas. 12.
He brought it; with it he sacrificed;
Agni was his *hotṛ*.
Vāyu is the Adhvaryu; Sūrya is the Udgātṛ;
Candramas is the Brahman.
Parjanya is the assistant priest;
the plants and trees are the cup-bearers;
the Viśve Devas are the Hotrakas.
The Atharvans and Aṅgirases are the guardians.
Those of old who were learned in the Vedas and possessed such knowledge, having approached a sacrifice that had been prepared, used to walk around it, saying:
"O immortals, let not this heated oblation burn up our offspring while we are negligent."
(GBr_1,1.13n) They call these very ones "protectors" (*parirakṣaka*) and "those who enter the assembly hall" (*sadaḥprasarpaka*), for they are perfected by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
(GBr_1,1.13o) Regarding this, Prajāpati indeed said:
(GBr_1,1.13p) "When the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at a sacrifice are unskilled, or when they have not practiced their vows, or are devoid of self-restraint (*brahmacarya*)."
(GBr_1,1.13q) They indeed call that a fracture of the sacrifice.
(GBr_1,1.13r) Following a fracture of the sacrifice, the sacrificer is fractured;
(GBr_1,1.13s) following a fracture of the sacrificer, the officiating priests are fractured.
Following the injury of the officiating priests, the sacrificial fees are injured;
following the injury of the sacrificial fees, the sacrificer is injured in his sons and cattle;
following the injury of his sons and cattle, the sacrificer is injured in the heavenly world.
"The fracture of the heavenly world follows; the security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) of that half [of the world] is shattered in which half they sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 13.
Those who know him thus, when there is a failure in the sacrifice or a defect in the sacrifice, should approach that Brahmin, saying:
"Homage be to you, O Blessed One!
May you mend for us the failure in the sacrifice."

(GBr 1,1.14d) Wherever there may be a fracture, one should kindle the fires there, prepare the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), and sprinkle the fires three times with the formula, "For the ear of the Earth," and circumambulate them three times sprinkling water.
(GBr 1,1.14e) While the work is being performed, he causes [the performer] to sip water three times and sprinkles him three times. (GBr 1,1.14f) He also sprinkles the sacrificial site.
Moreover, by means of the essence of the Vedas, whatever is torn in the sacrifice is joined together.
Just as one might join gold with salt, silver with gold, iron with silver, lead with iron, and tin with lead—in this very way, whatever is torn in this sacrifice is joined.
Following the joining of the sacrifice, the sacrificer is himself joined.
Following the union of the sacrificer, the officiating priests are united; following the union of the officiating priests, the sacrificial gifts are united;
following the union of the sacrificial gifts, the sacrificer is united with his sons and cattle.
"Following the union of sons and cattle, the sacrificer is united with the heavenly world;
following the union with the heavenly world, the security and prosperity of that half [of the world] is secured, in which half they sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 14.
Regarding this, Atharvan Deva, knowing [the truth], used to say: "Those who know the ritual should appease whatever deficiencies in the sacrifice there may be;

thus an expiation is performed in the sacrifice. Moreover, even if much that is contrary to the ritual order is performed in the sacrifice, no affliction whatsoever shall befall him, nor does he encounter an obstruction of the sacrifice. He strikes down repeated death, and he overcomes repeated rebirth."

"He who knows this has freedom of movement in all worlds; he shines forth—both he who, knowing thus, becomes the Brahman priest, and he for whom a Brahman priest knowing thus sits to the south of the sacrificial hall, and he for whom a Brahman priest knowing thus, seated to the south facing north, offers the oblations of clarified butter at the sacrifice"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 15.
In the lotus, Brahmā indeed created Brahmā.
That Brahmā, once created, fell into reflection:
"By what single syllable might I [attain] all desires, all worlds, and all..."
"May I experience all the gods, all the Vedas, all sacrifices, all sounds, all prosperities, and all beings, both stationary and moving"— with this thought,
he practiced the life of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*).

He beheld this syllable *om*, consisting of two letters and four measures, all-pervading, all-encompassing, the imperishable Brahman, the Vyahṛti of Brahmā, having Brahman as its deity. By means of it, he attained all desires,
all worlds, all gods, all Vedas, all sacrifices, all sounds, all prosperities, and all beings.
He experienced the stationary and moving beings; with his first color, he experienced the waters and moisture; with his second color, he experienced heat and the luminaries. // 16 //

(GBr_1.1.17a) By means of its first measure of tone, he pervaded the earth, Agni, the plants and trees, the Rigveda, the Vyāhṛti *bhūḥ*, the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt Stoma, the eastern direction, the spring season, and with respect to the self, speech, the tongue, and taste— thus these sense organs.

By its second vowel-syllable, he took possession of the intermediate space, the wind, the Yajurveda, the *vyāhṛti* "Bhuvaḥ," the *triṣṭubh* metre, the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*), the western direction, the summer season, the vital breath with respect to the self,
and the two nostrils as the sense of smelling odors— thus he took possession of the senses. 18.

By its third measure of tone, he pervaded heaven, the sun, the Sāmaveda, the *vyāhṛti* "Svar," the Jāgata metre, the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), the northern direction, the rainy season, light, and with respect to the self, the eyes and sight— thus [he pervaded] the sense organs. 19.

By means of the mere letter *va* of that [syllable *om*], he experienced the waters, the moon, the Atharvaveda, the stars, his own self as *om*, the progenitors (*janad*) as the Aṅgirases, the Anuṣṭubh metre, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), the southern quarter, the autumn season, the mind as the internal self, knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the senses. 20.
By the sound of its *m*, he experienced the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Vākovākya, Gāthās, Nārāśaṃsīs, Upaniṣads, and instructions;
the words *vṛdhat*, *karat*, *ruhat*, *mahat*, *tat*, *śam*, *om*—these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛtis*); lutes with many strings, sounding and well-tuned;
vocal and instrumental music, dance, song, and percussion; the celestial deity Caitraratha, the lightning-light, and the Bārhata Sāman.

The *chandas* meters, the *triṇava* and *trayastrimśa* *stomas*, the fixed upward direction, the seasons of winter and the cool season, and internally, the ear, sound, and hearing—thus he pervaded the sense organs. // 21 //
(GBr_1,1.22a) This very one-syllabled [Brahman] appeared at the beginning of the austerity of Brahman, the pure Atharvan of the *brahmaveda*. (GBr_1,1.22b) From that alone the mantras appeared.

(GBr_1,1.22c) Whatever in the mantras one makes deficient, damaged, or exhausted through lack of austerity, lack of service, or recitation on forbidden days, that he shall restore by means of the splendor of the Atharvans.
(GBr_1,1.22d) And may the mantras turn toward me, as embryos yearn to reach their mother.
(GBr_1,1.22e) He employs the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning;
(GBr_1,1.22f) by this very verse he should cause [the student] to attain restoration.
This very [breath] is yoked at the front of the sacrifice;
this is [yoked] at the back;
by means of this, the sacrifice is performed on all sides.
This has also been stated in a Rigvedic verse:
"That which is joined in the beginning, in the syllable, in the highest heaven.

A Brahmin who desires whatever object he may wish for should, having fasted for three nights, facing eastward and restraining his speech, sit upon sacrificial grass and repeat that very syllable a thousand times.
"His purposes and all his ritual actions are accomplished," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The city of Indra was filled with streams of wealth;
the Asuras besieged it,
and the gods were afraid.
"Who will slay these Asuras?
they asked. They beheld Oṃkāra, the eldest son of Brahmā, and they spoke to him.
"By means of your mouth, let us conquer these Asuras," [they said].
He replied,
"What will be my reward?"
"Choose a boon," [he said].
"I choose," [he replied]. He chose a boon.
"O Brāhmaṇas, you should not speak of the Brahman without having sent for me;
if you were to speak it, that would not be the true Brahman. "So be it," they replied.
(GBr_1,1.23p) Those gods were engaged in battle with the Asuras on the northern half of the sacrificial ground.

(GBr_1,1.23q) By means of the syllable *oṃ*, the gods caused the Asuras to perish from the Āgnīdhra fire-altar. (GBr_1,1.23r) Because they caused them to perish (*parābhāvayanta*), therefore the syllable *oṃ* is uttered first.
"Indeed, he who does not know this syllable *oṃ* would be without mastery; but he who knows it thus shall possess mastery over Brahman.
Therefore, in the *ṛc*, the *ṛc* becomes *oṃ*; in the *yajus*, the *yajus* becomes *oṃ*.
The *sāman* is in the *sāman*;
the *sūtra* is in the *sūtra*;
the *brāhmaṇa* is in the *brāhmaṇa*.
"Verse upon verse, the syllable *praṇava* upon the syllable *praṇava*"—this is the Brāhmaṇa passage. // 23 //
(GBr_1,1.24a) We inquire about the syllable *oṃ*: (GBr_1,1.24b) what is its root?
(GBr_1,1.24c) what is its nominal stem (*prātipadika*)?
What is the name? What is the verb? What is the gender? What is the number?
What is a case ending? What is a suffix? What is a vowel, a prefix, or a particle?
(GBr_1,1.24j) What indeed is grammar? (GBr_1,1.24k) What is the modification? (GBr_1,1.24l) What is the modifier?
How many measures does it have? How many syllables does it have? How many phonemes does it have?
How many syllables? What is conjunction? What are the places of articulation, the external efforts, and the internal efforts? What do the students recite?
"What is the metre? What is the color? These are the former questions; now follow the latter.
The Mantra, the Kalpa, the Brāhmaṇa, the Ṛg, the Yajus, and the Sāman—
why do the exponents of Brahman place the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning?
What is its deity?
What is its light?
What is its etymology? What is its locus?
"What is the primordial nature? What is the inner self?"— these are the thirty-six questions.
The preceding and following [sections] consist of three groups of twelve;
by means of these, we shall explain the syllable *oṃ*.
Indra asked Prajāpati:
"O Blessed One, having offered praise, I ask you.
"Ask, my son," he replied.
(GBr_1,1.25d) What is this syllable *oṃ*? (GBr_1,1.25e) Whose son is it? (GBr_1,1.25f) And what is its meter?
And what is this that is the phoneme?
And what is this that Brahmā becomes Brahman?
Therefore, indeed, he first took hold of that auspicious syllable *oṃ*.

In the Ṛgveda, the single-syllable *oṃ* is accented with the circumflex (*svarita*) and the acute (*udātta*). In the Yajurveda, the single-syllable *oṃ* is accented with the threefold tone (*traisvarya*) and the acute (*udātta*). In the Sāmaveda, the single-syllable *oṃ* is accented with the long and the protracted (*pluta*) acute (*udātta*).
(GBr_1,1.25m) In the Atharvaveda, the *oṃ* syllable consists of a single short, acute vowel.
(GBr_1,1.25n) It is said that the two syllables *a* and *u* are acute-acute, while the *m* sound constitutes one and a half morae (*ardhacatasro mātrāḥ*) and is a consonant.
(GBr_1,1.25o) That which is the first mora has Brahman as its deity and is red in color.
He who meditates on that [syllable] constantly shall go to the state of Brahman.
That which is the second *mātrā*, having Viṣṇu as its deity and black in color—
he who meditates on that constantly shall go to the state of Viṣṇu.
That third measure which has Īśāna as its deity and is tawny in color—
he who meditates on it constantly shall go to the station of Īśāna.
That fourth-and-a-half measure which has all the deities as its object, having become manifest, moves through the ether, resembling pure crystal in color.
He who meditates upon that constantly shall go to the nameless state. Furthermore, for a Brahmin who does not know the origin of the syllable *oṃ*, there must be a re-initiation (*punarupanayana*).
Therefore, the word of Brāhmaṇa is to be respected: Lātavya is his lineage, he is the son of Brahmā, Gāyatrī is his metre,
and white is his color.
The calf belongs to Puṃs;
Rudra is the deity;
Oṃkāra is [the essence] of the Vedas. // 25 //
(GBr_1,1.26a) What is the verbal root? (GBr_1,1.26b) The root *āp*.
(GBr_1,1.26c) Some [say] even the root *av*.
(GBr_1,1.26d) Due to the commonality of form, the commonality of meaning is more proximate;
(GBr_1,1.26e) therefore, because of the root *āp*, the syllable *oṃ* has the sense that "it attains everything. A word ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*) is meaningful;
[the rule] regarding the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is one of non-observation (*adarśana*).
It receives the designation "particle" (*nipāta*); and grammarians record it as having an acute accent (*udātta*) among the particles; that is the *avyayībhāva*.
It is a term expressive of its own meaning: it "never departs" (*na vyeti kadācana*).
That which does not change across the three genders, all case-endings, and all numbers—that is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
(GBr_1,1.26j) What undergoes modification? (GBr_1,1.26k) That which falls away.
(GBr_1,1.26l) The letters *ā* and *ka* are the modifications resulting from the root *āp*.

At the beginning, the syllable *oṃ* is transformed: the first part is the letter *a*, and the second is the letter *m*. Thus, the syllable *oṃ* is produced as a single phoneme consisting of two letters. // 26 //
(GBr_1,1.27a) "How many measures does it have?
(GBr_1,1.27b) It has three measures of the *ādeśa*; (GBr_1,1.27c) for it floats up at the beginning of the recitation.
The letter *ma* has the fourth [vowel] as its [corresponding].
As for its place of articulation:
both lips are its place of articulation.
The *nāda* and the *anupradāna* have two places of articulation;
the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) consist of a trace of the vowel *a*, while the remaining [vowels] as previously described are guttural;
and the former [vowels] reside in an open articulation (*vivṛtakaraṇa*).
And there exists no conjunction [of sounds] situated in the production of the second [consonants] through contact;
the teachers of old who studied the *saṃsthāna* taught that verbs, prefixes, unaccented vowels, circumflex accents, gender, case-endings, and number are [distinguished by their respective positions].
(GBr_1,1.27m) "They understand through hearing alone; they do not ask for the underlying cause.
(GBr_1,1.27n) Now, among those of the dark fortnight, the seer Pañcālacaṇḍa became an inquirer, saying: "May you sirs state the defects of the *udgītha* individually.
(GBr_1,1.27o) "In that regard, one should observe it according to the divisions of phonemes, syllables, words, and accents."
(GBr_1,1.27p) They praise speech as that which is "frequented by the seers" when it is inflected;
(GBr_1,1.27q) for that reason we say:
(GBr_1,1.27r) "This [speech] will be this [specific thing] among the phonemes."
"We learn it thus from those who know the six auxiliary sciences. "What is its metre? "The Gāyatrī is indeed its metre."
The *gāyatrī* among the meters of the gods is indeed explained as having one syllable and being white in color. There are two groups of twelve [syllables each].
This, indeed, is grammar: the statement of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the rules of phonetics (*śikṣā*), and the statement of the meters (*chandas*).
(GBr_1,1.27y) Now, the two subsequent groups of twelve are explained as the secret portion of the Veda (GBr_1,1.27z):
the Mantra, the Kalpa, the Brāhmaṇa, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_1,1.27aa) This is the Vyāhṛti of the four Vedas in their proper order: *oṃ*, *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*—these are the Vyāhṛtis. // 27 //

(GBr_1,1.28a) It is heard that [the Vedas] were uttered without due consideration (GBr_1,1.28b) at the beginning of the Dvāpara age; at that time, a certain portion of the sages fell under the influence of defects, and the thought occurred to them: "Soma must be drunk by three [at a time]; it is as if [the Veda] has reached its end.
(GBr_1,1.28c) Therefore, the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas] became diminished in their splendor.
(GBr_1,1.28d) Then the great seers lamented: (GBr_1,1.28e) "We have fallen into great sorrow and fear;
(GBr_1,1.28f) yet this has not been declared by all."
"Therefore, we approach the Blessed One alone,
[saying], 'May you be the refuge for us all.
Having said, "So be it," they remained silent.
"Not to those who have not approached [in due form]," he said;
"I shall approach [the teacher]," they thought, and they became humble. Having initiated them, he spoke to them.
"From the very beginning, you must perform my own *vyāhṛti*s.
Thus it is that my [sacrifices] are performed. Soma is not to be drunk except by those who know the *Bhṛgvaṅgiras* hymns;
otherwise, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) come to ruin.
"The sacrificer is defiled by the dust,
and the sacred revelation stands defiled"—
thus, through each successive union, you must govern offspring after offspring.
"In this way, his majesty shall not be overcome.
"So it is, so it is, O Blessed One," they replied, and as they did so, they were refreshed;
thus they became free from sorrow and fear.
Therefore, the exponents of Brahman place the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning. // 28 //
"What is its deity? "The deity of the *ṛc*s is Agni; that indeed is its light."
The Gāyatrī metre;
the Earth is the locus.
"I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the god, the officiating priest of the sacrifice, the invoker, the best bestower of treasures" (Ṛgveda 1.1.1).
Beginning with these words, they study the Ṛgveda;
for the *yajus* formulas, Vāyu is the deity,
and that indeed is the light.
The *traiṣṭubha* is the metre;
the intermediate region is the place.
"For food thee, for strength thee! Ye are the winds; may the god Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent work" [VS 1.1].
Beginning with these words, they study the Yajurveda;
the sun is the deity of the Sāmans,
and that indeed is the light.
The Jāgata metre;
heaven is the place.
"O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacrificial grass. [SV 1.1]
Beginning with these words, they study this Samaveda:
"For the Atharvans, the moon is the deity;
that indeed is the light."
All the meters;
water is the place.
"May the goddesses be for our aid" (Ṛgveda 10.9.4).
Having begun with these and other such words, they study the Atharvaveda:
"From water the multitude of beings, both stationary and moving, arises;
therefore every being consists of water, and everything consists of Bhr̥gu and Aṅgiras."
"Between these three Vedas, the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases are established"—thus [it is said]. "Ap" is the source of the waters, and by means of the syllable *oṃ*.
Vyāsa spoke this previously;
one who has been consecrated by the knowledge of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases may study other Vedas.

"One who has been consecrated elsewhere should not study the Bhṛgvaṅgiras [Atharvaveda], nor the Khila-śruti within the Sāmaveda. This [study] is through celibacy (*brahmacarya*). And he who knows this Atharvāṅgirasa, he knows everything—thus says the Brāhmaṇa. (29)
The syllable *oṃ* is the medicine for the self, pertaining to the inner self, and leading to the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of the self.
Having restrained the self, one should contemplate the reflection on the true nature of reality, which consists merely of [the cessation of] worldly attachment.
The meaning is that, having transcended the Vedas, one attains the fruit of the inner self, which is supreme above all.

"Knowledge accompanied by deliberation consists of these questions and answers"; having thus reflected upon the words according to their true meaning, one who knows the context shall indeed become a powerful master of the subject matter in all discourse—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 30.
(GBr 1.1.31a) Now, it is said that Glāva Maitreya once approached the learned Ekādaśākṣa Maudgalya.

(GBr 1.1.31b) Perceiving that he was living with him as a religious student (*brahmacarya*), he said: "What, indeed, my friend, is this that Maudgalya is studying, for which he lives here as a religious student? (GBr 1.1.31c) For his pupil had heard this from Maudgalya.
(GBr 1,1.31d) He goes to his teacher and reports: (GBr 1,1.31e) "This guest who has arrived today said of you, 'He studies poorly' (GBr 1,1.31f)— is he a wise man, my dear?"
"He recites the three Vedas, saying 'Bho!'—my dear, he has a disciple who is eloquent and desirous of victory; call him for me. He called him.
He said to him, "Sir," he replied. "What, my dear, is your teacher studying? he asked.
"He recites the three Vedas, saying 'Bho! [The son asked:
"But, my dear, since all the Vedas have been learned by us from his mouth, why does the teacher speak in this manner?"
"How indeed could the learned speak thus to those who are themselves learned?
For if I were to ask him this question, he would not wish to explain it;
for he does not study it."
Maudgalya said to his own pupil: "Go, gentle one, approach Glāva Maitreya;
study, sir, the Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī with twenty-four origins and twelve pairs, of which the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases are the eye."
"Tell me that in which all this is supported," [he said].
"If he, my dear, has studied poorly, the teacher will say, 'The student recites the Sāvitrī for one who is not a student of the Veda'; you should say that to him.
You have indeed told Maudgalya that he has studied poorly."
"As for that question which you asked me, you have not answered it; before a year has passed, you shall meet with calamity."
He went to where the other was;
he questioned him, but the latter did not understand.
He said to him: "You spoke of Maudgalya as one who has studied poorly;
he asked you a question which you did not answer. Before a year has passed, you shall meet with calamity."

(GBr_1,1.32g) Maitreya said to his own pupils: "Gentlemen, disperse yourselves according to your purpose, according to your homes, and according to your inclinations. (GBr_1,1.32h) I spoke ill of Maudgalya when he was studying poorly;
(GBr_1,1.32i) regarding the question he asked me, I did not answer it."
"I shall approach him;
I shall bring peace," he thought.
Then Maitreya, with fuel in his hand, approached Maudgalya at dawn, saying, "O sir, here I am, Maitreya."
"For what purpose? [He replied:
"I spoke to you, sir, as one who studies poorly.
Regarding that question which you asked me, I did not explain it."
"I will approach you;
I will bring peace," he said.
He replied, "In this very place, everything has already been approached and everything done; they say that you are traveling in a wretched vehicle."
"Moreover, this auspicious chariot of mine— [Patyal’s translation suggests the emendation *āhū rathaḥ*]—
I give that to you;
go by means of it."
He said, "In this matter, it is exactly as you have said regarding splendor and benevolence;
however, I shall indeed approach you as a pupil.
And so he approached him.
Having approached him, he asked: "What indeed do the sages call the excellent splendor of the god Savitṛ? What do they say of his *dhī*s? Tell me, if you know them.
"Savitṛ impels with those by which he moves," he replied. To him he spoke this: "The Vedas, the meters, are the excellent splendor of Savitṛ."
"The wise call the splendor (*bhargas*) of the god food; his thoughts are his actions.
"That I shall declare to you: 'May Savitṛ impel [those thoughts] by which he goes.
Having approached him with reverence, he asked: "Sir, please teach me: who is Savitṛ? What is Sāvitrī?"
The mind alone is Savitṛ; speech is Sāvitrī.
For wherever there is mind, there is speech; and wherever there is speech, there is mind.
These two are the two wombs; they form a single couple.
Agni himself is Savitṛ; the earth is Sāvitrī.
For wherever there is Agni, there is the earth; and wherever there is the earth, there is Agni.
These two are two wombs, a single couple.
Vāyu indeed is Savitṛ, and the intermediate space is Sāvitrī;
for wherever there is Vāyu, there is the intermediate space, and wherever there is the intermediate space, there is Vāyu.
These two are two wombs, a single couple.
The sun is indeed Savitṛ; the sky is Sāvitrī.
For wherever the sun is, there is the sky; and wherever the sky is, there is the sun.
These two are the two wombs; they form a single couple.
The moon itself is the Savitṛ; the lunar mansions are the Sāvitrī.
For wherever the moon is, there are the lunar mansions; and wherever the lunar mansions are, there is the moon.
These two are the two wombs, one couple.
Day indeed is Savitṛ, and night is Sāvitrī; for where there is day, there is night, and where there is night, there is day.
These two wombs are one couple.
The sun is indeed heat, and Sāvitrī is cold; for where there is heat, there is also cold, and where there is cold, there is also heat—
these two are the two wombs, a single couple.
The cloud is indeed Savitṛ, and the rain is Sāvitrī.
For where there is a cloud, there is rain; and where there is rain, there is a cloud. These two are two wombs, a single couple.
The lightning is indeed Savitṛ, and the thunder is Sāvitrī; for wherever there is lightning, there is thunder, and wherever there is thunder, there is lightning—
these two are two wombs, a single couple.
Prāṇa indeed is Savitṛ; food is Sāvitrī.
For wherever there is prāṇa, there is food; and wherever there is food, there is prāṇa. These two are the two wombs; they are one couple.
The Vedas themselves are Savitṛ; the meters are the Sāvitrī.
For where there are the Vedas, there are the meters; and where there are the meters, there are the Vedas.
These two are two wombs, a single couple.
The sacrifice is one [form] of Savitṛ, and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are the other form of Savitṛ.
For where there is the sacrifice, there are the sacrificial fees; and where there are the sacrificial fees, there is the sacrifice.
These two are two wombs, a single couple.

"Indeed, when they saw that Opākāri knew this, they said to him, 'Brahmacārī, you have completed your stay. Then those very people who had been sitting there became as if piled up like a funeral mound. Then he rose and went forth into homelessness. This indeed I know: that a Brahmacārī born from these wombs or from these pairs of parents shall not depart before his full span of life.
Brahman looked toward this world as its glory, its foundation, and its abode.
It performed austerity; if it were sustained in that vow, it became established in truth.
Having created the Brāhmaṇa by means of the Sāvitrī, Savitṛ assigned that Sāvitrī to him.
"That excellent glory of Savitṛ" is the first quarter of the Sāvitrī; Pṛthivī supplied the *ṛc*.
Through the *ṛc* one attains fire;
through fire, prosperity;
through prosperity, a wife.
Through a woman, a couple;
through a couple, offspring;
through offspring, ritual action.
Through action comes austerity;
through austerity, truth;
through truth, the Brahman.
(GBr_1,1.34p) A Brāhmaṇa [is consecrated] by the *brahman*;
(GBr_1,1.34q) the vow by the Brāhmaṇa;
(GBr_1,1.34r) indeed, by the vow the Brāhmaṇa becomes sharpened.

He becomes non-empty; he becomes uninterrupted. His thread is uninterrupted, his life becomes uninterrupted—he who knows thus, and he who, knowing thus, explains this first quarter of the Sāvitrī in this manner. // 34 //
"Of the god we meditate upon the splendor"—this is the second foot of the Sāvitrī.
With the intermediate space he joined the Yajus;
with the Yajus, Vāyu.
By means of the wind, the cloud;
by means of the cloud, the rain;
by means of the rain, the herbs and trees.
Through herbs and trees, [one attains] animals;
through animals, ritual action;
through ritual action, austerity.
Through austerity, truth;
through truth, the sacred word (*brahman*); through the sacred word, the Brahmin.

(GBr_1,1.35m) The vow of a Brāhmaṇa—(GBr_1,1.35n) by means of the vow, indeed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes sharpened; (GBr_1,1.35o) he becomes not empty, he becomes uninterrupted; his lineage remains uninterrupted and his life becomes uninterrupted for him who knows thus, and for him who, knowing thus, performs this [rite] with the Sāvitrī.
He explains the second quarter-verse. // 35 //
"May he who shall impel our thoughts"— this is the third foot of the Sāvitrī.
He established the Sāman as the day,
and from the Sāman, the Āditya.
By means of the sun, [one pervades] the rays;
by means of the rays, rain;
by means of rain, the herbs and trees.
(GBr_1,1.36g) By means of herbs and trees, [one sustains] animals;
(GBr_1,1.36h) by means of animals, ritual action;
(GBr_1,1.36i) by means of ritual action, austerity.
Through austerity, truth;
through truth, the Veda; through the Veda, the Brahmin.
(GBr_1,1.36m) The vow of the Brāhmaṇa.

(GBr_1,1.36n) By the vow, indeed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes sharpened; he becomes not empty, he becomes uninterrupted. (GBr_1,1.36o) His lineage remains uninterrupted and his life remains uninterrupted for him who knows this, and for him who, knowing thus, recites this [Sāvitrī] in this manner.
He explains the third quarter-verse. // 36 //
By such a Brahmin who knows this, the Brahman is indeed pervaded, swallowed, and grasped;
by the Brahman, space is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped;
by space, wind is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped.
Light, being overtaken, swallowed, and seized by wind; water, being overtaken, swallowed, and seized by light; earth, being overtaken, swallowed, and seized by water.

Food is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped by the earth; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped by food; the mind (*manas*) is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped by the vital breath.
Speech is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped by the mind;
the Vedas are pervaded, swallowed, and grasped by speech;
the sacrifice is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped by the Vedas.
Indeed, these twelve great elements are established in one who knows thus;
of them, the sacrifice is the most excellent.
Those who do not know it as it truly is think, "We know this very one," thinking, "We know him.
This sacrifice is established in the Vedas;
the Vedas are established in speech.
Speech is established in the mind;
the mind is established in breath;
breath is established in food.
Food is established on the earth;
the earth is established on the waters;
the waters are established on light.
Light is established in air;
air is established in space;
space is established in Brahman.
The Brahman is established in the Brāhmaṇa who knows the Brahman.
Indeed, he who knows this is a knower of the Brahman;
he obtains holy fame and fragrant scents.

"He who knows this, and he who, knowing thus, reveres this *Sāvitrī*—the mother of the Vedas, the perfection, the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*)—attains glory that is infinite and has his evil struck away. This is the Brāhmaṇa.
"The waters, generating the embryo... (PS 4.1.8).
The Person is the embryo of the waters;
he is the sacrifice. When the sacrifice is being led forward by the waters, it is extended toward the east.
Therefore, he first causes water for sipping to be brought.
When he sips, he sips three times;
he cleans his lips twice.

Having descended with life and cast off evil, having approached, having lifted [the vessel] with a *yajus*-formula, having applied the mantras, and having settled, he joins the branches facing eastward;

then, into his hand that is without the thumb, he pours water, saying: "Thou art immortality; thou art the under-spreading for immortality; I spread thee for the sake of immortality. Thus [he pours] water into the hand.
With the hymn beginning with "Bring them" (*ānīya*; *jīvā stha*), he sips water three times. When he sips first, he thereby causes the seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) to swell within him.
For those external constituents that are outside the body—namely, fire, wind, the sun, the moon, water, cattle, and other creatures—he thereby causes them to swell within this [body].
Water is immortality;
when he sips a second time, he thereby causes the seven vital airs (*apāna*) to swell within this [body].

For those external constituents of the body are as follows: the full moon, the eighth-day rite, the new moon, faith, consecration, sacrifice, and sacrificial gifts; by this [water], he causes them to swell within him.
Water is immortality. When he sips for the third time, he thereby causes the seven *vyāna* breaths to swell within him.

For those external constituents of the body are as follows: earth, atmosphere, heaven, the stars, the seasons, the seasonal periods, and the years; he causes them to swell by means of this [breath] within him.
Water is immortality.
The Puruṣa is Brahman.
Now, there is an *aprī* verse: "Therefore, indeed, the wise man [knows] this lotus as the Puruṣa. [Note:
The edition reads *athāprīṃgnigamo*, but see Patyal, p. 44.]
"This is the breath; he lies in the city, he lies in the body. Because he lies in the city (*puri*), they call this breath "the Person" (*puruṣa*) by an indirect name.
For the gods, as it were, love the indirect and dislike the direct.
When he sips water for the first time, he thereby secures for himself the oblations offered before the main sacrifice;
when he sips for the second time, he thereby secures for himself the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*);
when he sips for the third time, he thereby secures for himself the oblations offered at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
When he sprinkles twice, that constitutes the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

When he causes all the apertures and the entire body to swell, and whatever other ritual action involving mantras belonging to the giver might fail at the sacrifice, he secures all of that for himself by means of this.
When he employs the mantras preceded by *oṃ*, these are the *sarvamedha* sacrifices; these indeed are his.

In all worlds, among all gods, in all Vedas, among all beings, and among all creatures, there is freedom of movement and liberation from desire for him who knows this; and he does not perish even in the midst [of existence]. This has also been stated in a *ṛc*: "The waters are the form of Bhr̥gu and Aṅgiras; the waters consist of Bhr̥gu and Aṅgiras; every being consists of water; everything consists of Bhr̥gu and Aṅgiras. Within these three...
The Vedas followed the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases.
"The flower of the waters is form; space is the supreme purifier.
Having sipped water and sprinkled himself, he recites the mantra over himself: "O Indra, live!
Thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 39.
Thus ends the first chapter in the first part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_1,2.1a) "Oṃ! The Vedic student (*brahmacārī*) moves between both worlds" (ŚS 11.3.1a, PS 16.153.1a)—with these words he addresses the teacher.
(GBr_1,2.1b) "In him the gods become of one mind" (ŚS 11.3.1, PS 16.153.1b).
Thus he speaks of Vāyu;
"He goes immediately from the eastern ocean to the northern one" (ŚS 11.3.6,
PS 16.153.6), thus he speaks of Āditya.
(GBr_1,2.1d) Initiated, with long hair and beard—(GBr_1,2.1e) this one who is initiated, this one with long hair and beard, standing in the place of the teacher, is praised as "the teacher";
standing in the place of lightning, he is praised as "Vāyu"; standing in the place of heaven, he is praised as "Āditya."
This is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"The student, being warm...
Thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 1.

(GBr_1,2.2a) Indeed, when a Brāhmaṇa is born, he is born with seven faculties: spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), fame, sleep, anger, boastfulness, beauty, and merit as the seventh—[namely] odor. (GBr_1,2.2b) These very faculties of his depart when he enters upon the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*).
His sacrificial splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) goes to the deer;
his fame (*yaśas*) goes to the teacher (*ācārya*);
his sleep goes to the python.
(GBr_1,2.2f) Wrath [is] a boar;
(GBr_1,2.2g) praise [is] water;
(GBr_1,2.2h) a young girl [is] beauty.
(GBr_1,2.2i) A holy fragrance [belongs to] the plants and trees.

(GBr_1,2.2j) When he wears the skins of wild animals, by that he secures for himself that spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) which belongs to him among wild animals. (GBr_1,2.2k) Having bathed, he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
(GBr_1,2.2l) Whatever work he performs day after day for his teacher, by that he secures that glory which belongs to him [the teacher].
(GBr_1,2.2m) Having bathed, he indeed becomes glorious.
(GBr_1,2.2n) When, desiring to sleep, he lets sleep come upon himself, by that he secures that dream which belongs to him [the teacher] in the serpent.

When he has bathed and is sleeping, they say to him, "Sleep! Do not wake him! Because, when angry, he does not strike anyone with his voice, thinking himself as it were more wretched than man, by that he retains the anger which belongs to him in the wild boar. Indeed, when he has bathed, the angers enter into him who is more praiseworthy.

(GBr_1,2.2r) Now, one who prides himself on [his merit] should not bathe with water. (GBr_1,2.2s) By that means he secures for himself that praise which belongs to him in the waters. (GBr_1,2.2t) Having bathed, he is praised as more praiseworthy than others.
(GBr 1.2.2u) Now, this is the form of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*): that he should not look at a maiden when she is naked;
[if he does], he should have her face covered with a cloth or something similar.
By that, he obtains that form which belongs to him in his maidenhood.
Indeed, they look upon him when he has bathed as if upon a young girl.
Now, this is the holy fragrance of the student: the holy fragrance of the herbs and trees; having cut off [a portion] of that holy fragrance, he should not smell it.
Through that, he obtains the holy fragrance which belongs to him among the lords of plants and forests;
having bathed, he becomes one who possesses a holy fragrance. 2.
(GBr 1.2.3a) Now, this student, when approaching, approaches in four ways: with one foot he approaches the fire, with one foot the teacher, with one foot the village, and with one foot death.

(GBr 1.2.3b) In that he fetches fuel day by day and tends the fire morning and evening, by that he secures for himself that portion which belongs to him in the fire. (GBr 1.2.3c) In that he performs service for the teacher day by day, by that he secures for himself that portion which belongs to him in the teacher.

(GBr_1,2.3d) In that he enters the village day after day seeking only alms and avoids sexual intercourse, by that he secures for himself that foot of his which is in the village. (GBr_1,2.3e) In that, even when angry, he does not harm anyone with his speech, thinking himself as it were more wretched than man to man, by that he secures for himself that foot of his which is in death. (GBr_1,2.4a) For indeed, these five fires are established in the religious student.
There are two [fingers] on each hand, in the mouth, in the heart, and the generative organ is the fifth.
When he does not touch a woman with his right hand, by that he wins the world of those who perform daily sacrifices;
when he does so with his left, by that [he wins the world] of those who have gone forth as wanderers.
(GBr_1,2.4e) That which [is his] mouth, by that [he partakes] of the Agnipraskandins; (GBr_1,2.4f) that which is his heart, by that [he partakes] of the Śūras;
(GBr_1,2.4g) that which is his organ of generation, by that [he partakes] of the Gṛhamedhins.
If he carries off a woman with those [stealing implements], he remains as if without a fire.
Whatever he performs daily in the teacher's family, having performed that, he should say: "O Dharma, protect me; may I be protected.
For Dharma, being protected, protects him.
Day after day, his offspring indeed become more and more prosperous;
he establishes himself as a supporting verse (*dhāyyā*),
and he places his ancestors in the heavenly world.
(GBr_1,2.4n) One should not wear woven cloth.
(GBr_1,2.4o) He who wears woven cloth increases the *kṣatra*, not the *brahman*. (GBr_1,2.4p) Therefore, one should not wear woven cloth, [thinking]: "May the *brahman* increase, not the *kṣatra*."
(GBr_1,2.4q) One should not sit above [the fire].
For when one sits above, one makes one's own vital breath inferior. (GBr_1,2.4r) When the wind blows, (GBr_1,2.4s) one should sit below, lie down below, stand below, and walk below.
Thus indeed did the ancient Brahmins practice the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*).
When their son or brother was suffering, they would say to him, "Bring him here; let us initiate him.
Until the time of gathering the sacrificial fuel, he should eat food while intending to go to the heavenly world.
(GBr_1,2.4w) Then he says: "They say the rear; one should bathe him until the firewood is brought.
(GBr_1,2.4x) For these are not [ordinary] vows.
(GBr_1,2.4y) If the teacher should address him while he is lying down, he should rise and respond.

"If he [the teacher] should rise after him while he is lying down; or if he should approach him while he is standing; or if he should run after him while he is running away—it was thus indeed that the ancient Brahmins practiced the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*).
And this holy fame of theirs goes forth: 'Truly, here comes that one today. 4.
Janamejaya Pārīkṣita, while out on a hunt, was about to shoot two swans as they approached him; they said to him, "We have come to Janamejaya Pārīkṣita. He then spoke.
"Salutations to you both, O Blessed Ones! Who indeed are the Blessed Ones?
they replied, "The Dakṣiṇāgni and the Āhavanīya. He said, "Salutations to you both, O Blessed Ones; let that be explained."
"Here is a place of delight," they say; indeed, even the gods do not find delight here, for it is not that the gods do not find delight.
Moreover, from one place of delight, the gods proceed to another place of delight.
He said, "Homage to you both, venerable sirs; what is merit? "Brahmacarya," they replied.
"What is worldly? he asked.
“It is indeed celibacy,” [he said].
“Who knows that? Dantāvala Dhaumra replied.

(GBr_1,2.5p) Then, after some time had passed, Dhaumra Dantāvala approached Janamejaya Pārīkṣita. (GBr_1,2.5q) Rising for him, he himself offered a seat. (GBr_1,2.5r) Having greeted him, Janamejaya asked: "Sir, please teach me; what is meritorious?"
"Regarding 'celibacy' (brahmacarya): is it worldly? It is indeed celibacy itself."
To him he declared this: the student life for all the Vedas lasts forty-eight years.

Having divided that among the Vedas in four parts, one should practice the student life for twelve years; twelve years is the minimum, though one may even perform it for longer according to one's ability while still living at home after the ceremonial bath.
To him he gave a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh.
Some say that even one who is ill-reputed may be called a *brahmacārī* if he is a teacher; the ether is the [corresponding] deity with respect to the divine.
Now, with respect to the self, a *brahmacārī* is a Brāhmaṇa who is observant of his vows and observant of his conduct. 5.
"Brahman indeed delivered the creatures to Death;
he alone did not deliver the religious student (*brahmacārin*).
He said, 'I shall eat him.'"
"Why? [He replied:
"So that he may secure for himself that night which he might otherwise spend without having brought firewood;
therefore, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), having brought firewood day after day, should tend the fire in the evening and in the morning."
(GBr_1,2.6g) One should not place it on top; rather, one should establish it. (GBr_1,2.6h) If one were to place it on top, Parjanya would rain like a cloud on that day.
(GBr_1,2.6i) Those gods said, "This is indeed a Brāhmaṇa who will practice the life of a religious student."
"Tell him, 'Beg for alms! "Tell the householder, 'The householder's wife is one who frequents many [houses]! "What would she withhold from him if she does not give?
"He would appropriate her merit from sacrifices and charitable works, as well as her wealth."
Therefore, a housewife should give alms every day to a student of sacred knowledge, thinking, "Lest he should appropriate my merit from sacrifices and charitable works, as well as my wealth.
One should not let the seventh night pass; for by letting the seventh night pass, one ceases to be a student of sacred knowledge.
A student who has failed to attend to the sacred fuel and to beg for alms for seven nights must undergo initiation again.
(GBr_1,2.7a) He should not sleep on high beds, nor sing, nor dance, nor run, nor spit.
(GBr_1,2.7b) When he sleeps on high beds, garments are frequently ruined;
(GBr_1,2.7c) when he sings, frequent cries are set in motion.
When he dances repeatedly, they carry forth the deceased;
when he runs repeatedly, the offspring settle down;
when he spits, he spits upon his own center.
(GBr_1,2.7g) If he should spit, [one should recite: "From heaven now me... (ŚS 6.124.1, VaitS 12.7);
"Whatever here also of honey I... (PS 20.38.6, VaitS 12.8); "Whatever here also of sap of me... (PS 20.27.8).
"Whatever of this honey I have spat out here in forgetfulness, may Agni and Savitṛ place that back within my belly"— with these words he consecrates himself.

"Whatever of my essence has here fallen away and been forgotten, that we summon back here; may that swell within me again" (PS 20.27.8)—having thus [recited], one should not stand upon a cremation ground.
If he should nevertheless stand upon it, he should take water in his hand.
Having consecrated it with the mantra "If this [is] for the sake of desire for immortality" (PS 20.54.9), while reciting it and sprinkling [the water],
one should walk around and proceed above the place of the covenant.
(GBr_1,2.7l) "Whatever sin we have incurred by approaching that which is not the proper season, may it fall away like a blind man or a cripple; may the evil from which it comes not follow us.
(GBr_1,2.7m) Now, this student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) is indeed consecrated (*pariṣūta*) by the gods.
This has also been stated in a Ṛgvedic verse: "This, protected by the gods, moves unclimbed and radiant; in it are all cattle, in it are all sacrifices, in it is food together with the deities.
Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Generating the out-breath and the in-breath," so said the son of the great seer Vasiṣṭha at the mouth of the Śaṅkha cave: "Cold and heat shall manifest here as two springs.
And so it continues to this day.
Now, in the middle of Vipāś lies the first hermitage, named Vasiṣṭhaśilā.
The second was Kṛṣṇaśilā; upon it Vasiṣṭha performed penance.
Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni performed penance on the Jamadagni [rock].
Gautama and Bharadvāja performed austerities at Siṃhaprabhava; Guṅgu performed austerities at Guṅguvāsa; and the seer performed austerities at Ṛṣidroṇa.
Agastya performs penance at Agastyatīrtha; Atri performs penance in Divya; Svayambhū Kaśyapa performed penance on Kaśyapatuṅga.

(GBr_1,2.8m) Wolves, bears, hyenas, (GBr_1,2.8n) dogs, boars, *cilvaṭis*, and *babrukas*, as well as serpents and fanged creatures, become subdued by the sight of Kaśyapa Tuṅga at Saraṇavāṭa; there, perfection is attained.
(GBr_1,2.8o) For a thousand divine years, he remains standing on one foot in the forest of the seers as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
(GBr_1,2.8p) For a second thousand years, he held a stream of nectar upon his head.
(GBr_1,2.8q) For forty-eight thousand years of Brahma, Śiva performed austerities on the surface of the waters.
From that austerity thus performed, he performed yet further austerity.
Regarding this, these verses also speak; "Generating out-breath and in-breath," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One-footed, two-footed" (GBr 1.2.9b): Vāyu is one-footed; space is his foot.
The moon is two-footed; its two feet are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight. The sun is three-footed.
(GBr_1,2.9g) These worlds are his feet.
(GBr_1,2.9h) Fire has six feet.
(GBr_1,2.9i) Of that [fire], the earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the waters, the plants and trees, and these beings are the feet.
The Vedas are the goal of all these; the Self is established as the four branches of Brahman.
Furthermore, they say there are six: form and space. Form is represented by the *ṛc*.
The path of the Yajus; the splendor consisting of the Sāman; the creative power of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
"This very Brahman is the sacrifice, four-footed and twice established" (GBr 1,2.9q); of that, the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases are the establishment (saṃstha), and thus they say it is "once established."
In that he performs [the ritual] with the circles of the Hotṛ-verses, he thereby nourishes the earth;
for Agni moves within this [earth].
This is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Fire-clad, earth-kneed" (ŚS 12.1.21;
PS 17.3.2)—when the Adhvaryu performs with this *yajus*, he thereby causes the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) to swell;
in it, Vāyu does not settle, nor does any day whatsoever.
This has also been stated in a Rigvedic verse:
"Moving along paths in the intermediate space, it does not settle down on any day whatsoever.
The first-born source of the waters, the womb of cosmic order (*ṛta*), where indeed was it born, and from whence did it come into being? (RV 1.164.4).
(GBr_1,2.9y) That which the Udgātṛ performs with the Sāman, by that he causes the sky to swell;
(GBr_1,2.9z) for therein the bright Āditya moves.
(GBr_1,2.9aa) And this has also been stated in a Ṛg-verse:
"High-flying, ruddy, fair-winged" (ŚS 13.2.36;
PS 18.24.3). When he performs the *brahmārca* with the *kāṇḍas*, he thereby causes the waters to swell, for the moon moves within the waters.
This is also expressed by a Ṛgvedic verse: "The moon is within the waters. From those [waters] come the stalks of herbs and trees;
from them, the sacrifice proceeds by means of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, sprouts, juices, and fragrances.
Through the waters, the ears [of grain] are brought forth.
(GBr_1,2.9gg) Soma is pressed with water.
(GBr_1,2.9hh) Therefore, when he addresses the ears of the Brahmins to the ritual acts, he thereby gives his permission; for this is his portion.
(GBr_1,2.9ii) For this is his portion.

Just as one who is about to eat should first rinse with water and rinse again at the end, so too the sacrifice proceeds by means of water and is concluded in water; therefore, the Brahman priest causes the sacrifice to proceed through the *purastāddhoma* and *saṃsthitahoma* offerings.
For by means of the introductory oblations and the concluding oblations, he encloses the sacrifice on both sides.
For it was by drawing up the Vedas from between [the worlds] that the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases considered themselves drinkers of Soma;
for this Veda is of the nature of Soma.
This is also stated in a Rigvedic verse: "He who has drunk [the Soma] thinks he has drunk Soma.

Just as one quiets the rain that rises over this earth, smokes with light, and falls, even so does the Brahman priest quiet whatever is damaged in the sacrifice by means of the *bhṛgvaṅgiras* formulas and the *vyāhṛti*s.
Agni pacifies the Āditya;
these are the Aṅgirases;
they pervade all this.
"Vāyu, the waters, and the moon—these are the Bhrigus. They cause all this to swell; they become a single resting place," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 9.
There was once a wise man named Vicārī Kābandhi, the son of Kabandha Ātharvaṇa; he was a thinker, an investigator, and well-versed in the sacred scriptures.
Out of excessive pride in his own learning, he did not seek human wealth.
His mother said to him:

(GBr_1,2.10d) "It was they who spoke thus regarding food; it is they who now eat food among these Kurus, Pañcālas, Aṅgas, Magadhas, Kāśis, Kauśalas, Śālvas, Matsyas, Vaśas, Uśīnaras, and the Northern peoples.
(GBr_1,2.10e) But as for us, because of our excessive pride toward you, we have become unfit to be eaten.
(GBr_1,2.10f) My child, seek out a vehicle."
(GBr_1,2.10g) It came to King Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, the sovereign of the whole earth, as the Soma had been pressed.
(GBr_1,2.10h) Having entered the sacrificial hall, he addressed the officiating priests and the sacrificer:
(GBr_1,2.10i) "Those rivers which flow toward the east, those toward the south, those toward the west, and those toward the north—they are all called by distinct names."
(GBr_1,2.10j) As they reach the ocean, their individual names are cut away, and one speaks of them simply as "the ocean.

(GBr_1,2.10k) In the same way, all these Vedas are produced— along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*), the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), the explanatory treatises (*brāhmaṇa*), the esoteric teachings (*upaniṣad*), the histories (*itihāsa*), the etymological explanations (*anvākhyāna*), the ancient lore (*purāṇa*), the accents (*svara*), the phonetic refinements (*saṃskāra*), the glossaries (*nirukta*), the rules of instruction (*anuśāsana*), the methods of purification (*anumārjana*), and the dialogues of the sages (*vākovākya*).
As they approach that sacrifice, their specific name is lost; they simply call it "the sacrifice. // 10 //
(GBr_1,2.11a) Indeed, that sacrificial ground which is not sloping toward the east, nor sloping toward the north, which is artificial, or which is level and uneven, is cut off from the earth.

(GBr_1,2.11b) But this indeed is the sacrificial ground: that which is level, well-rooted, unburnt, firmly established, sloping toward the northeast, even, and as if strewn with grass—where one may know the Brahminhood of a Brahmin.
"Brahmā performs the office of the Brahmā," they said; "we do not know that Vedic metre by which we may go further.

He then questioned them: "Knowing what does the Hotṛ perform the duties of the Hotṛ? Knowing what does the Adhvaryu perform the duties of the Adhvaryu? Knowing what does the Udgātṛ perform the duties of the Udgātṛ? "What... [he asked].

"The learned Brahman performs the office of the Brahman," so says the Vedic verse; "but we do not find that by which we may proceed further," thus we say. Speech itself performs the office of the Hotṛ priest.
For the hymns and the *vaṣaṭ*-calls are accomplished through speech;
therefore we say: "Speech indeed is the Hotṛ, speech is the Brahman, speech is the deity.
Through the out-breath and the in-breath alone does the Adhvaryu perform the duties of the Adhvaryu.

(GBr 1,2.11j) Beings are led forth by the vital breath; the *praṇītā* waters are led forth by the vital breath. We say that the out-breath and the in-breath are the *adhvaryu*, the out-breath and the in-breath are the *brahman*, and the out-breath and the in-breath are the deity.
(GBr 1,2.11l) By means of the eye alone, the *udgātṛ* performs the office of the *udgātṛ*.
"For by the eye these beings see;
therefore, the eye alone is the Udgātṛ, the eye is the Brahman, and the eye is the god.
Thus, it is by the mind alone that the Brahman priest performs the office of the Brahman.
(GBr_1,2.11p) For by means of the mind one [reaches] the intermediate directions, the upward direction, and whatever else there is; that which one performs with the mind alone is Brahman.
(GBr_1,2.11q) We declare to you: the mind alone is Brahman; the mind is Brahman; the mind is the deity. // 11 //
"Just as, for instance, if here the sacrificer and the officiating priests were to call heaven 'earth,' or earth 'heaven,' no one else would approve of that;
even so he does not approve of this when one should say this.
But then, how is it?"

(GBr_1.2.12c) One should address the *hotṛ* as "Hotṛ," speech as "Speech," and the Brahman as "Brahman"; one should address the deity as "Deity" and the *adhvaryu* as "Adhvaryu," the out-breath and in-breath as "Out-breath and In-breath," and the Brahman as "Brahman";
one should address the deity as "Deity" and the *udgātṛ* as "Udgātṛ," the eye as "Eye," and the Brahman as "Brahman"; one should address the deity as "Deity."
One should say "Brahman" regarding the Brahmin; "Mind" regarding the mind; "Brahman" regarding the Brahman; and "God" regarding the god. 12.
(GBr_1,2.13a) "Indeed, these beings have various doctrines.

Those who perform sacrifices for one who drinks soma, those who perform sacrifices for one who drinks liquor, and those who perform sacrifices for a Brahmin who has discontinued the soma sacrifice—they should approach him in the morning with fuel in their hands, saying: 'We come to you, sir!
"For what purpose? [he asks].
"Those very questions which your honor asked us yesterday, may your honor explain those to us.
"So be it," he replied, and he explained those questions to them.
That by which one lays hold of both what exists here and what does not exist—that is Brahman.
He who knows that is a Brāhmaṇa; it is called "Brāhmaṇa" because he, having studied, declares [it] after his study. Thus [ends the section]. 13.
(GBr 1.2.14a) Now, therefore, concerning the places of sacrifice to the gods:
(14b) the self is a place of sacrifice to the gods;
(14c) faith is a place of sacrifice to the gods.
(GBr_1,2.14d) The officiating priests are the place of sacrifice for the gods; (GBr_1,2.14e) the earth is the place of sacrifice for the gods;
(GBr_1,2.14f) indeed, this very body is the place of sacrifice for the gods, which one inhabits whether one is moving about or not moving about.
This is the sacrifice;
this is the sacrificer; these are those who sacrifice.
(GBr_1,2.14j) This is the place for sacrifice to the gods; (GBr_1,2.14k) moreover, this is the place for sacrifice to the gods characterized by faith;
(GBr_1,2.14l) whenever one might establish it, that is the time.
(GBr_1,2.14m) Faith alone, however, should not pass him by;
(GBr_1,2.14n) that is the place of sacrifice for the gods. (GBr_1,2.14o) Now, this is the place of sacrifice for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
(GBr_1,2.14p) Wherever a learned Brāhmaṇa performs [the rite] with a mantra, that is a place for sacrifice to the gods. (GBr_1,2.14q) Now, this is a sacrificial ground belonging to the earth:
(GBr_1,2.14r) where waters stand still, where they flow, where they carry forth and carry upward—that is a place for sacrifice to the gods.

(GBr_1,2.14s) That which is level, with its roots [removed], not burnt, well-established, sloping toward the northeast, as if evenly strewn, and on whose front side there is a pit, a wave, a tree, a mountain, a river, or a path—
(GBr_1,2.14t) one must not leave even a space the size of the sacrificial ground remaining on the front side.
"They should not sit around the fire from the north," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 14.
Aditi, desiring offspring, cooked rice;
she ate the remnant,
and she conceived a fetus.
(GBr_1,2.15d) From that the Ādityas were born.
(GBr_1,2.15e) This rice-porridge which is being cooked is indeed made as a support, as a foothold.
(GBr_1,2.15f) The fuel-sticks are a span long.
For this much is the self, commensurate with Prajāpati. Indeed, that sacrificial body of Agni which was in the *aśvattha* tree, with that he united;
this ghee is his oily body.

In that he anoints the fuel-sticks with ghee, he thereby endows him with those two very bodies. In that he places [the sticks] after wiping them, for by a forward leap is vigor produced; in that he places them after wiping, it is indeed by a forward leap.
The year, indeed, is procreation;
Agni is procreation;
this is procreation.

(GBr_1,2.15p) When, for a year, he places a fuel-stick on the fire with a *ṛc*, the progenitor thereby causes him to be born from procreation itself. (GBr_1,2.15q) Man indeed does not possess the seasons; (GBr_1,2.15r) for he does not know which season he is born under.
That which is the constellation, that he attains; this rice-porridge which is being cooked is made into a womb; when fuel-sticks are placed [upon the fire], semen is thereby deposited.
In a year, indeed, seed that has been deposited comes to birth.
He who establishes the sacred fires when a year has elapsed establishes them as something already born. Prior to the completion of the year, the fires should be established during twelve nights.

For they are the image of the year—whether in three [days], or in two, or on the day before; these indeed are the days for one who is about to establish the sacred fires. The Ādityas, indeed, went from here to yonder world as the last.
(GBr_1,2.15bb) They are the guardians of the path; they drive away the one who desires to sacrifice. (GBr_1,2.15cc) Or rather, the Ādityas are the sharers of the remnants—[that which is left over].
(GBr_1,2.15dd) [That which is the remnant.]
(GBr_1,2.15ee) That he anoints the fuel-sticks with the remains of the food—having spoken to them alone, having spoken to them alone, he goes to the heavenly world. // 15 //
Prajāpati Atharvan, the god, having performed austerity, fashioned this *brahmaudana* to be consumed by four, consisting of four worlds, four gods, four Vedas, and four *hotṛ*-priests.
For these worlds are four: earth, the intermediate space, heaven, and the waters.
And these gods are four: Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, and Candramas.

(GBr 1.2.16d) "These Vedas are fourfold: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Brahmaveda. (GBr 1.2.16e) "Or these priestly offices are fourfold: the office of the Hotṛ, the office of the Adhvaryu, the office of the Udgātṛ, and the office of the Brahman.
(GBr 1.2.16f) And this has also been stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, seven are his hands;
bound in three ways, the bull bellows; the great god has entered mortals" (PS 8.13.3).
Thus it is said in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa (GBr 1.2.16g): "The four horns"—these are said to be the Vedas.
(GBr 1,2.16h) "Three are his feet" refers to the *savana*s (pressings).
(GBr 1,2.16i) "Two are his heads" refers to the *brahmaudana* and the *pravargya*.
(GBr 1,2.16j) "Seven are his hands" refers to the *chandas* (metres).

(GBr_1,2.16k) "Bound in three ways" is the mantra; the ritual manual (*kalpa*) and the explanatory text (*brāhmaṇa*). (GBr_1,2.16l) "The bull bellows"—this one, indeed, is the bull; he bellows that when he recites the liturgical hymns (*śastra*) at the sacrifices with *ṛc*s, *yajus* formulas, *sāman* chants, and sacred utterances (*brahman*).
(GBr_1,2.16m) "The great god has entered into mortals"—the sacrifice, indeed, is this great god.

(GBr_1,2.16n) "He has entered into mortals"—he who knows this refers to the *prāṇas*. (GBr_1,2.16o) "One should know the seven *pravatas*"; he says this of the *prāṇas*. (GBr_1,2.16p) "One should know the seven *parāvatas*"; he says this of the *apānas*.

“He who would know the head of the sacrifice”—this, indeed, is the head of the sacrifice, namely the *brahmaudana* accompanied by mantras. For if one were to approach that *brahmaudana* devoid of mantras, he would have approached the sacrifice headless.
Therefore, one should approach only the *brahmaudana* accompanied by mantras, not one devoid of mantras; so says the Brāhmaṇa. 16.
[Editorial Note: Brāhmaṇa] (GBr 1.2.17a) "By what means did Ātreya come to be?
(GBr 1.2.17b) "For darkness had seized the sun."
Atri dispelled that;
Atri perceived that;
and this very thing has been stated in a Ṛgvedic verse.
"From whom Atri drew up heaven" (ŚS 13.2.4c, PS 18.20.8c),
and "In heaven Atri established you for Sūrya to make a month" (ŚS 13.2.12ab,
PS 18.21.6ab)— having said this, he said to him, "Choose a boon."
He said, "May my offspring be worthy of receiving sacrificial gifts.
Therefore, it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "For this reason, the first sacrificial gift at a sacrifice is given to one of the Ātreya lineage. 17.
Prajāpati said to the Vedas, "Establish the sacred fires. Speech replied to them, "The horse is indeed the foremost among the ritual requisites.
They brought it forth from the formidable, cruel lake of water.
Speech said to them, "The horse should be appeased. They replied, "So be it.
Then the Ṛgveda approached him and said, "I shall appease the horse."
For him as he crawled forward, he created a great terror; he took refuge in this eastern direction,
and he said, "Truly, this horse is not yet appeased."
The Yajurveda approached him and said, "I shall quiet the horse.
To him as he crawled forward, it unleashed a great terror;
he fled toward this western direction.
He said, "This horse is indeed not yet at peace.
The Sāmaveda approached him and said, "I shall bring peace to the horse.
[The king asked,] "But with what will you bring peace?"
"The *Rathantara* is my *Sāman*, which is neither terrible nor cruel;
with it, let the horse be praised.
To him who had thus crept forward, he likewise released that same great terror.
He took possession of this northern direction.
He said, "This horse is not yet appeased.
Speech spoke to them, saying, "Go to Śaṃyu Ātharvaṇa!"
(GBr_1,2.18v) Having approached Śaṃyu Ātharvaṇa as he was seated, they said, "Salutations to you, O Blessed One; let the horse be healed.

"So be it."
He indeed performed a rite of pacifying water with the *Atharvaṇa* verses, the *Āṅgirasa* verses, the *Cātana* hymns, the *Mātṛnāman* hymns, and the *Vāstoṣpati* hymns; thus he brought about peace.
When that horse had been bathed and sprinkled, glowing coals were scattered from every pore of its body.

"Salutation to Śaṃyu Ātharvaṇa, who has fashioned me as worthy of sacrifice"—thus [he says].
Indeed, there will be other Brāhmaṇas hereafter who possess the most meager equipment;
they shall place [the fire] upon the footprint of the sun, or on that of an ox, a calf, a goat, a sheep, or a student of sacred knowledge.
"This earth, indeed, is the footprint of the Sun; upon that very footprint it shall be placed.

"‘When you first cried out as you were being born...’—these five [verses] (GBr_1,2.18kk).

The gods and the asuras were contending with one another.

(GBr_1,2.19d) Having become the Ṛgveda, he stood before him after going around.

(GBr_1,2.19k) The gods said to him, "Assume this form; with this form you conceal us most effectively, and with it you will be able to protect us.
