That is the Brahman-hood of the Brahman-priest.
Now, this form of Atharvan is he who is the turbaned Brahman-priest.
All the gods sat down to the south of him.

Indeed, it is from the Sadasya that this strength arises.
(GBr_1,2.19s) For they find a more spacious fold for a herd that is ill.
(GBr_1,2.19t) This southern quarter is indeed terrible, while the others are peaceful.

He creates himself and places himself within himself.
The gods said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "I choose."
He chose a boon:
"May they stand in this very *hotrā* office, purifying me, praising me, and reciting for me while I have become Indra.
They stood in that very *hotrā* office, purifying him, praising him, and reciting for him while he had become Indra.
Because they stood performing that very *hotrā*, purifying, praising, and reciting while Indra had become that [Soma], it became the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*.
That is the reason for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s name as *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*.
This *brāhmaṇācchaṃsīyā* is indeed the *hotrā* belonging to Indra.
"Choose a second boon," [he said].
"I choose," he replied, and he chose the boon.
"May they stand in this very *hotrā* office, purifying me while praising and reciting, having become Vāyu.
They stood in that very *hotrā* office, purifying him while praising and reciting, having become Vāyu.
Because they stood in that very *hotrā* office, purifying him while praising and reciting, having become Vāyu, he became the *potr̥*.
"That is the office of the Potṛ;
this Hotrā belonging to Vāyu is the Potrīyā.
Choose a third boon," [he said].
"Choose," he said. He chose this boon:
"May they stand over me, having become Agni, kindling me in this very office of the *hotṛ*, purifying me, praising me, and reciting for me."
While kindling him who had become Agni within that very *hotrā*, they remained there purifying, praising, and reciting.
Because they remained there kindling him who had become Agni within that very *hotrā*, purifying, praising, and reciting, that became the *āgnīdhra*.
That is the reason for the name *āgnīdhra* of the *āgnīdhra*.
"This is that same Hotṛ-function pertaining to Agni which belongs to the Āgnīdhra," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(GBr_1,2.20a) A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, bore this Agni Vaiśvānara.

"Come now, I shall display that splendor, sensory power, and vigor which are in me, so that he might indeed sustain me.
Having thus nourished himself, he milked this milk;
having shown it to this Brāhmaṇa, he offered it into his own self.
Having nourished his second self, he milked this ghee;
having shown it to this Brāhmaṇa, he offered it into himself.
Having nourished his third self, he milked this entire transformed variety of food.
Having shown this Brāhmaṇa to himself, he offered it into his own self;
having thereby replenished his fourth self, he beheld the Virāj, the wife of the Brāhmaṇa,
and gave her to him.
(GBr_1,2.20m) He became his very self. (GBr_1,2.20n) Then, about to cast away this Agni Vaiśvānara, the Brāhmaṇa established Agni Jātavedas.
(GBr_1,2.20o) He [Agni Vaiśvānara] said: "O Agni Jātavedas, place me here!"
He gave it the name Dvaita, which is both terrible and non-terrible.
It became a horse;
therefore, a horse does not pull a chariot by its forepart, nor does it carry a rider on its back.
He went to the gods;
he stood behind the gods;
therefore the gods were afraid.
He gave it to Brahmā;
he pacified it with this verse.
"They call you Agni Vaiśvānara; burning from your seats, you have gone forth. As such, speak for us among the gods; may we not come to harm under your protection. (PS 1.95.3;
also at VaitS 6.7)
(GBr_1,2.21b) He commences [the recitation] with these five *ṛc*s, beginning with:
"When you first cried out at birth" (*yad akrandaḥ prathamaṃ jāyamānaḥ*, *ṚV* 1.163.1). [The edition reads *pratamaṃ*.]
[Corrected p.
302] He became tranquil;
therefore, the horse is the most voracious among animals.
For he is indeed Vaiśvānara;
therefore, one gives the horse designated as "Agni" to the Brahmin,
for it has been bestowed upon the Brahmin.
He pressed out its essence;
that became the *rasa*.
Indeed, this is the *rasa*.
Although this is that very essence, they call it "chariot" by way of indirect designation;
for the gods, as it were, prefer the indirect to the direct, being averse to the manifest.
He arrived at the gods.
He remained behind the gods;
therefore the gods were afraid of him,
and they gave him to Brahmā.
(GBr_1,2.21q) He offered an oblation of clarified butter with this verse:
(GBr_1,2.21r) Having offered it over the chariot with the words, "The vigor of Indra, the vanguard of the Maruts" (ŚS 6.125.3, cf. PS 15.11.7), he mounted it with this verse.
"O Lord of the Forest, may you have strong limbs" (ŚS 6.125.1;
PS 15.11.8). Therefore, one gives the chariot used for the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnīdheya*) to the Brahman priest;
for it has been given to the Brahman.
The carpenter fashioned for him his eldest body as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
He saw it in five forms: in the *ṛc*, the *yajus*, the *sāman*, the peaceful, and the terrible.
Of these, he gave two to the Brahman: speech and light.
Speech, indeed, is the cow; light is gold.
Therefore, one gives to the Brahman priest the cow intended for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), which is to be consumed by four persons.
For she has been bestowed upon the Brahman.
When the cattle are being calmed, they cause [the sacrificer] to lose his sight;
he places that very sight within himself.
For what is sight, that is gold.
Therefore, he gives the gold belonging to the establishment of the sacred fires to the Brahman priest;
for what is given to the Brahman,
he places within his own self.
With that he kindled it;
what she did not deposit became *āglā*.
Having become *āglā*, she entered the ocean.
It burned the ocean;
therefore, even though the ocean is difficult to traverse,
it is indeed burnt by Vaiśvānara.
It rose up toward the earth;
it burned the earth;
it came to the gods.
She did not offend the gods;
those gods ran to Brahmā,
but he neither sang nor danced.
This is indeed *aglā*—
this is *kāruvidā*, this is *nama*.
Although he is actually *āglāhata*, they call him *āglāgṛdha* by an indirect name.
(GBr_1,2.21vv) For the gods, as it were, love what is hidden and hate what is manifest.

(GBr_1,2.21xx) Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should neither sing nor dance, lest he become an *āglāgṛdha*.
"Therefore, the first oblation belongs to Brahman and the latter belongs to Prajāpati; after the oblation to Prajāpati, the subsequent one belongs to Brahman alone"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 21.
The Atharvans and the Aṅgirases, as well as Bhṛgu and Cakṣus, beheld that Brahman;
they knew it, thinking, "This indeed is all that consists of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
Those gods offered the oblation belonging to Brahman into the Sāṃtapana fire.

(GBr_1,2.22e) For this Brāhmaṇa is indeed the Sāṃtapana fire. (GBr_1,2.22f) Of its vital energy, the gods partook of the vital energy, the ancestors of the ancestral offering with a well-disposed mind, and the Brāhmaṇas [partook] of the heavenly world through faith.
(GBr_1,2.22g) By means of that, the seers press [the Soma]; finally, women [press it] for themselves alone. Those outside [the community] press by both methods.
(GBr_1,2.22h) If no oblation pertaining to Brahman were offered at the sacrifice, men would be born from the oblations to Prajāpati as those who are not upright.
(GBr_1,2.22i) "He hears those worlds," said the father, for he who offers the Agnihotra is indeed the Āhavanīya, the Gārhapatya, and the Dakṣiṇāgni. [The edition reads *yāllokāñ*].
The gods rejoice in the beloved abode of the Āhavanīya fire;
of them, this Agni Sāṃtapana is the most excellent.
When his speech is satisfied, fire is satisfied;
when his breath is satisfied, wind is satisfied;
when his eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied.
When the mind is satisfied, the moon is satisfied;
when the ear is satisfied, the quarters and the intermediate directions are satisfied; when the fluids are satisfied, the waters are satisfied.
"When the body hairs are satisfied, the plants and trees are satisfied;
when the body is satisfied, the earth is satisfied.
Thus this foremost fire, Sāṃtapana, being satisfied, satisfies all that are to be satisfied"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 22.
(GBr_1,2.23a) "The Sāṃtapana [Agni], this oblation...

(GBr_1,2.23b) This indeed is the Sāṃtapana Agni: namely, the Brāhmaṇa for whom the rites of conception, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, the birth ceremony, the naming, the first outing, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the cutting of the beard, the initiation, the ritual bath, the Agnihotra, the observance of vows, and so forth, have been performed—he is the Sāṃtapana.
Now, he who is without sacred fires is like a clod of earth in a jar.

Just as a clod of earth thrown into a jar serves neither for the purpose of purification nor produces grain, even so is this Brāhmaṇa who is without sacred fires; for that Brāhmaṇa who is without sacred fires, there is no [attainment of] the divine.
One should not give him offerings for the ancestors, nor do the blessings of his Vedic study or the blessings of his sacrifices lead him to heaven.

"He is the skillful performer of this sacrifice" (ŚS 20.101.1, RV 1.12.1); such is the Brāhmaṇa. // 23 //
(GBr 1.2.24a) Now, Prajāpati, being about to sacrifice with Soma, spoke to the Vedas: "Which of you shall I choose as the Hotṛ, which as the Adhvaryu, which as the Udgātṛ, and which as the Brāhmaṇ?

(GBr 1.2.24b) They replied: "Choose one who knows the Ṛgveda as the Hotṛ, one who knows the Yajurveda as the Adhvaryu, one who knows the Sāmaveda as the Udgātṛ, and one who knows the Atharvāṅgirasa as the Brāhmaṇ.
(GBr 1.2.24c) Thus, his sacrifice becomes firmly established in the four worlds, among the four gods, in the four Vedas, and in the four offices of the Hotṛs—the four-footed sacrifice.
He who knows thus becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle.
Therefore, choose one who knows the *Ṛgveda* as the *hotṛ* priest, for he indeed knows the duties of the *hotṛ*;
Agni is indeed the *hotṛ*.
"The earth, indeed, is the abode of the *ṛc*s;
Agni is the deity; the *gāyatrī* is the meter; and 'bhūḥ' is the pure essence.
Therefore, choose him alone as the *hotṛ* priest for the conquest of this world."
For the conquest of this world,
for the total mastery of this world,
for the attainment of this world.
For the expansion of this world,
for the prosperity of this world,
for the exaltation of this world.
For the pervasion of this world,
for the sufficiency of this world,
for the completion of this world.
(GBr_1,2.24s) Now, if they do not choose a Hotṛ who knows thus, their sacrifice is left deficient even from the start.
(GBr_1,2.24t) Choose an Adhvaryu who knows the Yajus; for he knows the office of the Adhvaryu.
(GBr_1,2.24u) Vāyu, indeed, is the Adhvaryu.
The intermediate space is indeed the abode of the *yajus* formulas;
Vāyu is the deity, the *triṣṭubh* is the meter, and "bhuvaḥ" is the pure essence (*śukra*).
Therefore, choose him alone as the *adhvaryu*, saying, "of this very world."
(GBr_1,2.24y) Now, if they do not choose such an Adhvaryu, their sacrifice is left deficient from the very beginning.
(GBr_1,2.24z) Choose an Udgātṛ who knows the Sāmaveda; for he indeed knows the office of the Udgātṛ.
(GBr_1,2.24aa) He knows the Audgātra.
The Udgātṛ is indeed the sun; heaven is the abode of the Sāmans;
the sun is the deity; the Jāgata is the metre; "Svar" is the Śukra.
"Therefore, choose him alone as the Udgātṛ," [he said], "for this world.
Now, if they choose an Udgātṛ who does not know this, their sacrifice is depleted from the north.
Choose one who knows the Atharvāṅgirases as the Brahman priest.
For he knows the office of the Brahman priest;
the moon, indeed, is the Brahman;
and the waters are the abode of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
The moon is the deity; the lightning is the *uṣṇih* and *kakup* meters; "Om" is for the Atharvans; and "Śukraṃ janat" is for the Aṅgirases.
Therefore, choose that very one as the Brahman priest for the conquest of this world, for the total victory over this world.
For the conquest of this world,
for the attainment of this world,
and for the increase of this world.
For the prosperity of this world,
for the exaltation of this world,
for the pervasion of this world.
For the attainment of this world,
for the completion of this world;
yet if they do not choose such a knower as Brahman-priest, their sacrifice is depleted from the south, their sacrifice is depleted from the south.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_1,3.1a) Om. The earth slopes toward the south; (GBr_1,3.1b) from the south, the waters flow.
Therefore, the sacrificial grounds are as if elevated above that [general] ground wherever the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases have their dwellings.
(GBr_1,3.1c) Just as these waters carry these worlds along, even so do the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases carry all the gods along.

In this very way, this sacred utterance (*vyāhṛti*) carries all the Vedas: "Om" for the Ṛg-verses, "Om" for the Yajus-formulas, "Om" for the Sāman-chants; "Om" is the salutation for everything that is spoken.
Therefore, those who know it perform this as the final act in the sacrifice, saying: "O gods, O Brahmins, come, come!"
(GBr_1,3.1g) These indeed are the divine Brahmins, namely the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
(GBr_1,3.1h) Praising them, choosing them, and invoking them, people think [of them as such].
(GBr_1,3.1i) No one other than a knower of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases should come to the sacrifice when chosen.
(GBr_1,3.1j) By the splendor of the sacrifice, he obtains splendor; by vigor, vigor; by glory, glory.
(GBr_1,3.1k) No one other than a knower of the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* verses should come to the sacrifice when chosen, lest he should rob the sacrifice.

(GBr_1,3.1l) Just as a calf, having first sucked its mother, would then suck another cow, so should the *Brahman* priest, a knower of the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* verses, come to the sacrifice when chosen, lest he should rob the sacrifice.
"It would be like this: as if there were a cow, or a horse, or a mule, or a one-footed, two-footed, or three-footed creature—what could it carry? What could it eat?

Therefore, choose as the *hotṛ* priest one who knows the *Ṛgveda*, as the *adhvaryu* one who knows the *Yajurveda*, as the *udgātṛ* one who knows the *Sāmaveda*, and as the *brahman* one who knows the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*.
In this way, his sacrifice becomes firmly established in the four worlds, among the four gods, in the four Vedas, and in the four *hotrā* offices—the four-footed sacrifice."

"He who knows thus, and he who knows the priestly office of the officiating priests, and he who knows that which is to be sacrificed at the sacrifice, stands firm with offspring and cattle"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 1.
Prajāpati performed the sacrifice.

By means of the *ṛc* he performed the office of the Hotṛ; by means of the *yajus*, the office of the Adhvaryu; by means of the *sāman*, the office of the Udgātṛ; and by means of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases, the office of the Brahman.

Indeed, he performs this great sacrifice when he performs the office of the Hotṛ with the *ṛc*, the office of the Adhvaryu with the *yajus*, the office of the Udgātṛ with the *sāman*, and the office of the Brahman with the Atharvans and Aṅgirases.
(GBr_1,3.2d) Indeed, by means of the three Vedas, one wing of the sacrifice is perfected;
(GBr_1,3.2e) with the mind alone, the Brahman priest perfects the other wing of the sacrifice.
(GBr_1,3.2f) And this wind that blows is indeed the sacrifice.
(GBr 1,3.2g) Of that [sacrifice], the mind and speech are the two paths.
(GBr 1,3.2h) For by means of both the mind and speech the sacrifice proceeds. (GBr 1,3.2i) That [heavenly world] is the mind; this [earth] is speech.

(GBr_1,3.2j) If, while speaking, he should think, "A part of this sacrifice of mine has fallen away," (GBr_1,3.2k) then just as a one-legged man, when walking, or a one-wheeled chariot, when moving, comes to ruin, even so his sacrifice comes to ruin.
(GBr_1,3.2l) Following the ruin of the sacrifice, the sacrificer comes to ruin.
Following the failure of the sacrificer, the officiating priests fall into failure;
following the failure of the officiating priests, the sacrificial fees fall into failure;
and following the failure of the sacrificial fees, the sacrificer falls into failure with respect to his sons and cattle.
"Following the failure of his sons and cattle, the sacrificer falls into failure in the heavenly world;
following the failure in the heavenly world, the security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) of that half of the world in which they sacrifice falls into failure," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 2.

Regarding this, Śvetaketu Āruṇeya, having seen a Brahman priest speaking, said: "Half of this sacrifice has slipped away from me. Therefore, when the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, the restraining of speech (*vācoyamyam*) is performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*) until the two *antaryāma* cups; then, regarding those *pavamāna* chants which are [composed of] verses (*odṛcaḥ*), in them—
Now, regarding those stotras together with the śastras up until the *vaṣaṭ*-call:
if he should make a mistake in the *ṛc*, he should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire, saying, "Oṃ bhūr janat.
If [he makes a mistake] in the *yajus*, he should offer an oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, saying, "Oṃ bhuvo janat."
(GBr_1,3.3g) If [the fire] has gone out from the *sāman*, one should offer an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "oṃ svar janat.
(GBr_1,3.3h) If [it has gone out] from the unknown or from the *brahman*, one should offer an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire itself with the formula: "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janat oṃ.
(GBr_1,3.3i) That [is the expiation] for the *vākovākya*, for the *ṛc*s, the *yajus*es, the *sāmans*, and the *atharvāṅgirases*.
Furthermore, it has been said that by means of salt, the taste of the Vedas and the breach of the sacrifice are joined together.
Just as a man who walks on two feet, or a chariot with two wheels, proceeds without stumbling, even so his sacrifice proceeds without stumbling.
Following the non-failure of the sacrifice, the sacrificer attains non-failure; following the non-failure of the sacrificer, the officiating priests attain non-failure;
and following the non-failure of the officiating priests, the sacrificial fees attain non-failure.

Following the non-failure of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), the sacrificer attains non-failure with respect to his sons and cattle; following the non-failure of his sons and cattle, the sacrificer attains non-failure with respect to the heavenly world;

following the non-failure of the heavenly world, he attains non-failure with respect to the security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) of that half [of the world] in which they sacrifice—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 3.3.3r–r.

(GBr 1,3.4a) "Because he sat upon the Udumbara post for me, because he made the sound *hiṅ*, because he recited the *prastāva* for me, because he sang the *udgītha* for me, because he invoked the *subrahmaṇyā* for me"—thus are the sacrificial fees led to the Udgātṛ.

(GBr 1,3.4b) "Because he drew the cups for me, because he moved forward for me, because he listened for me, because he brought about unanimity for me, because he sacrificed for me, because he did not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call for me"—thus [are they led] to the Adhvaryu.

(GBr 1,3.4c) "Because he sat on the Hotṛ’s seat for me, because he sacrificed for me, because he recited the *śastra* for me, because he did not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call for me"—thus [are they led] to the Hotṛ.

"He has prepared my sacrificial ground; he has sent forth my *brahmāsada*; he has recited my *brahmajapa*s; he has offered for me the *purastāddhoma* and the *saṃsthita-homa* offerings; he has sacrificed for me; he has praised for me; he has not uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call for me"—thus [one says] regarding the Brahman priest. "He has performed for me with the most abundant *brahman*-power."
(GBr_1,3.4f) This indeed is the most abundant Brahman, namely the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases. (GBr_1,3.4g) Those who are Aṅgirases are the essence; those who are Atharvans are the remedy.
(GBr_1,3.4h) That which is the remedy is the immortal; that which is the immortal is Brahman.
(GBr_1,3.4i) "He indeed receives half of the share of the former priests; the other half belongs to the others, and half belongs to the Brahman," so says the Brāhmaṇa. // 4 //
The gods and the asuras engaged in battle. Thereupon, these three *hotrā* offices fell into disarray;
Indra appropriated their *ukthas* and *sāmans*.
He gave them to the Hotṛ.
Indeed, the Ājya-stotra became the portion of the Hotṛ; the Pra-uga-stotra became the portion of the Potṛ; and indeed, the Vaiśvadeva-stotra became the portion of the Hotṛ.
The Niṣkevalya belongs to the Neṣṭṛ;
the Marutvatīya indeed belonged to the Hotṛ;
and the Āgnimāruta belonged to the Āgnīdhra.
Therefore, this Āgnimāruta hymn is praised as being, as it were, most frequently practiced;
therefore, these— the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Āgnīdhra— become, as it were, desirous of reciting together, and the Āgnīdhra should wear a garment that is not soiled.
That [soma] became the most excellent of the Brahmanas.
He cut off half of them—the first portion for honor and the first foot—and this is what remains as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); so says the Brāhmaṇa. 5.
Uddālaka Āruṇi, it is said, once took up the office of a sacrificial priest for the people of the North.
He had a gold coin suspended around his neck, out of fear of being censured, thinking: "To whatever learned Brahmin might censure me, I shall give this to him.
Now, a fear of the Brahmins of the North seized him, thinking: "This Uddālaka, the Kaurupañcala, the Brahmin and son of a Brahmin, is coming!"
"He was chosen, yet he did not accept the office, saying, 'With what hero shall we contend?

They then took him up from the very point where he had fled, and they followed after him accordingly. They said to Svaidāyana Śaunaka, 'Svaidāyana, you are indeed the most learned in sacred knowledge (*brahmiṣṭha*) among us.'"
"O hero, let us contend with him," they said.
He held fast to him from whichever side he had approached, and they followed after him accordingly.
He then addressed them, saying, "O Svaidāyanas!"
"O Gautama's son!"—thus he called out to him in reproach, and he responded to what had been promised.
Indeed, Gautama’s son ran away with his garment tucked up.

(GBr_1,3.7a) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why is it that these creatures are first born hairy from the head; and why is it that for them other hairs, such as the beard and those under the armpits, grow later? (GBr_1,3.7b) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why is it that these creatures first become grey at the head; and why is it that in the end they all become grey?
(GBr_1,3.7c) He who knows the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices [should know]: why are these offspring born without teeth? Why are they born again as it were later?

(GBr_1,3.7d) He who knows the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices [should know]: why do their [teeth] fall out when they are seven or eight years old? Why are they born again? Why, in the end, do all of them fall out?
(GBr_1,3.7e) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why are the lower teeth born first and the upper ones later?

(GBr_1,3.7f) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why are the lower teeth smaller and shorter, while the upper ones are broader and longer? (GBr_1,3.7g) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why are these two tusks longer, and why are the two jaws as if equal?
(GBr_1,3.7h) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why are these two ears, being within, as if split open?
(GBr_1,3.7i) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why do men have beards while women are beardless?
(GBr_1,3.7j) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why is the body of these [women] continuous, as it were, and why are their bones more firm?

(GBr_1,3.7k) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why is it that in the first stage of life, the seed emitted by women does not result in conception; why is it that in the middle stage of life, the seed emitted results in conception; and why is it that in the final stage of life, the seed emitted does not result in conception?
(GBr_1,3.7l) He who would know the form of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why does this penis rise up and fall down?
(GBr_1,3.7m) Why does one breathe out only once? 7.

(GBr_1,3.8a) Now, he who knows the eight butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) in front, the five portions of the oblation (*havirbhāga*) in the middle, and the six portions for Prajāpati above, and who knows the eight butter-portions at the rear;
(GBr_1,3.8b) and he who knows the golden Gāyatrī with luminous wings, carrying the sacrificer by means of all sacrifices to the heavenly world;
(GBr_1,3.8c) and he who knows the *apaṅkti* with five feet and seventeen syllables, carrying the sacrificer by means of all sacrifices to the heavenly world.
(GBr_1,3.8d) Giving him a gold coin, he said, "Truly, you are well-versed in sacred lore, O Svaidāyana; I give this gold to one who knows gold.
(GBr_1,3.8e) Having accepted it, he went out. (GBr_1,3.8f) He departed for the place where the other was.
He asked him, "Is this the son of Gautama?
"This is Brahmā, the son of Brahmā," he replied. "If anyone should speak ill of him or even attempt to scrutinize him, his head would surely split apart, or his vital breaths would abandon him.
They cried out to one another in distress and fled away from where the other had been.
In the morning, with fuel in their hands, they approached him, saying, "We come to you.
He asked, "For what purpose?
They replied, "Those very questions that your honor asked us yesterday, may your honor explain those to us."
"So be it," he said;
then he explained these questions to them.

Because he first spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the east of the altar, therefore these creatures are born first with hair on their heads. Because he subsequently spreads the sacrificial seat (*prastara*) as it were behind [the grass], therefore for them the beard, the armpit hair, and other body hairs grow as it were later.
Because he throws the sacrificial seat into the fire before the sacrificial grass, therefore these creatures become grey-headed first on their heads.
Because he finally throws everything into the fire, therefore in the end all become grey-haired.
Because the *prayāja* offerings are without *puronuvākyā* verses, therefore these offspring are born toothless.
Because the oblations (*havis*) have *puronuvākyā* verses, therefore they are born with teeth as it were later on.
Because the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are without invitatory verses (*puro’nuvākyā*), therefore these [daughters] of seven or eight years of age become estranged from their husbands.

Because the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*) are with invitatory verses, therefore they are born again. Because the *samiṣṭayajus* offering is without an invitatory verse, therefore finally all [the sons] are estranged.
(GBr_1,3.9j) Because he recites with a *gāyatrī* verse and sacrifices with a *triṣṭubh* verse, therefore the lower teeth are born first and the upper ones later.
(GBr_1,3.9k) Because he recites with a *ṛc* verse and sacrifices with a *yajus* formula, therefore the lower teeth are smaller and shorter, while the upper ones are broader and longer.
(GBr_1,3.9l) Because he pours the two long libations forward, therefore these two tusks are longer.

Because the two *saṃyājyā* verses have identical meters, therefore the two jaws are as it were equal. Because he pours the butter together during the fourth fore-offering (*prayāja*), therefore these two ears are as it were split open within.
Because he utters the *abhihiṅkāra* after muttering the *japa*, therefore men are bearded, while women are beardless.
Because he recites the *sāmidhenī* verses continuously, therefore their bodies are, as it were, continuous.

Because the *sāmidhenīs* have wood for their oblation, therefore their bones are, as it were, more solid. Because the *prayāja* offerings have clarified butter for their oblation, therefore, when seed is infused in them during the first stage of life, it does not come to fruition.

Because they proceed with the oblations of curds and the sacrificial cake in the middle [of the sacrifice], therefore in the middle stage of life, the emitted seed comes to fruition. Because the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) have clarified butter as their oblation, therefore in the final stage of life, the emitted seed does not come to fruition. Because he breathes out once at the final after-offering, therefore this penis rises upward and falls downward.

(GBr_1,3.9v) If one were not to exhale, there would be swelling; (GBr_1,3.9w) if one were to exhale repeatedly, there would be discharge. Therefore, one exhales once, so that there shall be neither swelling nor discharge. // 9 //

Now, as for those eight butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) mentioned previously: there are five fore-offerings (*prayāja*), two libations of ghee (*āghāra*), and two butter-portions. Of the butter-portions, the first belongs to Agni and the second to Soma;
of the sacrificial food-portions (*havirbhāga*), that which belongs to Soma is indeed the oblation itself, while the cake (*puroḍāśa*) belongs to Agni.

(GBr_1,3.10d) The cake for Agni-Soma, the fire Sviṣṭakṛt—these are the five middle portions of the oblation. (GBr_1,3.10e) Now, as for the six portions belonging to Prajāpati: the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, that which he cuts off for the *agnīdh*, the portion for the Brahman, the portion for the sacrificer, and the *anvāhārya* rice as the sixth.

(GBr_1,3.10f) Then, as for the eight subsequent portions: the eight butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), the three after-offerings (*anuyāja*), the four offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), and the *samiṣṭayajus* as the eighth.
Now, that golden Gāyatrī with wings of light who carries the sacrificer by means of all sacrifices to the heavenly world—that is the altar itself.
Those eight butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) which are in front are its right wing;
and those eight butter-portions which are behind are its left wing.
The oblations are the self;
the Gārhapatya fire is the hindquarters;
the Āhavanīya fire is the head.
The two wings are made of gold and silver.
Now, because they do not see the sun from the front [of the altar], the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) is without light.
Furthermore, that five-footed *paṅkti* verse consisting of seventeen syllables—which carries the sacrificer to the heavenly world by means of all sacrifices—is indeed the *yājyā*.
Of that [formula], "Oṃ śrāvaya" has four syllables; "astu śrauṣaṭ" has four syllables;
and "yaj" has two syllables.
"ye yajāmahe" consists of five syllables;
"vaṣaṭ" consists of two syllables. This is the *paṅkti* [verse], consisting of five feet and seventeen syllables. It carries the sacrificer to the heavenly world by means of all sacrifices.

"Therefore, wherever there is sovereignty, or wherever they shall carry him [the dead], one should choose as Brahman priest only one who knows this, and not one who does not know this"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 10.

(GBr_1,3.11o) To which deity does that which has been kindled belong?

(GBr_1,3.11x) To which deity does that which is being carried away belong?
(GBr_1,3.11y) To which deity does the fire belong when it is being placed? (GBr_1,3.11z) To which deity does it belong when it has been placed?
(GBr_1,3.11aa) To which deity does the fuel belong?

(GBr_1,3.11cc) To which deity did you look at the Gārhapatya fire?
(GBr_1,3.11dd) To which deity does the subsequent oblation belong?
"To which deity did you offer when you led the *sruk* spoon three times toward the north?
To which deity did you offer when, having placed the *sruk* on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), wiped it, and rubbed your hands toward the north?

(GBr_1,3.11kk) To which deity did you offer the water with the ladle when it was not washed?
(GBr_1,3.11ll) To which deity [did you offer it] when it was washed? (GBr_1,3.11mm) To which deity did you offer the water with the ladle to the west of the Āhavanīya fire? [ed. udaka]
"To which deity did you dedicate the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles when you wiped them?
To which deity did you dedicate the handle of the *sruk* at night when you rubbed it? To which deity did you dedicate it in the morning when you rubbed it?"
"If you know this, O Gautama, then your oblation is offered; but if you do not know it, your oblation is unoffered"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 11.
He said: "The portion for Rudra is in the cow when she is being milked;
that for Manu is when she has been called to the udder;
that for Vāyu is when she has been let loose."
The Vairāja is the calf being led forward; the Jāgata is [the milk] being drawn up;
the Āśvina is [the milk] being milked.
The milk for Soma when it has been milked;
that for Bṛhaspati while it is being prepared;
that for Heaven and Earth while it is being carried away.
The oblation for Agni is [the portion] being placed on the fire; that for Vaiśvānara is [the portion] already placed on the fire;
that for Viṣṇu is [the portion] being ignited by the sprinkling of butter.
The Maruta oblation is that which has been set ablaze;
the Pauṣṇa is that which has been vomited up;
the Vāruṇa is that which has been poured out.
The offering to Sarasvatī was brought back with water;
the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ was being removed;
the offering to Dhātṛ had been removed.
The Vaiśvadeva cup when being lifted;
the Sāvitra cup when already lifted; the Bārhaspatya cup when being moved forward.
(GBr_1,3.12v) When being carried away, it belongs to Heaven and Earth;
(GBr_1,3.12w) when being set down, it belongs to Indra;
(GBr_1,3.12x) when having been set down, it is for strength.
The fuel-stick belongs to Agni. When I offered the first oblation, I placed myself in the heavenly world thereby.
When I looked at the Gārhapatya fire, it was for the continuity of this world.
The subsequent oblation belongs to Prajāpati;
therefore it is more full, for it is performed by the mind alone.
Having offered with the ladle, I led it up three times toward the north; by that, I have gratified the Rudras.
(GBr 1,3.12ee) When, having placed the ladle on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and wiped it, I wiped my hands from the north, I thereby gratified the plants and trees.

(GBr 1,3.12ff) When, having wiped for a second time and arranged the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*pitryupavīta*), I offered the *svadhā* oblation to the ancestors from the south, I thereby gratified the ancestors. (GBr 1,3.12gg) When I first tasted [the food], I thereby gratified the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
That which was the second [portion], by that [I offered] to the embryos;
therefore embryos live without eating. That which was at the end, the whole of it, I ate; by that I satisfied all the gods.
(GBr_1,3.12kk) In that I poured water with the ladle from the unpurified [water], by that I drove away the *sarpa-itara-janas* (the serpent-like non-people).
(GBr_1,3.12ll) In that [I poured] from the purified [water], [I drove away] the *sarpa-puṇya-janas* (the serpent-like virtuous people).
(GBr_1,3.12mm) In that I poured water with the ladle behind the Āhavanīya fire, by that I drove away the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
"In that I have wiped the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles, by that I have sent forth the Seven Seers (*saptarṣis*).
In that I have rubbed the handle of the *sruc* at night, those who enter [their homes] at night, the right-shouldered ones, them I have sent upward.
In that I have rubbed it in the morning, those who go forth in the morning, the right-shouldered ones, them I have sent upward"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 12.
"Indeed it is so, sir, as you have said. But let me ask you something more. "Ask, Prācīnayogya," [he replied].

"Quickly, the householder who offers oblations without knowledge is deprived of everything. [The other asked: "But with what knowledge do I offer? What is your knowledge, and what is the atonement?"

(GBr_1,3.13cc) Having smeared the fire-places with a ball of cow-dung from an ox, having placed the oblation nearby, and having churned the fire, he should offer it, saying: "Svāhā to out-breathing and in-breathing! Svāhā to equalizing-breathing and diffusive-breathing! Svāhā to upward-breathing and form! (GBr_1,3.13dd) Then, in the morning, having replenished the fires in their proper places, he should offer as before.
"That knowledge is mine; that is my atonement.

Now, if they should be unable to produce fire, or if no wind should blow from any direction, what danger could come from that? He who offers oblations without knowing this—his sacrifice and his offerings become in vain.
"But with knowledge indeed do I offer," he said.
"What is that knowledge? What is the expiation?
"Having smeared the sacrificial sites with a ball of cow-dung from an ox, and having set out the materials for the oblation—"
With the hymn beginning, "May Vāta breathe forth the medicine" (PS 19.46.7–9), he should offer oblations into himself alone.
Then, in the morning, having churned the fire and established the fires in their proper places, he should offer oblations as before.
"That is my knowledge, that is my atonement," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 13.
"Exactly so, O Venerable Sir, it is just as you have said.
Nevertheless, I shall indeed approach you as a pupil.
"If you had not spoken thus, your head would have fallen off," [said Śākalya].
"Come now, I shall tell you that whereby it will not fall away from you:
for indeed, when one who knows this eats and drinks, speech is satisfied by that;
and when speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied."
When fire is satisfied, the earth is satisfied;
when the earth is satisfied, those beings that depend upon the earth are satisfied.
Indeed, when one who knows this eats and drinks, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is satisfied by that.
When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is satisfied, the wind (*vāyu*) is satisfied;
when the wind is satisfied, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is satisfied;
when the intermediate space is satisfied, those beings that depend upon the intermediate space are satisfied.
Verily, when one who knows this eats and drinks, the eye is satisfied by that;
when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied;
when the sun is satisfied, the sky is satisfied.
When the one in heaven is satisfied, those beings that depend upon heaven are satisfied.
Indeed, when one who knows this eats and drinks, his mind is satisfied by that;
when the mind is satisfied, the moon is satisfied.
When the moon is satisfied, the waters are satisfied;
when the waters are satisfied, those beings that depend upon the waters are satisfied.
Indeed, when one who knows this eats and drinks, the ear is thereby satisfied.
When the ear is satisfied, the quarters and the intermediate directions are satisfied.
When the quarters and the intermediate directions are satisfied, those beings that depend upon the quarters and the intermediate directions are satisfied.
Indeed, for one who, knowing this, eats and drinks, his very right hand is the *juhū* ladle.
The left hand is the *upabhṛt* ladle,
the throat is the *dhruvā* ladle,
and food is the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
"The vital breaths are the lights.
For one who knows this, and for one who, knowing thus, performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice, the *agnihotra* becomes ever-sacrificed, ever-offered, ever-eaten, and ever-drunk; such is the Brāhmaṇa. 14.
The Priyamedhas, the Bharadvājas, thinking themselves to be knowers of sacrifice,
used not to approach any knower of the Veda;
they thought they knew everything.
They were unaware of this together;
they did not agree regarding the *agnihotra*.
One of them offered the *agnihotra* once, another twice, and another thrice.
(GBr_1,3.15g) Of them, he who had offered the Agnihotra once was asked by the other two: "To whom do you offer?
(GBr_1,3.15h) [He replied: "In truth, this entire universe is Prajāpati; (GBr_1,3.15i) 'I offer to Prajāpati alone in the evening,' and 'to Prajāpati in the morning.'"
(GBr_1,3.15j) Of them, those two asked the one who sacrificed twice, "To whom do you sacrifice? (GBr_1,3.15k) He replied, "To Agni and Prajāpati in the evening; to Sūrya and Prajāpati in the morning.

(GBr_1,3.15l) Those two asked the one who sacrificed thrice, "To whom do you sacrifice? He replied, "To Agni and Prajāpati in the evening; to Anumati and Prajāpati [in the evening]; to Sūrya and Prajāpati..."
"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," [he said] at the morning [offering].
Of them, he who offered twice prospered;
he became the most abundant.
By means of offspring one surpassed the other two, and by means of prosperity the other two surpassed him.
The offspring of the former entered into a state of common birth with the offspring of the other two.
Therefore, the oblation should be offered twice: both with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and with the mind (*manas*).
"He who knows this and he who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, attain that very prosperity which he attained"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 15.
(GBr_1,3.16a) From what indeed was Svāhā produced? (GBr_1,3.16b) By whom was she created? (GBr_1,3.16c) Or what is her lineage?
How many syllables,
how many words, and how many phonemes?
What is its prior cessation?
Where does it abide? What is its substratum?
"Tell me, what is the deity and what is the form of Svāhā?
"Svāhā is indeed born of truth; she was created by Brahmā."
The Lāmagāyana-sagotra has two syllables;
it is one word.

(GBr_1,3.16p) And the three colors— white, lotus-colored, and golden— (GBr_1,3.16q) are the condensed unity of all meters in the Vedas; at the end of the colors are the four Vedas in the body, (GBr_1,3.16r) the six limbs are the herbs and trees, and the hairs are the [plants].
The sun and moon are her two eyes;
she is *svāhā*, she is *svadhā*, and she is employed in sacrifices as the *vaṣaṭ* call;
Agni is her deity.
"The form of a Brāhmaṇa" refers to the Brāhmaṇa. 16.
Now, moreover, there were indeed sages named Kārava who possessed little wealth;
they saw this Agniṣṭoma consisting of a single *gī* and they performed it.
"With that they sacrificed; they went to heaven.
"He who should desire, 'May I go to heaven,' let him sacrifice with this Agniṣṭoma consisting of a single quality," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 17.

(GBr 1,3.18a) Now, therefore, we shall explain the distribution of the Savanīya animal. (GBr 1,3.18b) Having set aside the portions for the sacrificial cuttings, the two jaws together with the tongue belong to the Prastotṛ; (GBr 1,3.18c) the throat together with the uvula belongs to the Pratihartṛ.
The hawk is for the chest of the Udgātṛ;
the right side with the shoulder is for the Adhvaryu;
the left is for the Upagātṛs.
The left shoulder belongs to the Pratiprasthātṛ; the right hip belongs to the Adhvaryu; the three ribs belong to the Brahman; and the lower thigh belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
The right thigh belongs to the Potṛ; the left hip belongs to the Hotṛ;
the lower leg belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
The right arm belongs to the Acchāvāka;
the right arm belongs to the Neṣṭṛ; the left arm belongs to the Sadasya.
The shoulder blade and the spine belong to the master of the house;
the tail belongs to the wife;
she causes a Brāhmaṇa to accept it.

The rectum, the heart, and the two kidneys are for the *āgnīdhra*; the fingers are for the *ātreyī*; the right arm is for the *gṛhapati* who bestows the vow; and the left arm and the two right feet are for the *gṛhapati*.
The householder takes hold of both feet of the wife who has received the vow;
their lips [are joined] together,
and the householder alone instructs her.
The *maṇika* bones, the three shoulder-blades, and the *kīkasā* bones belong to the *grāvastut*;
the three *kīkasā* bones and half of the *apāna* belong to the *unnetṛ*;
from here upwards, [the organs] belong to the *camasādhvaryus*, and the *kloman* belongs to the *śamitṛ*.
The head belongs to the Subrahmaṇya;
the skin belongs to him who invokes the *śvas-sutyā* (the sacrifice to be performed tomorrow).
In this way, they indeed amount to thirty-six.
The cow has thirty-six cuttings;
the *bṛhatī* meter has thirty-six syllables;
and the heavenly world is indeed of the nature of the *bṛhatī*.
By means of the Bṛhatī, indeed, the gods sacrifice in the heavenly world;
by means of the Bṛhatī they are established in the heavenly world.
Those who thus distribute [the verses] are established with offspring and cattle.

(GBr_1,3.18kk) Now, if those who are of different character, or evil-doers, or fire-eaters, or other people should plunder [the victim], even so does their sacrificial animal become plundered; it does not lead to heaven.
(GBr_1,3.18ll) Indeed, Śrutārṣi knew this division of the sacrificial animal for the gods. He taught it to Girija Bābhravya, and from him another [taught it] to human beings.
"Thereupon he came hither among men," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
[Among humans] (GBr_1,3.19a),
now therefore follows the consecration (dīkṣā) (GBr_1,3.19b).
For what reason indeed do they call one "consecrated" (dīkṣita)?
"He dwells in the most excellent thought"—
it is because he dwells in this thought that they call him "the consecrated" (*dīkṣita*) by an indirect name;
for the gods, as it were, love the indirect and dislike the direct.

(GBr_1,3.19f) For what reason is one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) not expected to rise [in greeting] and not expected to offer salutation, even though he is one who ought to be risen for and saluted?
(GBr_1,3.19g) Those who ought to be risen for and saluted—the *Atharvāṅgirases*—enter into him.
(GBr_1,3.19h) What, then, is his *Atharvaṇa* portion?
(GBr_1,3.19i) When they offer into the self alone and not into another—
(GBr_1,3.19j) thus indeed do the Atharvaṇas who perform the Odanasava sacrifice offer into the self alone and not into another.
(GBr_1,3.19k) Now, what is his *Āṅgirasa*?
When one does not utter the names of oneself and others, then indeed in that *āsād* the names of both oneself and others are not uttered. They speak speech that is discerning and pleasing;
they cause the Brahmin to discern and cause him, the son of Prajāpati, to be pleased.
This very one is the milker of the vow, the Atharvāṅgirases;
for they are dependent upon her.
For what reason, then, does one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) not eat food, and why do they not utter his name?
(GBr_1,3.19r) "He who is established in food becomes established in name," they say; those who eat his food eat his evil.
(GBr_1,3.19s) But those who take his name strike away the evil from his name.
(GBr_1,3.19t) Moreover, they say that he becomes the embryo of the Vedas.
Regarding him who is unborn, unperceived, and has not purchased the *soma*, they say that his food is unfit to be eaten.
He is born at dawn during the initiations; they purchase the *soma* for him. Regarding him who is now born, perceived, and has purchased the *soma*, they say that his food becomes fit to be eaten.
For what reason, then, are the *saṃsavas* (the pouring out of remains) sought to be avoided?
Whichever of the two is more vigorous, he steals away the sacrifice of the other. For what reason, then, should one not meditate on the gods, nor study when [the sacrifice] has concluded?
It is for the sake of the *saṃsava* alone.
When it lightens, thunders, and rains, the gods press the Soma and consume it;
so too do the learned Brahmins who have studied the Vedas press it.
For them, their fathers and grandfathers partake of every essence.
"He should not meditate on the divine when [the teacher] has passed away, nor should he study," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 19.
The teachers had returned home and were sitting together.
Yajña, intending to undergo initiation, assumed the form of a Brāhmaṇa and approached them, saying:
"If you have all come together in this manner, well then, let me be initiated among you."
Patyal proposes *apasamavatasthur*, [ed. *dikṣā*] (GBr 1,3.20d).
They said, "We do not recognize you at all; we do not know you.
For who would undergo initiation with one who is thus unknown? (GBr 1,3.20e).

"Now, whether you will undergo initiation or not, or if you shall initiate yourselves in this manner, you will surely become bewildered; your sacrifice will be bewildered. Therefore, all of you must undergo initiation."
(GBr_1,3.20i) "Or rather, you shall initiate only one person; you shall be the *gṛhapatis* and the *ṛtviks* for a non-deficient (*ahīna*) sacrifice. (GBr_1,3.20j) They sat there silently, reflecting.
(GBr_1,3.20k) He said, "Why indeed do you sit in silence?"
(GBr_1,3.20l) "We ask you further.

(GBr_1,3.20m) "Ask," they said. "Now, regarding this initiation that you are about to undergo: during this year that follows, will you engage in sexual intercourse, or will you not? [Patyal notes that *upamay etasmin* occurs in two BORI manuscripts and suggests...]

"Fie! they said, "How can we approach those who have not been initiated? We shall not approach them."
"You will indeed become despisers of the Brāhmaṇas;
for that seed of yours which has been in this year-long [penance] would have become Brāhmaṇas, and you would have attained awakening.
"Or rather, we shall go there, or we shall not go," they said.
"You who have been consecrated will indeed become outcasts;
the path leading to the gods will no longer appear to you,
for the path leading to the gods will be hidden from you."
"Therefore, we take refuge in the Blessed One alone, so that we may reach the end of the year in safety"—thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 20.
He said: "Twelve vital essences indeed depart from one who has been consecrated.
A consecrated person must not offer the Agnihotra oblation, nor should he perform the Full Moon sacrifice."
One should dwell in this [world] by means of the New Moon sacrifice;
one should not perform the sacrifice to the ancestors.
One should not go to that place which one desires to reach with the mind;
one should not sacrifice with the *iṣṭi* offering;
nor should one speak at random with speech.
(GBr_1,3.21j) He should not engage in sexual intercourse;
(GBr_1,3.21k) he should not consume food according to his desire; (GBr_1,3.21l) he should not sacrifice with the animal sacrifice.
One should not go where one cannot see with the eye;
one should wear a black antelope skin and wear a tuft of hair on the crown of the head.
One should clench the fists;
one should extend the three fingers beginning with the thumbs;
one should grasp a deer horn.
(GBr_1,3.21s) He should rub himself with that.
(GBr_1,3.21t) Now, if the speech of one who is consecrated should fail, or if his fists should be opened, he should mutter these [verses]. 21.

(GBr_1,3.22a) May the Agnihotra and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice, both becoming fulfillers of desires, enter me from the front toward the back along with the earth. (GBr_1,3.22b) May the Vāsativī and the Amāvāsya sacrifice, both [becoming fulfillers of desires], [enter me] from behind toward the front—in the same manner. (GBr_1,3.22c) May the Mind and the Pitṛyajña sacrifice, both [becoming fulfillers of desires], [enter me] from the right toward the north—in the same manner.
(GBr_1,3.22d) "And speech and the *iṣṭi* sacrifice from the north, both moving toward the south"—this is the same [as before].
(GBr_1,3.22e) "And semen and food from here upward, both"—this is the same [as before].
(GBr_1,3.22f) "And the eye and the *paśubandha* sacrifice from yonder downward, both becoming fulfillers of desires for the sake of imperishability."

"He has entered into union"—thus indeed, he who is consecrated places treasures within himself; for him there is no affliction whatsoever, nor does he encounter any obstacle to the sacrifice; he strikes down repeated death and transcends rebirth.
"He who knows this has freedom of movement in all worlds; he shines. "And he who, knowing thus, undergoes initiation," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 22.

Now, if the wife of one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should become pregnant, he should have a mess of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) prepared in the milk of a cow that has recently calved and whose calf is of the same color as herself; having poured clarified butter over it, removed it from the fire, drawn it out, and uttered the *abhihiṅkāra* over it, he should add the ritual residues (*saṃpāta*) from the rites for detecting pregnancy and for producing a male child, and she herself should eat it.
Food is indeed semen;
the *hiṃkāra* is the male, for thus it is said: "May the wife of one who has been consecrated obtain a son from that which belongs to the consecrated."
"One should sacrifice by this very same procedure"—this is the Brāhmaṇa. 23.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_1,4.1a) Om. This indeed is the sacrifice, which is he who blows here.
(GBr_1,4.1b) Those who undergo initiation for the sake of the year-long rite seek after him.
(GBr_1,4.1c) Among them, the master of the house is the first to be initiated.
This world, indeed, is the Gṛhapati;
for upon this world everything here is established,
and upon the Gṛhapati all those engaged in the sacrificial session (*sattra*) are established.
Verily, they undergo consecration for the sake of stability, so that he may find firm standing.

(GBr_1,4.2a) Then he consecrates the Brahman priest. The moon is indeed the Brahman with respect to the divine, and the mind with respect to the self. (GBr_1,4.2b) By means of the mind itself, he thus joins together the plants.
(GBr_1,4.2c) Therefore, whoever knows the plants, he alone is the Brahman-plant.
He unites it with this verse.
Therefore, no other person should undergo initiation between these two;
for if another were to undergo initiation between these two, he would destroy this world with the plants.
(GBr_1,4.2g) They would indeed become parched; therefore, no other person should undergo initiation between these two. // 2 //
(GBr_1,4.3a) Then he consecrates the Udgātṛ.
(GBr_1,4.3b) Āditya, indeed, is the Udgātṛ with respect to the divine; the eye is [the Udgātṛ] with respect to the self.
(GBr_1,4.3c) Parjanya is Āditya.
From Parjanya rain is born;
rain alone thereby sustains the plants.
Therefore, no other person should undergo initiation between these two.
If another were to undergo initiation between these two, he would cause this world to be destroyed by rain;
they would indeed be subject to drought.
Therefore, no one else should undergo initiation between these two. 3.
(GBr_1,4.4a) Then he consecrates the Hotṛ priest.
(GBr_1,4.4b) Agni is indeed the Hotṛ with respect to the divine; Speech is [the Hotṛ] with respect to the self.
(GBr_1,4.4c) Food is rain.
He thus firmly unites both speech and Agni with food;
therefore, no other person should undergo initiation between these two.
If another were to undergo initiation between these two, he would destroy this world with food.
They would surely be hungry;
therefore, no other person should undergo consecration between these two [days]. 4.
(GBr_1,4.5a) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ consecrates the Adhvaryu.
(GBr_1,4.5b) Vāyu indeed is the Adhvaryu with respect to the divine; Prāṇa is [the Adhvaryu] with respect to the self.
(GBr_1,4.5c) Rain is food.
He thus joins together the wind and that vital breath with food;
therefore, no other should undergo initiation between these two.
If another were to undergo initiation between these two, he would destroy this world by means of the vital breath.
They would surely be subject to death;
therefore, no other person should undergo initiation between these two.
(GBr_1,4.6a) Then he consecrates the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin for the Brahman;
(GBr_1,4.6b) then he consecrates the Prastotṛ for the Udgātṛ;
(GBr_1,4.6c) then he consecrates the Maitrāvaruṇa for the Hotṛ.
Then the Neṣṭṛ consecrates the Pratiprasthātṛ for the Adhvaryu;
he follows him.
Indeed, the others conform to the arrangement of these nine.
There are indeed nine vital breaths; by means of the vital breaths the sacrifice is extended. Then he consecrates the Potṛ for the Brahman.
(GBr 1,4.6j) Then he consecrates the Pratihartṛ for the Udgātṛ;
(GBr 1,4.6k) then he consecrates the Acchāvāka for the Hotṛ;
(GBr 1,4.6l) then the Unnetṛ consecrates the Neṣṭṛ for the Adhvaryu.
He initiates him [the sacrificer] accordingly; then he initiates the Brahman at the Āgnīdhra fire-altar;
then he initiates the Subrahmaṇya for the Udgātṛ.
(GBr_1,4.6p) Then he initiates the Grāvastut for the Hotṛ.
(GBr_1,4.6q) Then another person—either a *snātaka* or a student (*brahmacārī*)—initiates him.
(GBr_1,4.6r) "One who is already purified should not purify," they say.
This is that initiation in its proper sequence.

Those who undergo initiation in this manner do not find atonement for the Sattrins even while they are about to be initiated. "The security and prosperity of those [Sattrins] is secured in that half [of the year] in which they are initiated," so says the Brāhmaṇa. // 6 //
By means of faith, the gods fashioned the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering; from Aditi, the *prāyaṇīyā*; from Soma, the purchase (*kraya*); and from Viṣṇu, the guest-offering (*ātithya*).
From Āditya [comes] the Pravargya; from Svadhā the Upasads;
from Agni and Soma the day of fasting.
(GBr_1,4.7g) To the gods who travel at dawn, the morning litany; (GBr_1,4.7h) to the Vasus, the morning pressing;
(GBr_1,4.7i) to the Rudras, the midday pressing.
The third pressing belongs to the Ādityas;
the purificatory bath belongs to Varuṇa; the concluding offering belongs to Aditi.
To Mitra and Varuṇa, the Anūbandhyā cow;
to Tvaṣṭṛ, the victim for Tvaṣṭṛ;
to the goddesses, the Devikās, the oblations for the deities.
(GBr_1,4.7p) From desire [comes] the ten-night sacrifice;
(GBr_1,4.7q) from the world of heaven, the Udavasānīyā offering;
(GBr_1,4.7r) that, indeed, is the birth of the Agniṣṭoma.
"He who thus knows this birth of the Agniṣṭoma, having become possessed of the self and possessed of the world through the Agniṣṭoma, goes even unto the gods," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, when they sacrifice with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, they sacrifice to Faith (*śraddhā*) alone as the divine deity;
Faith the goddess becomes their deity.
Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as Faith the goddess.
Now, when they sacrifice with the Prāyaṇīyā offering, they sacrifice to the goddess Aditi as the deity; they become the goddess Aditi as their deity,
and those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the goddess Aditi.
Now, when they proceed to the purchase, they thereby worship the divine Soma as the deity;
Soma, the god, becomes their deity. Those who proceed in this manner attain union with and residence in the same world as the divine Soma.
Now, when they perform the guest-offering (*ātithyā*), they worship the god Viṣṇu as the deity;
Viṣṇu the god becomes their deity.
Those who undertake this attain union with the god Viṣṇu and residence in the same world as him.
Now, when they undertake the Pravargya rite, they worship the divine Āditya as the deity;
Āditya becomes the divine deity. Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as the divine Āditya.
Now, when they perform the *upasads*, they worship the goddess *svadhā* as the deity;
they become the goddess *svadhā* as their deity.
Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the goddess *svadhā*.
Now, when they enter upon the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*), they worship the two deities Agni and Soma as the gods.
Agni and Soma become the two deities.
Those who enter upon this attain union with and residence in the same world as the two deities Agni and Soma.
Now, when they perform the morning recitation (*prātaranuvāka*), they worship the deities who travel at dawn;
the gods who travel at dawn become their deities.
Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the gods who travel at dawn.
Now, when they proceed to the morning pressing, they worship the Vasus as the deities;
the Vasus become the deities.
Those who proceed to this attain union with and residence in the same world as the Vasu gods.
Now, when they approach the midday libation, they worship the Rudras as the deity;
the Rudras become the gods as the deity.
Those who approach this attain union with and residence in the same world as the Rudra gods.
Now, when they proceed to the third pressing, they worship the Ādityas, the gods, as the deity.
The Ādityas become the gods who are the deity.
Those who proceed to this attain union with and residence in the same world as the Āditya gods.
Now, when they go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), they worship the god Varuṇa as the deity;
Varuṇa the god becomes their deity.
Those who perform this rite attain union with and residence in the same world as the god Varuṇa.
Now, when they sacrifice with the *udayanīyā* offering, they sacrifice to the goddess Aditi as the deity;
Aditi the goddess becomes their deity.
Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the goddess Aditi.
Now, when they sacrifice with the *anūbandhyā* cow, they sacrifice to the two gods, Mitra and Varuṇa, as the deities.
Mitra and Varuṇa become the two gods, the deities.
Those who perform this rite attain union with and residence in the same world as the two gods, Mitra and Varuṇa.
Now, when they sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, they sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ as the deity;
Tvaṣṭṛ the god becomes their deity.
Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as the god Tvaṣṭṛ.

Now, when they proceed with the Devikā oblations which take place during the Upasad days—namely Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu—the divine Devikās are the deities. Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as these divine Devikā deities.
Furthermore, when they undertake the ten-night Atirātra sacrifice, they worship whichever deity they desire.
Desire is the god, the deity they become; they attain union with and residence in the same world as the god Desire for those who undertake this.
Now, when they sacrifice with the *udavasānīyā* offering, they sacrifice to the heavenly world itself as the god, the deity.
Heaven is the world, the god, and the deity. Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as heaven, the world, the god, and the deity.
This, indeed, is the birth of the Agniṣṭoma.
He who thus knows this birth of the Agniṣṭoma, having indeed attained that Agniṣṭoma, becomes firmly established in the heavenly world.
He who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle; having become one with the self and the same world as the Agniṣṭoma, he goes even unto the gods—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 8.
(GBr 1,4.9a) By means of day and night, the gods fashioned the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra;
(GBr 1,4.9b) from the half-months, the Caturviṃśa day;
(GBr 1,4.9c) from Brahman, the Abhiplava.
From the Kṣatra [comes] the Pṛṣṭhya;
from Agni, the Abhijit;
from the Waters, the Svarasāmans.
From Sūrya [they go] to the Viṣuvat; the Svarasāmans have been declared as those that turn back;
from Indra [they go] to the Viśvajit.
The Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods] have been declared;
the Gava and Āyus [one-day rites] belong to Mitra and Varuṇa;
the ten-night rite belongs to the Viśvedevas.
From the quarters comes the ten-night period, the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite;
from these worlds comes the *chandoma* three-day rite;
from the year comes the tenth day.
The Mahāvrata of Prajāpati;
the Udayanīya Atirātra from the heavenly world;
that indeed is the birth of the year.
"He who thus knows this birth of the year, having become one with the year in soul and one with its world, goes even unto the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 9.
Now, when they perform the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, they sacrifice to the two deities, the gods Day and Night.
They become the gods Day and Night;
those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the two gods, Day and Night.
Now, when they undertake the twenty-fourth day, they worship the half-months as the deities;
the half-months become the gods who are the deities.
Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as those gods who are the half-months.
Now, when they perform the *abhiplava* [six-day period], they sacrifice to the god Brahmā as the deity;
they become the god Brahmā as the deity.
Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the god Brahmā.
Now, when they perform the *pṛṣṭhya* [rite], they worship the divine Kṣatra as the deity;
they become the divine Kṣatra as the deity.
Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the divine Kṣatra.
Now, when they perform the Abhijit sacrifice, they worship Agni as the deity;
Agni becomes the god and the deity. Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as Agni, the god.
(GBr_1,4.10p) Now, when they perform the Svarasāman chants, they sacrifice to the goddesses as deities; the waters become the goddesses as deities.
(GBr_1,4.10q) Those who perform this attain union with and residence in the same world as the goddesses, the waters.
(GBr_1,4.10r) Then, when they perform the Viṣuvat day, they sacrifice to the Sun as the god-deity.
The Sun is the deity; they become the deities.
They attain union with and residence in the same world as the divine Sun, those who undertake this.
Thus have been declared the Svarasāmans in their regular order.
Now, when they perform the Viśvajit sacrifice, they worship the god Indra as the deity;
they become Indra, the god, as their deity.
Those who perform this attain union with the god Indra and residence in the same world as him.
The *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [six-day periods] have been explained.
Now, when they perform the *gavām ayana* and *āyuṣaḥ ayana*, they worship the two deities Mitra and Varuṇa;
Mitra and Varuṇa become the two deities.
(GBr_1,4.10bb) Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as the two gods, Mitra and Varuṇa.
(GBr_1,4.10cc) Now, when they undertake the ten-night rite, they worship all the gods as their deity. (GBr_1,4.10dd) All the gods thus become their deity.
(GBr_1,4.10ee) Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as all the gods.
(GBr_1,4.10ff) Now, when they undertake the six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭhya* rite of the ten-night sacrifice, they worship the goddesses, the quarters, as the deities;
the quarters become the goddesses, the deities.
Those who undertake this [sacrificial session] attain union with and residence in the same world as the goddesses of the quarters.
Now, when they undertake the three-day period consisting of the *chandomas*, they sacrifice to these very worlds as the gods and deities;
for these worlds become the gods and deities.
Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as these worlds and these gods.
Now, when they undertake the tenth day, they sacrifice to the year itself as the god and the deity;
the year becomes the god and the deity.
Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as the god Saṃvatsara.
Now, when they undertake the Mahāvrata, they worship Prajāpati himself as the deity;
they become Prajāpati, the god, as their deity.
(GBr_1,4.10qq) Those who undertake this attain union with and residence in the same world as Prajāpati, the god.
(GBr_1,4.10rr) Now, when they undertake the *udayanīya* Atirātra sacrifice, they worship the heavenly world itself as the god and the deity.
(GBr_1,4.10ss) They become the heavenly world, the god, and the deity.

Those who practice this attain union with and residence in the same world as the god of heaven. This, indeed, is the birth of the year. He who knows this birth of the year attains that very year and becomes firmly established in the heavenly world.
"He who knows this becomes established through offspring and cattle; having become one with the year, with its own self, and with its world, he goes even unto the gods—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 10.

(GBr_1,4.11a) This very Saṃvatsara is established both with respect to the divine and with respect to the self. (GBr_1,4.11b) He who thus knows this Saṃvatsara as established both with respect to the divine and with respect to the self finds a firm foundation.
(GBr_1,4.11c) He who knows thus finds a firm foundation through offspring and cattle. // 11 //
This very year, indeed, is composed of the *bṛhatī* metre:
two syllables are the two six-day periods of the days; two are the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [six-day periods];
[and] the *gavām ayana* and *āyus* [twelve-day periods], and the ten-night period.
Thus, indeed, they amount to thirty-six;
the cow has thirty-six cuttings,
and the Bṛhatī meter consists of thirty-six syllables.
The heavenly world indeed belongs to the Bṛhatī;
by means of the Bṛhatī, the gods sacrifice in the heavenly world;
through the Bṛhatī, he becomes firmly established in the heavenly world.
He who knows thus becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. 12.
This very year indeed consists of three *mahāvrata*s:
there is a *mahāvrata* on the twenty-fourth day, a *mahāvrata* on the *viṣuvat* day, and the *mahāvrata* itself is the [third] *mahāvrata*.
Those of old who knew this thus performed the sacrifice with these three *mahāvrata*s.
They were radiant, speakers of truth, and firm in their vows.

If those who today approach this [fire-altar] in such a manner were to do so as an unbaked clay vessel would dissolve when water is poured upon it, even so would the sacrificers perish as they ascend over it.
However, for one who knows thus, that which was conquered and secured by him through truth, austerity, and his vow remains his own. 13.

"Now, if one should approach the Mahāvrata after having approached or not approached the twenty-fourth day, how does it become free from injury? One should say: 'By means of that very Atirātra which they perform before the Viṣuvat.
The Pṛṣṭhya is fashioned from the Abhiplava."
From the *pṛṣṭhya* comes the *abhijit*; from the *abhijit*, the *svarasāman*s;
from the *svarasāman*s, the *viṣuvat*.
From the Viṣuvat come the Svarasāmans;
from the Svarasāmans comes the Viśvajit;
from the Viśvajit come the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods].
(GBr_1,4.14j) From the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [six-day periods] come the *gavām ayana* and the *āyus*.
(GBr_1,4.14k) From the *gavām ayana* and the *āyus* comes the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*).
(GBr_1,4.14l) From the ten-night rite comes the *mahāvrata*.

(GBr_1,4.14m) After the Mahāvrata comes the Udayanīya Atirātra. (GBr_1,4.14n) The Udayanīya Atirātra is for the sake of the heavenly world, for the sake of food, and for the sake of firm standing. // 14 //
"Now, if one were to approach the Mahāvrata without having approached the twenty-fourth day that precedes the Viṣuvat, how does it become free from injury?
"One should say: 'By means of that very Atirātra which they perform before the Viṣuvat.
"The Pṛṣṭhya is fashioned from the Abhiplava."
From the *pṛṣṭhya* comes the *abhijit*; from the *abhijit*, the *svarasāman*s;
from the *svarasāman*s, the *viṣuvat*.
From the Viṣuvat comes the Svarasāman;
from the Svarasāmans comes the Viśvajit;
from the Viśvajit come the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava.

(GBr_1,4.15j) By means of the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [six-day periods], one reaches the *gavāmayana*; (GBr_1,4.15k) by means of the *gavāmayana*, the ten-night period (*daśarātra*); (GBr_1,4.15l) now, the *mahāvrata* did not stand firm for the gods, thinking: "How has he reached the *viṣuvat* day with upward-moving *stomas*, while I am left with those that turn back?"
Those gods desired,
"Let us find that sacrificial rite with its ascending stomas by which we may attain this day.
Thereupon, they beheld this twelve-night sacrifice with ascending stomas.
They brought it; they sacrificed with it;
then it stood apart from them.
The Great Vow stands firm for him; he finds support, he finds support through offspring and cattle—he who knows thus. 15.
"Now, if one were to undertake the Mahāvrata day without having undertaken the twenty-fourth day leading up to the Viṣuvat, how does it become free from injury?
"One should say: 'By means of that very Atirātra which they perform before the Viṣuvat.
Regarding this, they say: "How many days of the year are directed forward, and how many are directed backward?"
(GBr_1,4.16d) Those which they perform only once are directed away;
(GBr_1,4.16e) but those which they perform again and again are directed hitherward—thus indeed should they meditate upon them.
(GBr_1,4.16f) For they conform to the recurrence of the two six-day periods. // 16 //
"Now, if one were to approach the Mahāvrata without having approached the twenty-fourth day, and without having approached the Viṣuvat, how does it become free from injury?
"One should say: 'By means of that very Atirātra which they perform before the Viṣuvat.
"They perform the Abhiplava first, prior to the Viṣuvat."
The *pṛṣṭhya* comes after;
the *abhiplava* is the father and the *pṛṣṭhya* is the son.
Therefore, in their earlier years, sons depend upon their father.
They perform the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] before the *viṣuvat*, and the *abhiplava* after it.
The *abhiplava* is indeed the father and the *pṛṣṭhya* is the son;
therefore, in his final stage of life, the father lives off his sons—he who knows thus.
This has also been stated in a *ṛc*:

"A hundred autumns stand before us, O gods, during which you have ordained the aging of our bodies; where sons become fathers—do not harm us in the midst of our journey toward old age" (*Ṛgveda* 1.89.9).
Indeed, his sons depend upon him as a father during the earlier stage of life, and he, having known this, depends upon his sons as a father during the final stage of life. 17.
Now, this is the Great Bird (*mahāsuparṇa*).

Those six months which they undertake from the equinox (*viṣuvat*) onwards constitute its right wing; and those six [months] which they undertake subsequently in reverse order constitute its left wing.
The self (*ātman*) of the year is indeed the equinox (*viṣuvant*); the limbs and the two wings [are the rest].
For where there is the self, there are the wings; and where there are the wings, there is the self.
"Indeed, the self does not exceed the two wings, nor do the two wings exceed the self.
Thus, one should say regarding this: "It is known thus by some of the later [teachers], and by others of the later; and indeed by some of the earlier, and by others of the earlier. 18. [Ed. būyāt]
Regarding this they say: "Since the year consists of twelve months, how then can one obtain this day? [The answer is: "One obtains it through the Vaiṣuvata day.
"Is it known to both those who are behind and those who are ahead?
He should reply: "It is known to both those who are behind and those who are ahead."
The central day of the year (*viṣuvān*) is indeed the self (*ātman*) of the year, and the months are its limbs.
For where there is the self, there are the limbs; and where there are the limbs, there is the self.
"Indeed, the limbs do not exceed the self, nor does the self exceed the limbs.
Thus, indeed, this is known among some as "of the later days" and among others as "of the earlier days"; one should say, "both of the later and of the earlier. This, indeed, is the year. 19.
Regarding this they say: "How is it that the *abhiplava* periods have light on both sides, while the *pṛṣṭhya* period has light on only one side?
These worlds indeed have light on both sides—by means of fire here and by means of the sun yonder.
For he who burns as if crushing everything is the light of these [worlds].
(GBr_1,4.20d) Indeed, these two divine wheels, established upon the *pṛṣṭhya*, roll along crushing evil.
(GBr_1,4.20e) Therefore, if one proclaims the evil of those who know this and have been consecrated, these very divine wheels cut off his head.
(GBr_1,4.20f) The ten-night period is the support.
"The *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* [sacrifices] are the two wheels;
the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*) is the axle-socket. One should perform the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* as the framework," so said Vāsyu.
"One should transpose the *stotras* and *śastras* of those two."

(GBr_1,4.20j) He who causes them to circulate—therefore these vital breaths (*prāṇas*), though diverse, dwell together in this person through their single rising within the body. If he were not to cause them to circulate, the sacrificer would surely be liable to die. (GBr_1,4.20k) For he indeed is liable to die who is blind or deaf.
(GBr_1,4.20l) Nine *agniṣṭoma* sacrifices are completed in each month.
There are indeed nine vital breaths; by means of the vital breaths the sacrifice is extended;
there are twenty-one *ukthya* chants.
There is one Ukthya and one Ṣoḍaśin; the Ukthya is indeed food,
and the Ṣoḍaśin is virility.
Having ascended in that manner, they ascend to the heavenly world. 20.
(GBr 1.4.21a) Now, therefore, follows the ascending of the days.
(GBr 1.4.21b) By means of the *prāyaṇīya* Atirātra, they ascend to the *udayanīya* Atirātra; by means of the twenty-four-fold [Stoma], to the Mahāvrata;
(GBr 1.4.21c) by means of the Abhiplava, to the subsequent Abhiplava.
By means of the *pṛṣṭhya* [shadaha], one reaches the further *pṛṣṭhya*;
by means of the *abhijit*, the further *abhijit*; and by means of the *svarasāman* days, the further *svarasāmans*.

"Now we shall attain this day," they say—that is, the *vaiṣuvata* day. Regarding the question, "Is it of the days preceding or of those following?", one should say: "Of both the preceding and the following."
This, indeed, is that year.
(GBr_1,4.22a) Now, therefore, follows the succession of the days.
(GBr_1,4.22b) The *prāyaṇīya* *atirātra* leads on to the twenty-fourth day.
(GBr_1,4.22c) The twenty-fourth day leads on to the *abhiplava*.
The *abhiplava* leads to the *pṛṣṭhya*;
the *pṛṣṭhya* to the *abhijit*;
and the *abhijit* to the *svarasāmans*.
The Svarasāmans [lead] to the Viṣuvat;
the Viṣuvat [leads] to the Svarasāmans;
the Svarasāmans [lead] to the Viśvajit.
The Viśvajit [is preceded] by the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava;
the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava by the Gavāyuṣī;
the Gavāyuṣī by the Daśarātra.
The ten-night rite leads to the Mahāvrata;
the Mahāvrata leads to the concluding Atirātra;
the concluding Atirātra is for the sake of the heavenly world, for the acquisition of food, and for firm establishment.
[Ed. 'tiratraḥ] (GBr_1,4.23a) The Ādityas and the Aṅgirasas indeed contended for the world of heaven, saying, "We shall first go to heaven; we shall first go!
(GBr_1,4.23b) Those Ādityas, by means of light Sāmans, four Stomas, and two Pṛṣṭhya-stotras, leaped up to the world of heaven.
Because they leaped forward (*abhyaplavanta*), it is therefore called the *Abhiplava*.
Following after them, the Aṅgirases touched the heavenly world with heavy Sāmans, with all the *stomas*, and with all the *pṛṣṭhya* chants;
because they touched it (*abhyaspṛśanta*), it is therefore called the *Spṛśya*.
Although this very [sacrifice] is actually tangible, they call it "pṛṣṭhya" by an indirect name;
for the gods, as it were, prefer the indirect and dislike the direct.
