The pṛṣṭhya was fashioned from the abhiplava.
From the *pṛṣṭhya* comes the *abhijit*; from the *abhijit*, the *svarasāman*s;
from the *svarasāman*s, the *viṣuvat*.
After the Viṣuvat day come the Svarasāman days; after the Svarasāmans comes the Viśvajit;
after the Viśvajit come the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods].
The *gavāmayana* and the *āyus* sacrifices consist of the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* periods;
the *daśarātra* consists of the *gavāmayana* and the *āyus*.
Indeed, these are the forests of the sacrifice, the shavings of the sacrifice.

Between every hundred of those chariots there is an interval; just as those who have entered the forests, having overcome hunger and thirst, float along while destroying evil, even so do these float along who approach [the sacrifice] knowing [this].
But those who approach it unknowingly, they [float] like one from one stream to another, from one shallow place to another.
"From the equal they go to the equal, from happiness to happiness, from fearlessness to fearlessness"—thus indeed do we reach the completion of the year; so says the Brāhmaṇa. 23.
Kausurubindu, the son of Kausāmbeya, was about to depart. He dwelt as a student with Uddālaka Āruṇi.
The teacher asked him: "Boy, how many days of the year did your father consider there to be?
"How many indeed? he replied.
"Ten," he said;
"Or rather ten," he said;
"The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is the Virāj."
"But how many are there? "Nine," he said. "Yes, nine," he replied.
"There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*); by means of the vital breaths the sacrifice is extended.
But how many are there really?"
"Eight," he said.
"Indeed, eight," he said.
"The Gāyatrī has eight syllables."
"The Gāyatrī is the sacrifice.
"But how many [feet] does it have? "Seven," he said.
"Seven indeed," he said,
"for there are seven meters; by means of the meters, the sacrifice is performed."
"But how many are there, indeed? "Six," he said.
"There are six, indeed," he said.
"There are six seasons;
[it is] for the attainment of the seasons.
"But how many are there really?"
"Five," he said;
"five indeed," he said;
"the *paṅkti* meter has five feet."
"The sacrifice consists of five parts.
"But how many [parts] are there?
"Four," he said.
"Or rather, there are four," he said. "There are indeed four Vedas; by means of the Vedas, the sacrifice is performed."
"But how many are there?
"Three," he said.
"Indeed, there are three," he said.
The sacrifice is indeed threefold;
the sacrifice is extended by means of the pressings (savana).
"But how many [pressings] are there? he asked.
"Two," he said.
"Two indeed," he said.
"For man has two feet."
The person has two foundations.
The sacrifice, indeed, is the person.
But how many [foundations] does it actually have?
"It is one," he said. "Or rather, it is one," he said.
"Day after day, indeed, [it constitutes] the entire year. 24.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_1,5.1a) Om. The Abhiplava is a six-day period.
(GBr_1,5.1b) For there are six days: Jyotis, Go, Āyus, Go, Āyus, Jyotis.
(GBr_1,5.1c) The Abhiplava is a five-day period.
For there are indeed five days; for that which is the first day is also the last day,
and there is the four-day *abhiplava*.

For there are four *stomas*: the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, and the *ekaviṃśa*. The *abhiplava* is a three-day period (*tryaha*) consisting of three repetitions: *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*.
The *abhiplava* is a two-day rite;
for there are indeed two *sāmans*, namely the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*.
The *abhiplava* is also a one-day rite.
For it is by means of the *stomas* of the one-day sacrifice that [the rite] is extended;
twelve *stotras* remain over from the four *ukthya* offerings;
that is the seventh, the *agniṣṭoma*.
"In this way, indeed, seven Agniṣṭomas are completed in a month," so says the Brāhmaṇa. // 1 //
(GBr_1,5.2a) Now, therefore, follows the firm footing. (GBr_1,5.2b) Those who consecrate themselves for the year-long sacrifice cross over the ocean.
(GBr_1,5.2c) For them, the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra is indeed the landing-place.
"For they cross by means of a ford;
just as one might cross the ocean by means of a ford, so is that.
The twenty-fourth day is a firm footing, like a place where the water reaches the armpits or the throat, from which one may rest and then swim across."
The *abhiplava* is for swimming;
the *pṛṣṭhya* is for swimming with a support.
The *pratiṣṭhābhijit* is like a place where one might rest before swimming—whether it be at chest-deep water or neck-deep water; such is that [sacrifice].
The first Svarasāman is one whose navel is burnt; the second is one whose knee is burnt; the third is one whose ankle is burnt.
The island is the support; it is the Viṣuvat day. It is like that place where, having been scorched up to the armpits or up to the neck, they would rest before plunging into the water.
The first Svarasāman below [the Viṣuvat] is as if scorched at the ankles; the second is as if scorched at the knees.

The third [day] is the *nīvidagdha*. The *gādha* is the foundation, the *viśvajit*; it is like that which is burnt at the armpit or burnt at the throat—that from which, having rested, they would swim across. The *pṛṣṭhya* is to be swum across; the *abhiplava* is to be swum across; the *gavāyus* are to be swum across; the *daśarātra* is to be swum across.

The firm foundation is the Mahāvrata, just as a ford that is knee-deep or armpit-deep, from which one may rest before bathing; such is that [rite]. For them, the Udayanīya Atirātra is indeed a *tīrtha* (ford), for they emerge by means of a ford.
(GBr_1,5.2v) It is just as if they were to draw water from the ocean by means of a watering place; such is that.
(GBr_1,5.2w) Now Śvetaketu Āruṇeya used to say, "I shall indeed consecrate myself for a year.
(GBr_1,5.2x) His father, looking up at his face, said, "Do you know, O long-lived one, the ford and the foundation of the year?"
"He knows"—this is what the Brāhmaṇa says, for he who knows this spoke thus. 2.
The person, indeed, is the year.
His two feet are the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, for with the two feet they set out; that which is white in them is the form of the day.
That which is black is the form of the night;
the nails are the form of the stars; the body hair is the form of the herbs and trees.
The two thighs are the twenty-fourth day;
the chest is the *abhiplava*;
the back is the *pṛṣṭhya*.
The head is indeed the *trivṛt* (threefold), for the head consists of three things: skin, bone, and marrow, together with the brain.
The neck is the *pañcadaśa* (fifteenfold), for there are fourteen ribs on this side;
the fifteenth is strength.
Therefore, with these minute [channels], he carries a heavy burden;
therefore, there are fifteen neck-vertebrae,
and the chest consists of seventeen.
There are eight other collarbones and eight others; the chest is the seventeenth.
Therefore, the chest is seventeenfold.
The belly is twenty-onefold.
For there are indeed twenty *kuntāpa* hymns within his belly; the belly is the twenty-first.
Therefore, the belly is the twenty-first, and the two sides are the thirty-third.
There are thirteen other ribs; there are thirteen other sides. Because of that, the sides are the *triṇava* [stoma];
the backbone is the *trayastrimśa* [stoma].
For there are indeed thirty-two vertebrae (*pṛṣṭīkuṇḍīla*) in this [body],
and the backbone (*anūka*) is the thirty-third;
therefore, the backbone is the thirty-third.
Of that [year], this very right arm is the Abhijit; these three vital breaths in the right side are the Svarasāmans;
the self is the Viṣuvat.
Of that [sacrifice], these three vital breaths on the left side are the Svarasāmans in the forward direction; this left arm of his is the Viśvajit;
the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods] have been declared.
The two downward vital breaths are the *gavāyus* chant;
the limbs are the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*);
the mouth is the *mahāvrata*.
(GBr_1,5.3kk) His two hands are indeed the Udayanīya Atirātra;
for by means of the two hands they rise up. 3.
Man, indeed, is the year.
His out-breath is the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra,
for by means of the out-breath they set forth.
The day is one that must be commenced with speech;
whatever one undertakes, it is speech that undertakes it; by means of speech alone one undertakes it.
(GBr_1,5.4g) His very right hand is the Abhiplava.
(GBr_1,5.4h) Of that [hand], this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing. (GBr_1,5.4i) It is in the place of the Gāyatrī.
Therefore, this [meter] is the smallest for her;
this is its morning pressing, this is its midday pressing, and this is its third pressing,
in the place of the *triṣṭubh*.
Therefore, this [earth] is his most excellent [form];
this is his morning pressing, this is his midday pressing, and this is his third pressing,
in the abode of the Jagatī.
Therefore, this [earth] is the most excellent of these two.
Of it, this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing;
it is established in the station of the *paṅkti* metre.
The *paṅkti* is indeed broad;
therefore, among these [metres], it is the broadest.
Of it, this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
In the abode of Virāj is food; for prosperity is indeed food,
and Virāj is the eating of food.
For the attainment of food and prosperity;
therefore, this [earth] is the most excellent of them.
Of that [Soma], this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
In the abode of the *atichandas*,
for the *atichandas* is indeed the abode of the meters;
therefore, this plank is the widest.
Of that [year], this is the morning pressing, this is the midday pressing, and this is the third pressing.
This is the abhiplava from here; this is the abhiplava from there; this is the self from here; the pṛṣṭhya is from there.
The abhiplava moves back and forth.
The *pṛṣṭhya* chant stands as it were; for thus one stands with the limbs,
and one stands with the self.
Of that [sacrifice], this very right ear is the Abhijit. Of that [ear], what is white in the right eye is the first Svarasāman;
what is black is the second.
That which is the white circle is the third;
the nose is the Viṣuvat day; the first downward-facing Svarasāman is indeed the [black] circle; that which is black is the second.
That which is white is the third; its left ear is the Viśvajit;
the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [sacrifices] have been declared.
The two downward breaths are the Gāyatrī and the Āyuṣ;
the limbs are the Daśarātra;
the mouth is the Mahāvrata.
Of that [sacrifice], the Udayanīya Atirātra is indeed the udāna;
for by means of the udāna they rise up. 4.
The person, indeed, is the year.
"Person" is one [name];
"year" is one [name].
In this regard, that is equal:
two days and nights are one year;
these are the two vital breaths in a person.
In this regard, it is equal:
there are three seasons of the year,
and these three vital breaths in a person.
In this regard, it is equal:
there are six seasons of the year,
and these six vital breaths in the person.
In this regard, it is equal to that:
there are seven seasons of the year,
and these seven vital breaths in a person.
In this regard, that is equal:
there are twelve months in a year,
and these twelve are the vital breaths in a person.
In this regard, it is equal:
there are thirteen months in a year,
and there are these thirteen vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person.
In this regard, it is equal:
there are twenty-four half-months in a year,
and this person consists of twenty-four parts.
Twenty finger-breadths and four finger-joints—
herein they are equal;
for there are twenty-six half-months in a year.
"This Puruṣa is the twenty-sixth;
the two supports are the twenty-sixth"—
in this regard, they are equal.
"There are indeed three hundred and sixty days and nights in a year;
there are just as many vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person. In this respect, they are equal."
There are seven hundred and twenty days and nights in a year;
there are exactly that many bones and marrow in a person. In this respect, they are equal.
"There are indeed one hundred and forty-four half-days and half-nights in a year;
so many, too, are the gross pieces of flesh in a person. In this respect, they are equal."
"There are indeed two hundred and eighty foot-days and foot-nights in a year;
so many, it is said, are the ligaments that bind a person.
In this respect, they are equal."
"Indeed, there are ten thousand and eight hundred muhūrtas in a year; there are exactly as many hair-pores on a person. In this respect, they are equal."
As many times as there are fifteen muhūrtas, so many are the prāṇas;
as many times as there are fifteen prāṇas, so many are the apānas;
as many times as there are fifteen apānas, so many are the vyānas.
(GBr_1,5.5ww) As many times as there are vyānas, fifteenfold, so many are the samānas;
(GBr_1,5.5xx) as many times as there are samānas, fifteenfold, so many are the udānas;
(GBr_1,5.5yy) as many times as there are udānas, fifteenfold, so many are these [etādīs].
As many as these [former] ones were, so many are these [present] ones; as many as these [present] ones are, so many are the pores of perspiration;
as many as the pores of perspiration are, so many are the paths for rapid movement.
(GBr_1,5.5ccc) As many as there are swift paths, so many are the pores of the skin;
(GBr_1,5.5ddd) as many as there are pores of the skin, fifteen times that many are the raindrops from a raining cloud;
(GBr_1,5.5eee) this is the measure of a hundred *krośas*.

This has also been stated in a *ṛc*: "Whether moving about elsewhere from his toil, walking, sitting, or even sleeping, how many hundreds of times does a person breathe in and breathes out in a single moment throughout his years? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8).
"And how many times does a person breathe in and breathes out in equal measure during the eight hundred *muhūrtas* that they say constitute a year, measured by days and nights?"—
thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 5.
"The equality of the year must be understood," Vāsyu used to say.
"They perform one *atirātra* sacrifice before the *viṣuvat* day and one after it. They perform fifty-three *agniṣṭoma*s before the *viṣuvat* day and fifty-three after it."
They perform one hundred and twenty *ukthya* rites before the *viṣuvat*, and one hundred and twenty after it;
they perform six *ṣoḍaśin* rites before the *viṣuvat*, and six after it; they perform thirty six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*) before the *viṣuvat*, and thirty after it.
This is the equality of the year.
He who knows this equality of the year becomes one with the year, attains its world, and merges with the gods—thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 6.
(GBr 1,5.7a) Now, therefore, the sequence of sacrifices:
(GBr 1,5.7b) the establishment of the fires;
(GBr 1,5.7c) from the establishment of the fires, the full-offering.
From the full oblation comes the Agnihotra;
from the Agnihotra come the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
from the New and Full Moon sacrifices comes the Āgrayaṇa.
From the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice come the Cāturmāsya sacrifices;
from the Cāturmāsya sacrifices comes the Paśubandha;
from the Paśubandha comes the Agniṣṭoma.
From the Agniṣṭoma [comes] the Rājasūya;
from the Rājasūya, the Vājapeya;
from the Vājapeya, the Aśvamedha.

(GBr_1,5.7m) From the horse sacrifice comes the human sacrifice; (GBr_1,5.7n) from the human sacrifice, the all-sacrifice; (GBr_1,5.7o) from the all-sacrifice, those sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees.
(GBr_1,5.7p) Those who were without sacrificial fees stood against those with sacrificial fees;
(GBr_1,5.7q) those without sacrificial fees stood against those with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee.
These, indeed, are the sequences of the sacrifice.
"He who thus knows these sequences of the sacrifice, having become one with the self and one with the world through the sacrifice, attains the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. // 7 //
Prajāpati desired, "May I attain infinity. He established the sacred fires and performed the full-oblation sacrifice;
he beheld only an end.
Having sacrificed with the Agnihotra, he saw only the end;
having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he saw only the end;
having sacrificed with the Āgrayaṇa, he saw only the end.
Having sacrificed with the Cāturmāsya offerings, he saw only the end;
having sacrificed with the Paśubandha, he saw only the end;
having sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma, he saw only the end.
Having sacrificed with the Rājasūya, he assumed the name "Rāja" (King).
He saw only the end;
having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, he assumed the name "Samrāj" (Sovereign).
He saw the very end;
having sacrificed with the Aśvamedha, he gave himself the name Svarāj;
he saw the very end.
Having sacrificed with the Puruṣamedha, he gave himself the name Virāj;
he saw only the end.
Having sacrificed with the Sarvamedha, he gave himself the name Sarvarāj.
He saw only an end.
Having sacrificed with Ahīna rites accompanied by sacrificial fees, he saw only an end. Having sacrificed with Ahīna rites without sacrificial fees, he saw only an end.
He performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) with *atirātra* rites at both ends;
he bestowed speech upon the *hotṛ*,
breath upon the *adhvaryu*, sight upon the *udgātṛ*, mind upon the *brahman*, his limbs upon the *hotraka*s, and his own self upon the members of the assembly (*sadasya*s).
(GBr_1,5.8y) Having thus given himself away for infinity, he attains infinity.
(GBr_1,5.8z) Therefore, with those sacrificial fees which he brought, he ransomed himself.
(GBr_1,5.8aa) For this reason, one should hasten with this Jyotiṣṭoma-Agniṣṭoma, which is a means of self-ransom, involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee and serving to pacify the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
"For he who departs without having performed the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice departs without having ransomed himself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(GBr_1,5.9a) "When those who sit for the year-long session undergo initiation for the sake of the year, how is it that their *agnihotra* remains uninterrupted?
(GBr_1,5.9b) "One should say: 'By means of the vow (*vrata*).
(GBr_1,5.9c) How is it that their *darśa* sacrifice remains uninterrupted?"
"One should say, 'With curds and with the sacrificial cake.
[Question: How does this become uninterrupted by the Full Moon sacrifice?
[Answer: One should say, 'With clarified butter and with the sacrificial cake.'"
"How is it that the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice is not omitted for them? "By means of the rice-pap offering to Soma," he should say.
"How is it that the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are not omitted for them?"
"One should say, 'With the curdled milk' (payasyā).
How is it that their animal sacrifice remains uninterrupted?
One should say, 'By means of both the animal and the sacrificial cake.'"
(GBr_1,5.9m) "How is it that their Soma sacrifice remains uninterrupted?
(GBr_1,5.9n) "By means of the cups," he should reply.
(GBr_1,5.9o) "How is it that their Gṛhamedha sacrifice remains uninterrupted?"
"He should say, 'With parched grains and mixed grain-offering' (dhānākarambhaiḥ).
[Question: How does the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) remain uninterrupted for them? [Answer: He should say, 'By means of the domestic fires (aupāsana). "
"How is their pairing uninterrupted?
"By the *hiṃkāra*," he should say.
"This is the union of the sacrificial rites within the year."

"He who thus knows this completion of the sacrificial rites within the year, having become possessed of the self and sharing the same world as the sacrifice, goes even unto the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 9.
The gods, indeed, consecrated themselves for a thousand years.

Of them, five hundred years had passed when this entire [ritual] was mastered—the *stomas*, the *pṛṣṭhas*, and the *śastras*. Those gods were as if distressed, saying, "We recognize that sacrificial rite which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice."
"For what man indeed could sacrifice for a thousand years?
Thus they perceived that [the syllable *om*] as the unfailing essence in the midst of the sacrifice;
by means of that unfailing essence, they perceived whatever differentiation existed within the Veda—whether in the *ṛc*, the *yajus*, the *sāman*, the peaceful, or the terrible.
(GBr_1,5.10g) These, indeed, are the five *vyāhṛtis*: *o śrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*, and *vauṣaṭ*.
(GBr_1,5.10h) Those gods said, "Come here! We recognize that sacrificial rite which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice.
(GBr_1,5.10i) "For what man is there who would sacrifice for a thousand years?"
(GBr_1,5.10j) Then they beheld this *Tāpaścita* as the direct path of the thousand-year sacrifice.
(GBr_1,5.10k) For those indeed are the *stomas*, those the *pṛṣṭhas*, and those the *śastras*.
(GBr_1,5.10l) He indeed undergoes the consecrations for twelve months, the *upasad*s for twelve months, and the soma-pressings for twelve months.
(GBr_1,5.10m) Now, in that he undergoes the consecrations for twelve months and the *upasad* rites for twelve months, by that he attains these two, Agni and Arka.
(GBr_1,5.10n) And in that he performs the soma-pressings for twelve months, by that he attains this Great Litany (*mahaduktha*).
(GBr_1,5.10o) Those gods said, "Come, let us seek to understand that sacrificial rite which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice."
"For what man indeed could sacrifice for a thousand years? Thus they perceived this year as the direct manifestation of the Tāpaścita;
for those same *stomas* become its [the year's] *pṛṣṭhas*, and those same [stomas] become its *śastras*.
Those gods said, "Let us strive for this: let us recognize that sacrificial rite which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice;
for what man indeed could perform it for a thousand years?
Thereupon, they perceived this twelve-day rite as the direct embodiment of the year.
For those indeed are the *stomas*, those the *pṛṣṭhas*, and those the *śastras*.
He indeed undergoes the twelve-day rite with initiations for twelve days, with *upasad* rites for twelve days, and with soma-pressings for twelve days.
Now, in that he undergoes the twelve-day rite with initiations for twelve days and with *upasad* rites for twelve days, by that he attains these two, Agni and Arka.
(GBr_1,5.10y) Now, as for the twelve days of soma-pressings, by means of them he obtains this Great Recitation (mahaduktha).
(GBr_1,5.10z) Those gods said, "Let us strive here; let us recognize that sacrificial rite which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice.
(GBr_1,5.10aa) "For what man indeed could sacrifice for a thousand years?"
(GBr_1,5.10bb) Then they perceived this Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha as the direct form of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha).
(GBr_1,5.10cc) For those same *stomas* are used, those same *pṛṣṭhas*, and those same *śastras*.
(GBr_1,5.10dd) Those gods were as if saying, "We recognize that sacrificial performance which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice."
"For what man indeed could sacrifice for a thousand years?
Thus they perceived this Viśvajit as the direct [completion] of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha;
for those same *stomas* are used, those same *pṛṣṭhas*, and those same *śastras*.
Those gods said, "Let us strive here; let us recognize that sacrificial rite which is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice.
For what man indeed could perform it for a thousand years? That very Viśvajit sacrifice is the counterpart of the thousand-year sacrifice.
"This Viśvajit is indeed Prajāpati of all creatures," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 10.

Prajāpati said to the person Nārāyaṇa, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! He replied, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! Thus indeed you address me. Even three times he said this. Then the Vasus healed him with the morning libation, the Rudras with the midday libation, and the Ādityas with the third libation.
"The sacrificial site itself is the remnant; 'the sacrificial site'—such is the blessing. Indeed, I know this regarding the sacrifice:

"The Vasus [attained] the morning pressing, the Rudras the midday pressing, and the Ādityas the third pressing; the sacrificial site itself is the remnant; 'the sacrificial site'—such is the blessing. Surely those who know such blessings would have you perform the sacrifice for them.

(GBr_1,5.11e) "Truly, these are ignorant when the Hotṛ does not know the Ṛgveda, the Adhvaryu does not know the Yajurveda, the Udgātṛ does not know the Sāmaveda, and the Brahman does not know the Bṛhaduktha and Aṅgiras hymns.
(GBr_1,5.11f) "Perform the sacrifice! Come now, I shall explain that to you:
(GBr_1,5.11g) how these days of recitation (*ukthāhāni*) become like a thread on a gem, or like a gem on a thread."
Therefore, one should appoint as Brahman-priest whoever is all-knowing.
For he who knows the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases is indeed the learned, all-knowing Brahman-priest;
these are indeed the pacifiers and protectors of this entire universe.
Therefore, after the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, the Brahman priest causes [the sacrificer] to recite [the formula]. 11.
"You are a hawk, having the *gāyatrī* as your meter; I take hold of you;
carry me safely across."
When he says, "Thou art a falcon," he thereby refers to Soma;
for having become fire, this [Soma] indeed causes [beings] to tremble in this world. Because he causes them to tremble (*saṃśāyayati*), therefore he is called the falcon (*śyena*).
(GBr_1,5.12g) That is the reason for the falcon’s nature as a falcon.

(GBr_1,5.12h) When he says, “O you of the *gāyatrī* metre, I take hold of you,” he takes hold of Agni, who is present in this world at the morning pressing, by means of the *gāyatrī* metre and with the Vasu deities.
(GBr_1,5.12i) When he says, “Safely carry me across,” it is by means of the *gāyatrī* metre itself and with the Vasu deities.
"At this morning pressing, may Agni, the god, safely carry me across in this world," he says;
by means of the Gāyatrī metre and the Vasu gods, he who knows thus attains safety at the morning pressing in this world through Agni, the god.
Then, during the midday Pavamāna, he causes him to recite: "Thou art the sovereign, having the Triṣṭubh as thy metre."
"I take hold of you;
carry me across to well-being.
When he says, "You are the sovereign," he is indeed saying this regarding Soma.
(GBr_1,5.13e) Having become this very wind, he shines as a sovereign (*samrāj*) in the world of the intermediate space.
(GBr_1,5.13f) Because he shines as a sovereign, therefore he is a sovereign.
(GBr_1,5.13g) That is the sovereignty of the sovereign.

(GBr_1,5.13h) When he says, "O you who have the *triṣṭubh* metre, I take hold of you," [he means] by means of the *triṣṭubh* metre, with the Rudra deities, at the midday pressing, for Vāyu who is present in the world of the intermediate space. (GBr_1,5.13i) When he says, "Safely carry me across," [he means] by means of that very *triṣṭubh* metre, with the Rudra deities, at the midday pressing, in the world of the intermediate space, with the deity Vāyu, "safely carry me across."

(GBr_1,5.13j) By means of that very *traiṣṭubha* metre, with the Rudra deities, at the midday pressing, and with the god Vāyu in the world of the intermediate space, he who knows this attains well-being. (GBr_1,5.14a) Then, during the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "Thou art tone (*svara*), thou art song (*gaya*), thou art the *jagatī* metre; I take hold of thee.
(GBr_1,5.14b) I take hold of thee.
"May it be well; carry me across," he says.
When he says, "Thou art the light (*svar*)," he is indeed speaking of Soma;
for having become the sun, he shines (*svarati*) in yonder world.
Because it sounds forth (*svarati*), therefore it is called *svaras*; that is the reason for the name *svaras*.
When he says, "Thou art a cow (*gaya*)," he is indeed speaking of Soma.
(GBr_1,5.14i) Having become this very moon, he goes to all the worlds; (GBr_1,5.14j) because he goes (*gacchati*), therefore he is *gayas*; that is the etymology of *gayas*.

When he says, "I take hold of you, following the *jagatī* metre," he takes hold of Sūrya, who is present in that world at the third pressing, by means of the *jagatī* metre and the Āditya deities. When he says, "Safely carry me across," he means, "By means of the *jagatī* metre and the Āditya deities, safely carry me across to Sūrya, the god, in that world at the third pressing"; thus, by means of the *jagatī* metre, he [safely carries him across].
Through the Chandas, the Ādityas, and the gods at the third pressing, he who knows this attains well-being in yonder world with the god Sūrya. 14.
(GBr_1,5.15a) Then, at the conclusion of each pressing, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "In me is splendor; in me is greatness; in me is glory; in me is everything.
(GBr_1,5.15b) The earth indeed is splendor, the intermediate space indeed is greatness, the sky indeed is glory, and the waters indeed are everything.
(GBr_1,5.15c) Fire indeed is splendor, wind indeed is greatness, the sun indeed is glory, and the moon indeed is everything. [ed. ādityā]
The Vasus alone are *bhargas*; the Rudras alone are *mahaḥ*; the Ādityas alone are *yaśas*; the Viśvedevas alone are *sarvam*.

The Gāyatrī alone is *bhargas*; the Triṣṭubh alone is *mahaḥ*; the Jagatī alone is *yaśas*; the Anuṣṭubh alone is *sarvam*. The eastern direction alone is *bhargas*; the western direction alone is *mahaḥ*; the northern direction alone is *yaśas*; the southern direction alone is *sarvam*.

Spring indeed is *bhargas*; summer indeed is *mahaḥ*; the rainy season indeed is *yaśas*; autumn indeed is *sarvam*. The *trivṛt* [stoma] indeed is *bhargas*; the *pañcadaśa* [stoma] indeed is *mahaḥ*; the *saptadaśa* [stoma] indeed is *yaśas*; the *ekaviṃśa* [stoma] indeed is *sarvam*.
The *Ṛgveda* indeed is *bhargas*; the *Yajurveda* indeed is *mahaḥ*; the *Sāmaveda* indeed is *yaśas*; the *Brahmaveda* indeed is *sarvam*.
The Hotṛ alone is *bhargas*, the Adhvaryu alone is *mahaḥ*, the Udgātṛ alone is *yaśas*, and the Brahman alone is everything.
Speech alone is *bhargas*, breath alone is *mahaḥ*, sight alone is *yaśas*, and mind alone is everything. 15.

When he says, "In me, splendor," this refers to the earth among the worlds, Agni among the gods, the Vasus among the classes of gods, the Gāyatrī among the meters, the eastern direction among the directions, spring among the seasons, the Trivṛt-stoma among the stomas,
the Ṛgveda among the Vedas, the office of the Hotṛ among the offices of the priests, and speech among the senses.

When he says, "Mightiness in me," he thereby names the atmosphere of the worlds, Vāyu of the gods, the Rudras of the divine hosts, the Triṣṭubh of the meters, the western quarter of the directions, the summer of the seasons, the fifteenfold Stoma of the Stomas, the Yajurveda of the Vedas, the office of the Adhvaryu of the priestly offices, and the out-breath of the vital powers. 17.

When he says, "Glory in me," he thereby declares for himself the heaven among the worlds, the Āditya among the gods, the Ādityas among the hosts of gods, the Jāgata among the meters, the northern quarter among the directions, the rainy season among the seasons, the seventeen-fold hymn-form (*saptadaśa-stoma*) among the *stomas*, the Sāmaveda among the Vedas, the office of the Udgātṛ among the officiating priests, and sight among the senses. (17)

When he says, "In me is everything," he thereby refers to the waters among the worlds, the moon among the gods, the Viśve Devas among the hosts of gods, the Anuṣṭubh among the meters, the southern quarter among the directions, the autumn among the seasons, the Ekaviṃśa among the Stomas,
the Brahmaveda among the Vedas, the office of the Brahman among the Hotrakas, and the mind among the senses. (GBr_1,5.18)
This very one, when divided tenfold, becomes four;
for there are indeed ten syllables in the four *virāj* meters,
and embryos subsist upon that.
Prosperity is indeed the Virāj;
glory is the eating of food.
Thus, he establishes prosperity, the Virāj, glory, and the eating of food as his firm foundation.
As they establish themselves, everything here establishes itself;
he who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. 20.
(GBr_1,5.21a) Dadhyaṅ Āṅgirasa once approached the god Anarvāṇ, thinking, "May we attain the fulfillment of the sacrifice.

(GBr_1,5.21b) That Dadhyaṅ Āṅgirasa said: "Verily, he who knows the seventeenfold Prajāpati as present in the sacrifice—his sacrifice does not fail, nor does the lord of the sacrifice fail. (GBr_1,5.21c) Thus he spoke.
These, indeed, are the five *vyāhṛtis*: *o śrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*, and *vaṣaṭ*.

Dadhyañc Āṅgirasa said: "We do not know whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins, or whether we belong to that seer or to another. And the Pitṛs, who are free from enemies and possessors of the Truth (*ṛtāvant*), pour themselves forth upon the *svadhā* offering, saying: "Let us speak! Let us speak!"
"He went [thinking], 'Either Svāyaṃbhuva or the Ṛtāvants shall rejoice; we will not speak.
Therefore, while the *pravara* is being pronounced, one should cause him to recite these three verses beginning with 'The gods, the fathers...'.
He who goes and performs the sacrifice becomes successful, as well as he who does not speak, and he who does not speak—so says the Brāhmaṇa. (21)
"In former times, they used to offer this animal sacrifice to Savitṛ in the east; nowadays, however, it is offered to Prajāpati," so they say, "for he who is Savitṛ is Prajāpati.
Therefore, having piled up the fires, they should perform that sacrifice with it.
(GBr_1,5.22d) They should indeed have common hearths until the Ukha-sambharaniya [offering].
(GBr_1,5.22e) At the Ukha-sambharaniya, having distributed the fires, they should sacrifice with that [offering].
(GBr_1,5.22f) They should indeed have separate hearths until the Dikshaniya [offering].

Having piled up the fires at the Dīkṣaṇīyā offering, they should sacrifice with it; those fires should remain on the same hearths until the Udavasānīyā offering. Having piled up the fires at the Udavasānīyā offering, they should sacrifice with it.
(GBr_1,5.22j) They should indeed have separate hearths.
(GBr_1,5.22k) Now, if the sacrificer should fall ill, he should remain seated after placing the fires on his sides until he is recovered.
(GBr_1,5.22l) If he should die, they should burn him with those very fires.
(GBr_1,5.22m) "The other sacrificers sit with the fires of the horse," so they say;
(GBr_1,5.22n) the Brāhmaṇa for that is the same as that which was [stated] previously at the morning libation;
(GBr_1,5.22o) the blessings in the Pitṛmedha have already been explained. // 22 //

The evening and morning fire-oblations, the cooked offering from the pot, the new-moon sacrifice, the bali-offering, the ancestral sacrifice, the eighth-day rite as the seventh, and the animal sacrifice.
Thus, these are the *pākayajñas*:

the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices (*paurṇamāsa* and *āmāvāsya*), the first-fruits sacrifice (*naveṣṭi*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), and the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) as the seventh.
Thus, these are the Havis-sacrifices: the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin,
the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma as the seventh.
Thus are these [verses] for the Soma-pressing:
"Who indeed are the gods of the *pravovāja* hymns? Who indeed are the gods who go to heaven? Who indeed are the gods possessing oblations? What indeed does he approach, seeking favor?"
The seasons indeed are the *pravovāja* hymns; the months are the gods who shine toward heaven;
the half-months are the possessors of the oblation. That [Soma] goes forth, seeking the gods.
How many indeed are its nights, how many days, how many hymns of praise (*stotra*), and how many recitations (*śastra*)?
How many indeed are the pressings (*savana*) of the year, and how many are its *stotriya* verses and syllables?
(Two *atirātra*s, six hundred *agniṣṭoma*s, two hundred and twenty *ukthya*s,
twelve *ṣoḍaśin*s, sixty *ṣaḍaha*s, and the *vaiṣuvata* day.)
Three hundred and twenty days and one day belong to this year; so many are its pressings—three thousand and eighty when fully chanted.
There are two hundred and sixty-six *stotra* and *śastra* hymns, and ten thousand (*ayuta*) belong to him;
the *stotriya* verses number ninety thousand, two hundred thousand (*niyuta*), and ninety-six.
Eight hundred thousand, thirty-four thousand, and ninety-four steps—
this much is the middle measure of the gods for the year measured by the seers.
(GBr_1,5.23k) One ten-thousand, thirty hundred-thousands, two ten-thousands,
as well as eight hundred and nine syllables— of such extent is the supreme self of Prajāpati.
The first *vaṣaṭ*-call ends with the offering; this is well-arranged limb by limb in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
When one desires the healing power of the meters, that which is offered in many ways as four hundred oblations into the fire—[that is the essence].
(GBr_1,5.23m) At the morning pressing, the twenty-onefold hymn is chanted with the Gāyatra-stoma;
at the midday pressing, it is arranged with the seventeenfold; and the third pressing with the thirty-threefold. // 23 //
(GBr_1.5.24a) Through faith, the ascetic Vaiśvānara, desiring offspring, poured his seed with fervor;
from that was born the world-conquering Soma-jambha, and from the seer Aṅgiras arose as a seer.
(GBr 1.5.24b) He who has conquered that world beyond through faith in the fourfold sacrifice of the seers— faith which is more excellent than [mere ritual]—
and for whom the Vedas, joined with drops of Soma, flow forth, carrying him to the world of the righteous.
The *ṛc*s, rejoicing in their delight, carry his four portions by means of the *uktha* recitations and *śastra* chants;
and the *yajus* formulas, both those performed and those yet to be performed, carry his four portions by means of the *graha* libations and the sacrificial offerings.

(GBr 1,5.24d) Upon the *audumbarī* post, by means of the sound of the *sāman*, with the *viṣṭuti*s and the *stoma*s, and by means of the *chandas*, they carry the *sāman*s and the four portions; together with the chanting, the *stoma*, and the *prastāva*.
Praising with expiatory rites and remedies, the peaceful Atharvans and Aṅgirases,
as well as the Brahman priest rejoicing in his office as Brahman, joyfully carry the four unmixed portions.
(GBr 1,5.24f) May he who knows Brahman be your benefactor; may the auspicious and wise one protect this Dharma through his insight.
Let him not cause you to fall away from immortality, from sacrifice, and from ritual action—through which even the Aṅgirases departed.

Do not utter a cry; do not be cursed; do not be one who transgresses. May you not cause me distress when joined together; may you establish the worlds for me. Guard against divine fear; protect the dharma that is uplifted, the sacrifice, the timely portion, the praise, and the protection.
The Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa recite one quarter, and the Acchāvāka together with the Grāvastut recite another;
praising with Ṛg-verses day after day, they sustain Agni, the quarter belonging to the earth, through sacred knowledge.
The Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Unnetṛ—praising the intermediate space with the Yajus formula—they maintain one placed foot; they sustain Vāyu as the foot with the Brahman.
The Udgātṛ, concealing [the chant] with the Sāman, should give the *stobha* on the Udumbara post attentively, even with a faltering voice.
The Prastotṛ, being learned, should then perform the excellent praise; and the Subrahmaṇya and the Pratihartṛ likewise in the sacrifice.

(GBr_1,5.24k) Praising with the *sāman*, they place one foot in heaven; by means of the *brahman*, they sustain the sun as the fourth foot. The *brahman* priest indeed [sustains] one foot of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*; together with the *potṛ* and the *agnīdh*, they sustain the other foot.
Guarded by the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases, they maintain the lunar quarter within the waters through the sacred word (*brahman*);
the *hotṛ*-priests, engaged with the Vedas, separately extol it in sixteen ways as it is divided fourfold.
The wise, consecrated, faithful, and protected priests carry forward the sacrifice;
from the south, the one belonging to the Brahman recites this sacred utterance (*vyāhṛti*): "Oṃ! Let there be life! (*oṃ janat*).
The ancients declare that the seventeenth is the Sadasya;
the eighteenth is the consecrated wife among the consecrated, who is faithful and devoted here in this sacrifice.
The nineteenth became the *śamitṛ*, the twentieth was the householder (*gṛhapati*) himself pressing the soma at the sacrifice;
O Aṅgiras, carry these twenty-one [deities] when the rite is completed.
The world praised by the Vedas is unconquered by various dwellings. // 24 //
There are seven Soma-pressings and seven Pākayajñas; likewise, there are seven Haviḥ-yajñas, making twenty-one in total.
All these sacrifices go to the Aṅgirases—both those which the seers create anew and those which were created by the ancients.
(GBr 1,5.25b) Within these Vedas, they also gather for the officiating priests a single enclosure;
may that curse, which clings to the whole [body], be cast away from him as a withered stalk, scattered among the offspring.
The sacrificial gifts, when being led back while the Soma is pressed and the ritual framework is spread out, turn back;
those who do not turn back go with their blessings in vain; performing no sacrifice, they do not cross over to the higher worlds.
(GBr_1,5.25d) A period of twelve years' studentship is prescribed for each Veda;
thus are all the Vedas established in their respective duties.
They possess common mantras, ritual manuals, and Brāhmaṇas; however, that entire arrangement is recorded as being distinct within the various Vedas.
The earth is the station of the Ṛgveda; the atmosphere is the station of the Adhvara sacrifice;
the sky is the station of the Sāmaveda; and the waters are traditionally held to be the station of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
Fire is the deity of the Ṛgveda; the Yajurveda has Vāyu as its deity;
Āditya is the deity of the Sāmaveda; and the Moon and Lightning are the deities of the Bhṛgvaṅgirases.
The *trivṛt* hymn-form belongs to the *Ṛgveda*; the sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) were born together with the *pañcadaśa*.
The *sāmaveda* was born with the *saptadaśa*, while the *ekaviṃśa* is commensurate with the Brahman.

Speech is said to be the internal aspect of the Ṛgveda, breath that of the Yajurvedas; the eyes are the internal aspect of the Sāmaveda, and the mind is traditionally held to be that of the Bhṛgvaṅgirases.
(GBr_1,5.25j) They say that the Gāyatra was born together with the Ṛg-verses, and the Yajus-formulas were born together with the Jāgata and the Triṣṭubh.
The seers declare that the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases arose from the Uṣṇih and Kakubh meters, and the Sāmans from the Jagatī.

With the *ṛc*s [they conquer] the earth, with the *yajus* the intermediate space, and with the *sāman* the heavens; the world-conquering Soma-chewers, protected by the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases, may this four-footed sacrifice carry up to heaven.
Well-praised with *ṛc*-verses, adorned with *yajus*-formulas, highly lauded, victorious through the *sāman*-chants, with Soma as its teeth,
and protected by the Atharvans and Aṅgirases, the four-footed sacrifice ascended to heaven.

Knowing the *ṛc*s, one knows the earth thoroughly; knowing the *yajus* formulas, one knows the great intermediate space; the wise singer of the *sāmans* knows heaven; and he who knows the *bhṛgvaṅgirases* knows all the worlds.

Whatever mantras people mutter in the village or in the forest, though they do not understand their manifold meanings, all those sacrifices go to the Aṅgirases; for that which is the lowest limit of Brahman is indeed the goal.
By means of this triple knowledge, one goes to Triviṣṭapa, Tridiva, and the highest Nāka.
Beyond that are the great worlds of Brahman belonging to the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases; that is their goal.
"That is the goal of the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases," so says the Brāhmaṇa. // 25 //
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
Thus ends the preceding Brāhmaṇa. Now, when he throws away a blade of grass from the seat of the Brahman priest, he thereby purifies it. Then he sits down, saying: "In this seat of Arvāgvasu, I sit."
Arvāgvasu, indeed, is the Brahman of the gods, and Parāgvasu is that of the Asuras.
He places him first with this [formula]:
"May he extend the sacrifice uninjured."
(GBr_2,1.1f) Then, having sat down, he mutters: "Bṛhaspati is the Brahman.
(GBr_2,1.1g) For Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa is indeed the Brahman of the gods;
it is toward him that he seeks permission. (GBr_2,1.1h) While the *praṇītā* waters are being carried forward, he restrains his speech until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
"This indeed is the door of the sacrifice;
he thus makes it non-empty,
because after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been performed, there is the impulsion for the *anuyāja* offerings."

(GBr_2,1.1l) This, indeed, is the second door of the sacrifice. (GBr_2,1.1m) He makes that very door non-empty. (GBr_2,1.1n) That the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are laid around is for the protection of the sacrifice.
He lays down the enclosing-sticks for the sake of the self-nature of the sacrifice;
he cleanses the enclosing-sticks;
verily, he purifies them.
(GBr_2,1.1r) Three times the middle one; (GBr_2,1.1s) these three are the vital breaths;
(GBr_2,1.1t) verily, he conquers the vital breaths.
Three times he [offers] toward the southern half.
There are indeed three worlds;
verily, he conquers the worlds.
Three times he offers on the northern part; for there are indeed three worlds of the gods;
verily, he conquers the worlds of the gods.
He fans it three times; for there are indeed three paths leading to the gods, and he thus conquers them.
These [fans] indeed become twelve.
Twelve indeed are the months of the year;
by this he gratifies the year itself. Moreover, he places the year itself for him, for the attainment of the heavenly world. 1.
Prajāpati indeed excluded Rudra from the sacrifices. He desired:
"May this intention of mine be fulfilled—that he who has excluded me from the sacrifices [be thwarted]."
Having drawn near to the sacrifice, he pierced it;
that which was pierced he cut out,
and it became the *prāśitra*.
He raised it up;
they brought it for Bhaga;
he looked upon it.
His eye fell away;
therefore they say, "Bhaga is indeed blind.
Moreover, he does not even desire that which he desires.
They brought it to Savitṛ;
he accepted it, but he cut off his two hands.
They gave him two golden ones in exchange.
Therefore he was praised as "the one with golden hands.
They brought that [oblation] for Pūṣan;
he ate it.
His teeth were ground away; therefore they say, "Pūṣan is toothless, his portion is ground flour.
They brought that [portion] to Idhmāṅgirasa.
He ate it; his head fell off;
the sacrifice itself restored him.
This very one is the sacrificial fuel;
indeed, the ancient ones were the kindling-sticks.
They brought that as sacrificial grass for Aṅgirasa.
He ate it;
his limbs and joints fell apart,
and the sacrifice itself restored him.
This very thing is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*);
the ancient *prastara* bundle is indeed that.
They brought it to Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa.
Bṛhaspati was afraid, thinking, "In this way, he will surely meet with misfortune.
He beheld this mantra:
"I gaze upon you with the eye of Sūrya... [PS 20.57.11]
"Thus he spoke:
'For nothing whatsoever harms the eye of the sun.'"
He was afraid, thinking, "It will harm me as I receive it.
He said, "On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, and with the hands of Pūṣan, being impelled by the command, I receive you.
Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he received it with those deities.
Having spread out blades of grass, he places it upon the sacrificial ground with its handle pointing eastward, saying, "I set thee on the navel of the earth.
For the earth is the pacifier of foods; by means of her, he indeed pacified it. He was afraid, thinking, "It might harm me as I eat it."
"I eat you with the mouth of Agni," he said.
For nothing harms the mouth of Agni. He was afraid, thinking, "It might harm me once I have eaten it."
"I set you down in the belly of Indra," he said;
for nothing whatsoever harms the belly of Indra.
"In the belly of Varuṇa," [he said]; for nothing whatsoever harms the belly of Varuṇa. // 2 //
(GBr_2,1.3a) Then they say: "The belly of a Brāhmaṇa.
(GBr_2,1.3b) [He offers with: "Thou art his self; do not injure my self within my self, svāhā!
(GBr_2,1.3c) Food indeed is the self of all beings; by that very means he pacified it.
He consecrates the portion that has been tasted with:
"The fire named Nṛmaṇas, who has entered into the Brāhmaṇas—may this *prāśitra* be well-offered into him; may it not harm me in the highest heaven" (PS 20.57.15).
He consumed it with the entire Brahman;
therefore, it did not injure him. Consequently, one should appoint as the Brahman priest whoever is most proficient in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*).

Bṛhaspati is indeed all the *brahman*. With the whole *brahman*, he indeed raises up the sacrifice from the south. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) depart from him who eats [the food] that has been pierced.
Having cleansed himself with water, he touches his vital breaths, saying: "May speech be in my mouth. The vital breaths are indeed immortality;
water is immortality.
(GBr_2,1.3n) He summons the vital breaths back to their respective places.
(GBr_2,1.3o) Regarding this, some say: "They brought it to Indra.
(GBr_2,1.3p) Those gods said: "Indra is indeed the most powerful and the strongest among the gods."
(GBr_2,1.3q) "Bring this to him," they said.
(GBr_2,1.3r) So they brought it to him. (GBr_2,1.3s) He made it into a couch with the *brahman* formula.
Therefore they say, "Indra is Brahman.
It is the size of a barley grain;
for [the poison] that is the size of a barley grain does not harm.

Because he pours [the clarified butter] below, therefore the flowing [of blood] from below does not harm offspring with disease; because he pours it above, therefore the flowing [of blood] from above does not harm offspring with disease;
if he were to pour it on both sides, the flowing [of blood] from both sides would be fatal to offspring with disease.
If he were to bring it across the boundary, he would pierce that which is unpierced of the sacrifice.
He carries it around by the front; he carries it around by the proper path. Indeed, the sacrifice is torn asunder when one carries the *prāśitra* around.
When he says, "O Brahman, I shall set forth," [it is because] Bṛhaspati is indeed all the *brahman*. With this entire *brahman*, he joins the sacrifice from the south.
Moreover, the sacrifice is supported right here where the Brahman priest is; the sacrifice is supported precisely there.
Therefore, he immolates it from that very [place].
If he were to strike it with his hand, it would become trembling;
if with his head, it would become afflicted with headache.
"If one were to remain silent, the sacrifice would not be undertaken," [they say]; "One should simply say, 'It is the foundation,' for the sacrifice is indeed supported by speech."

(GBr_2,1.4m) Wherever the Brahman priest is, and wherever the sacrifice is established, from there he hands it over to him. (GBr_2,1.4n) He places it in the Āgnīdhra fire; thus he gratifies the seasons, which have Agni as their mouth. (GBr_2,1.4o) He places it in the Āgnīdhra fire; thus he gratifies the seasons, which have Agni as their mouth. (GBr_2,1.4o) He places it in the Āgnīdhra fire; thus he gratifies the seasons, which have Agni as their mouth. (GBr_2,1.4p) Now, for the stability of the subsequent oblations,
(GBr_2,1.4q) he then offers the libation upon the kindled fire; (GBr_2,1.4r) he cleanses the enclosing sticks.
He indeed purifies them; he wipes them once each time,
for at this point the sacrifice has turned away.
It amounts to four;
moreover, cattle are four-footed;
[this is] for the attainment of cattle.
"O God Savitṛ, this they have proclaimed to you," he says for the sake of impulsion; "Bṛhaspati is the Brahman," he says,
for he is most rich in sacred knowledge (*brahmiṣṭha*).

"May he protect the sacrifice; may he protect the lord of the sacrifice; may he protect me; may he protect me in my ritual action," he says, for the sake of the sacrifice, for the sake of the sacrificer, and for the attainment of cattle. 4.
"Indeed, no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given on the full moon day nor on the new moon day;
this rice which is being cooked—that is the sacrificial fee given for the success of the sacrifice.
Verily, one sacrifices with a sacrifice when he performs this [offering], and moreover, one makes a meritorious gift (*pūrta*) when this rice is cooked."
(GBr_2,1.5d) He who cooks this [oblation] is indeed one who has performed sacrifices and meritorious works. // 5 //

(GBr_2,1.6a) Indeed, two kinds of gods come to the house of the sacrificer: some are Soma-drinkers, others are non-Soma-drinkers; (GBr_2,1.6b) some are eaters of oblations, others are non-eaters of oblations.
(GBr_2,1.6c) These Brahmins are indeed the gods who do not eat oblations.
(GBr_2,1.6d) He who has not previously sacrificed has these deities as his [deities]. (GBr_2,1.6e) For they indeed rule over the offspring and cattle of such a person.
(GBr_2,1.6f) Being unpropitiated, they depart from him, taking away his food and strength.

In that he brings the *anvāhārya* mess of rice, he thereby gratifies those very [priests]; he says, "It is to be carried around for those seated to the south"; thus he performs the sacrifice with a sacrifice that possesses sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
By means of oblations he gratifies the gods who eat the offerings, and by means of sacrificial gifts he gratifies the human gods;
they, being gratified, bestow upon him food and strength.
The gods and the asuras were indeed contending.
Those gods sacrificed to Prajāpati alone;
the asuras, however, offered their oblations while being in mutual opposition to one another.
Those gods saw this rice-porridge;
they offered it as a portion to Prajāpati.
Seeing that portion, Prajāpati turned back toward the gods.
(GBr_2,1.7g) Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(GBr_2,1.7h) He who, knowing this, cooks this rice-porridge, prospers in himself; his hateful rival is defeated.
(GBr_2,1.7i) Prajāpati indeed apportioned the sacrificial portions to the gods.
He thought, "I am within," and he saw this uncooked rice;
he set that aside as his own portion.
This is indeed the portion of Prajāpati;
it should be unlimited,
for Prajāpati is unlimited.
Thou art the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor, full of milk; thou art imperishable;
for imperishability, I take thee.
May you not perish for me there in yonder world and here; protect my out-breath and in-breath; protect my equalizing breath and diffusive breath.
Protect my form as *udāna*;
you are strength (*ūrj*); bestow strength upon me.
"May you not fail me as I act; may you not deceive me as I give.
Through you, may I prosper in the presence of Prajāpati."
He who knows thus, he who knows thus, prospers in the very presence of Prajāpati. 7.
(GBr_2,1.8a) Or rather, those who here have prospered through sacrifices—they are these lights, which are those stars over there.
(GBr_2,1.8b) That is the "star-nature" of the stars, in that they do not perish.
(GBr_2,1.8c) The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the two points of completion of the sacrifice.

(GBr_2,1.8d) Or those who, without having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, sacrifice with the Soma sacrifice—for them these are the lights, namely those stars that seem to fall. (GBr_2,1.8e) Just as here on earth, when a place is not well-established, people push one away, saying, "You shall not settle here! You shall not settle here!", even so these [stars] push them away from yonder world. (GBr_2,1.8f) They, being thus pushed away, fall down. // 8 //
(GBr_2,1.9a) If the moon should rise after the sacrificial oblation has already been set aside, one should divide those rice grains into three portions.
(GBr_2,1.9b) Those that are of medium size, he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ.
(GBr_2,1.9c) Those that are the largest, he should offer as a pap in curd to Indra Pradātṛ.
(GBr_2,1.9d) Those which are the smallest, for those he prepares a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
(GBr_2,1.9e) These indeed are the cattle that are left over; it is them he thereby obtains.
(GBr_2,1.9f) It is them he thereby obtains.
He wins them;
Agni is indeed the giver of the middle one, Indra is the giver of the eldest,
and that which is this smallness among cattle is Viṣṇu’s Śipiviṣṭa.
He obtains that very thing;
he secures cattle for himself. 9.
The earlier full moon is Anumati;
the later is Rākā.
The earlier new moon is Sinīvālī; the later is Kuhū.
The moon indeed is both the Ordainer and the Disposer;
when full it dwells with one [form] and when not full with the other—that is a pair.
When it beholds one and not the other—that is a pair.
That the moon is born from the new moon is a union;
from that very union he causes cattle to be born for him. 10.

(GBr_2,1.11a) One should not sacrifice with two [verses]. (GBr_2,1.11b) For if one were to proceed with the first while [the rite] is currently being performed, he would make a failure; (GBr_2,1.11c) and if he were to proceed with the second while [the rite] is currently being performed, he would make a failure with the first.
There is no *iṣṭi* sacrifice, nor is there a *yajña*;
consequently, one is born with a shamed face and lacking in confidence;
therefore, one should perform only a single sacrifice.
He is indeed born bold;
disregarding that, he should sacrifice with two [offerings].
With the first, he seizes the very mouth of the sacrifice; he sacrifices with the second.
By the first [offering] one obtains the deity, and by the latter, the sense-organ;
by the first one secures the world of the gods, and by the latter, the world of men;
one approaches many sacrificial rites—this sacrifice is indeed named Sumanā.
If the moon should rise in the west after one has already begun the sacrifice on that very day, it becomes prosperous for him in this world. 11.
One who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
Agni, indeed, is all the deities, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice;
thus he undertakes both the deities and the sacrifice for the sake of prosperity.
"He surely prospers.
"Both undertakings together," they say, "are successful;
even one who is bound by the horns is released."
The new moon sacrifice (*darśa*) is the first of these two, and the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) is the latter.

Now, as for the fact that the full moon sacrifice is commenced later, it is just as if it were performed first. Therefore, when one commences the full moon sacrifice, one should offer a pap (*caru*) to Sarasvatī and a cake on twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) to Sarasvant; for Sarasvatī is the new moon, and Sarasvant is the full moon.
He undertakes both of these together for the sake of prosperity;
he indeed prospers. 12.
One whose well-known sacrifice is omitted should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Path). He whose well-known sacrifice is omitted goes astray from the path.
Agni, indeed, is the maker of the path among the gods.
He should approach him with his own portion;
he leads him along that path.
An ox is the sacrificial fee.
For he leads one along the path. 13.
(GBr_2,1.14a) He who, having established the sacred fires, is about to travel abroad, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.
(GBr_2,1.14b) For he who, having established the sacred fires, travels abroad, frequently transgresses his vow; whether he approaches a woman or eats meat on the day of his vow.
(GBr_2,1.14c) Agni, indeed, is the lord of vows among the gods.
Fire has entered his vow;
therefore, one causes him to undertake that vow. 14.
One who has established the sacred fires and sheds tears born of distress should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.
For he who has established the sacred fires has been brought near to the gods;
therefore, he must not shed tears for this reason.
For the gods do not shed tears;
Agni, indeed, is the observer of vows among the gods;
it is to Agni that this man's vow has gone.
Therefore, one causes him to undertake this vow. 15.
(GBr_2,1.16a) One whose father and grandfather have not drunk Soma should offer a bull let loose to Indra and Agni.
(GBr_2,1.16b) Verily, he whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma is deprived of sensory power and vigor.
(GBr_2,1.16c) In that it is for Indra, he thereby endows him with sensory power and vigor.
(GBr_2,1.16d) He whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma is deprived of his virility by the deities.
(GBr_2,1.16e) Since this [offering] belongs to Agni, and Agni indeed is all the deities,
(GBr_2,1.16f) he thereby endows him with all the deities.
He becomes one who has been let loose;
for the Soma-draught of one whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma is, as it were, let loose.
Therefore, this [offering] is the fulfillment of the cattle of that deity. 16.
When the plants had ripened, the gods indeed entered into a race for them.
Indra perceived, "Agni will surely be the first to win these. He said, "Whichever of us two wins first, let that be won by us both."
Agni won them;
Indra won them after him.
Thus, although it belongs to Indra and Agni, it is called *āgnendra*.
At that time, there was indeed only one grain of barley, one of rice, one of bean, and one of sesame.
Then the Viśvedevas said, "We shall spread this out; let there be a share for us.
Therefore, the Vaiśvadeva oblation is offered upon the ground.
(GBr_2,1.17j) Then he spreads it out with this very [formula].
(GBr_2,1.17k) It should be in milk, for the sake of its being dedicated to the Viśvedevas; for milk belongs to the Viśvedevas.
Then these two said, "Truly, you are not spreading this out for us; it is established in me. Yonder sun cooks by means of rain; this will not overcome it from here.
"Let there be a share for us," they said.
Indeed, a share is made for them for the sake of victory alone.
(GBr_2,1.17p) Moreover, it is for the sake of stability. That [verse] which is addressed to Heaven and Earth—(GBr_2,1.17q) plants indeed belong to Soma;
(GBr_2,1.17r) Soma is the sovereign king of plants.
(GBr_2,1.17s) Those that are domestic and those that are wild—their share is this: the *śyāmāka* grain.
(GBr_2,1.17t) That which is *śyāmāka* belongs to Soma; he thus makes it a sharer.
(GBr_2,1.17u) If one were to eat of the new crop without having performed the *āgrayaṇa* offering, he would be eating the portion of the gods that has not been duly apportioned.
The Āgrayaṇa is indeed produced from the year;
the Brahman is the year. Therefore, the Brahman should insert [the verses] at the beginning of the *pūrva-homas* and the *saṃsthita-homas*.
A one-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee;
for it is the image of the year,
and it is indeed seed that has not yet been procreated.
For the sake of procreation. 17.
Now, this is the Apratiratha hymn:
"The two arms of Indra are firm and virile.
By means of this, indeed, Indra conquered the Asuras.
(GBr_2,1.18c) By means of this, the sacrificer becomes invincible and conquers his rival.
(GBr_2,1.18d) He should offer it in battle; he indeed becomes invincible.
(GBr_2,1.18e) By means of this, Bharadvāja indeed equipped Pratardana for combat.
He became a ruler.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become a ruler," one should arm him with this;
he indeed becomes a ruler.
By this, indeed, Indra conquered the Virāj.
He recites ten verses;
the Virāj consists of ten syllables. By means of this, the sacrificer appropriates his rival through the power of the Virāj.
Regarding this, some indeed recite eleven [verses], saying:
"The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables, and the thunderbolt (*vajra*) is of the *triṣṭubh* nature;
by means of the thunderbolt, he thus drives away the demons."
(GBr_2,1.18o) From the south, the Rakṣases sought to strike at the sacrifice of the gods. (GBr_2,1.18p) They drove them away with the Apratiratha hymn.
(GBr_2,1.18q) Therefore, the Brahman priest proceeds while muttering the Apratiratha hymn.
That the Brahman priest goes while muttering the Apratiratha hymn is for the conquest of the sacrifice and for the striking away of the Rakṣases—for the striking away of the Rakṣases. 18.
(GBr 2,1.19a) Now, therefore, follows the performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
(GBr 2,1.19b) One should perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices on the full moon day of Phālguna.
(GBr 2,1.19c) For the full moon of Phālguna is indeed the mouth of the year; the later Phālgunī days are the head, and the earlier ones are the tail.

Just as the two ends of a moving object meet together, even so the two ends of the year meet together. When one sacrifices with the Cāturmāsya offerings on the full moon of Phālguna, one thereby sets the year in motion from its very beginning;
moreover, these Cāturmāsya sacrifices are indeed healing sacrifices.
Therefore, they are performed at the junctions of the seasons;
for indeed, disease arises at the junctions of the seasons.
These are the eight oblations.
There are indeed eight oblations for four full-moon sacrifices;
the Vaiśvadeva is the combination of four full-moon sacrifices.
Now, as for the fact that they churn the fire: the Vaiśvadeva is Prajāpati.
It is for the sake of procreation indeed;
thus he brings forth this divine embryo.
Now, as to why there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses: Prajāpati is seventeenfold.
For the attainment of Prajāpati.
Now, as for the fact that they recite the two Ājyabhāga verses containing the word *sat*: they indeed become "possessing the real" (*sadvantau*).
And as for the two Virāj verses being the *saṃyājyā*s: the Virāj is indeed food and prosperity; it is for the attainment of food and prosperity.

Now, as for the fact that there are nine *prayāja*s, nine *anuyāja*s, eight oblations (*havīṃṣi*), and the *vājina* as the ninth—thereby one attains the *virāj* consisting of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatrīyā*).
Furthermore, they say it is the ten-syllabled *virāj*: namely, the *prayāja*s, the *anuyāja*s, the oblations, the two *āghāra* libations, and the two *ājyabhāga* portions.
Now, when he first sacrifices to Agni and Soma among the deities— Agni and Soma being indeed the mouth of the gods—
he thereby gratifies the gods from the very mouth.
Then, when he sacrifices to Savitṛ— Savitṛ is indeed that one who shines yonder.
By that [offering], he gratifies him alone.
Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices to Sarasvatī: Sarasvatī is indeed speech;
by this [offering], he gratifies speech.
Now, as for why he sacrifices to Pūṣan: Pūṣan is indeed that one who shines yonder;
it is him he gratifies thereby.
And as for why he sacrifices to the Maruts, the Self-strong: the Maruts, the Self-strong, are indeed terrible.
By that very act, he gratifies them.
Now, when he sacrifices to the Viśvedevas, these indeed are the Viśvedevas, namely all the gods;
by that very act, he gratifies them.
Now, when he sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, Heaven and Earth are indeed the two foundations; it is for the sake of stability. And when he sacrifices to the Vājins, the Vājins are indeed cattle.
By this, he gratifies the cattle;
moreover, the *vājins* are indeed the seasons;
by this, he gratifies the seasons.
Moreover, the *vājins* are indeed the *chandas*;
by this he gratifies the *chandas*. Furthermore, the *vājins* are indeed the divine horses.
In this regard, the gods together with the horses become beloved and gratified.
Then, when he subsequently sacrifices with the Full Moon sacrifice, his Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has thus been performed during the waxing fortnight.
By means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, Prajāpati indeed created offspring.
Once created, they ate Varuṇa’s barley before they had brought forth [their own offspring];
Varuṇa then bound them with the nooses of Varuṇa.
Those creatures went to their father Prajāpati and petitioned him: "Learn that sacrificial rite by which, having sacrificed, he gratified Varuṇa;
when Varuṇa is gratified, they shall be completely released from the bonds of Varuṇa and from all evil."
Then Prajāpati saw this sacrificial rite, the Varuṇapraghāsas;
he took it up and sacrificed with it.
By means of that [sacrifice], he gratified Varuṇa.
Varuṇa, being gratified, released the creatures from the bonds of Varuṇa and from all evil.
Indeed, the creatures of this man are likewise released from the bonds of Varuṇa and from all evil.
(GBr_2,1.21m) He who knows thus—
(GBr_2,1.21n) Now, when they lead forward the fire, it is that very same fire which they churn out at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice that they lead forward here.
(GBr_2,1.21o) As for the fact that it is churned out, its Brāhmaṇa explanation has already been stated.

(GBr_2,1.21p) Now, as for the fact that there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "sad," and the two *saṃyājyā* verses are *virāj*s—the *brāhmaṇa* explanation for these has already been stated.
(GBr_2,1.21q) Furthermore, there are nine *prayāja*s, nine *anuyāja*s, and these nine oblations.
(GBr_2,1.21r) However, there are exactly five common *saṃcara* oblations, ending with the one for Pūṣan.
The Brāhmaṇa concerning them has been stated. 21.
Now, as for the fact that there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni: Indra and Agni are indeed strength and splendor; he thus establishes strength in splendor.
Then, as for the curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Varuṇa: Varuṇa is indeed Indra.
And he is indeed the vessel of milk;
therefore the *āmikṣā* belongs to Varuṇa.
Now, as for the *payasyā* belonging to the Maruts: the Maruts are indeed supported in the waters.
(GBr_2,1.22g) "For water is milk.
(GBr_2,1.22h) Now, the Maruts are dependent upon Indra; the milk belongs to Indra.
(GBr_2,1.22i) Therefore, the curd-mixture belongs to the Maruts.
Now, as for the cake on one potsherd for Ka: Ka is indeed Prajāpati;
it is for the attainment of Prajāpati.
Moreover, "Ka" is also the name of bliss.
He bestows that very happiness upon himself;
furthermore, when he gives a pair of cattle, that is the form of procreation.
They are the Ukthya and the Vājina.
Now, when he sacrifices to Varuṇa in the waters, he gratifies him in his own abode.
Then, when he subsequently sacrifices with the Full-moon sacrifice, it is as if the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings have been performed for him during the waxing fortnight.
The Sākamedha offerings are indeed an Indra-sacrifice.
Just as a great king, having arrayed his army divisions in front, would proceed along a secure path, even so he sacrifices to the deities in front.
Just as that Great Vow (*mahāvrata*) of Soma is, so too is this Great Vow of the sacrifice (*iṣṭimahāvrata*).

(GBr_2,1.23d) Now, as to why he sacrifices first to Agni Anīkavant among the deities: Agni is indeed the mouth of the gods; thus he gratifies the gods from the very mouth. (GBr_2,1.23e) And as to why he sacrifices at midday to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas: Indra is indeed the Maruts Sāṃtapanas.
The midday pressing belongs to Indra;
therefore, he offers these [oblations] conjoined with Indra. Now, as for the fact that they perform the Gṛhamedhīya rite in the evening: the Gṛhamedhīya is indeed an act for nourishment.
The evening is the nourishment of cattle;
therefore, they perform the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice in the evening.

Consequently, when on the following day they perform the rite with a full ladle mixed with the scrapings of the previous Gṛhamedhīya, they thereby connect the morning rite with the ritual action of the preceding day.
(GBr_2,1.23m) Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices to the *marutaḥ krīḍinaḥ* in the morning: the *marutaḥ krīḍinaḥ* are indeed Indra;
therefore, he sacrifices to them as being associated with Indra.
(GBr_2,1.23n) And as for the fact that they lead forward the fire: it is that very same fire which they churn at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice that they lead forward here.
(GBr_2,1.23p) Regarding that which is churned, its Brāhmaṇa has been explained.

(GBr_2,1.23q) Now, as for the fact that there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "sat," and the two *saṃyājyā* verses are *virāj*s—regarding these, their Brāhmaṇa has been explained.

(GBr_2,1.23r) Now, as for the nine *prayāja*s, the nine *anuyāja*s, and the eight oblations (*havīṃṣi*)—of these, the six recurring oblations (*ṣaṭsaṃcarāṇi havīṃṣi*) ending with the one for Indra and Agni are indeed common to all.
The Brāhmaṇa concerning them has been stated.
Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices to Mahendra at the end: the chief indeed takes his place at the end;
therefore, he sacrifices to him at the end.
Now, as for the cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman: he who shines yonder is indeed Viśvakarman;
it is him that he gratifies thereby.
And as for the bull that he gives: the sacrificial rite belongs to Indra. 23.

Now, as for the fact that they perform the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) in the afternoon: the ancestors indeed possess the afternoon; therefore, they perform the sacrifice to the ancestors in the afternoon. Regarding this, they say: "Since the ancestors possess the latter half of the month (*aparapakṣa*), why do they sacrifice to them in the former half of the month (*pūrvapakṣa*)?"

"These ancestors are indeed gods; therefore, they sacrifice to them during the first fortnight. Now, as to why he recites one *sāmidhenī* verse three times: the ancestors, it is said, [partake] only once.
Therefore, he recites each *sāmidhenī* verse three times.
Now, as to why he does not recite the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) of the sacrificer: it is so that he may not exclude the sacrificer from the invocation.
Then, as to why he invokes Soma accompanied by the fathers, or the Somavat fathers, the Barhiṣad fathers, and the Agniṣvātta fathers.

(GBr_2,1.24j) Some do not invoke their own greatness, saying, "This is the greatness of the sacrificer"; however, it is established that one should indeed invoke it, for this is the greatness of Agni.
(GBr_2,1.24k) He causes the announcement with: "Oṃ svadhā! (GBr_2,1.24l)
"Let there be *svadhā*," he responds;
for the utterance *svadhā* belongs to the ancestors.

Now, as to why he draws out two portions containing the *barhis* from the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s: the *barhis* is indeed offspring; [he does this] thinking, "Lest I place offspring among the ancestors."
These indeed become six;
for there are six seasons,
and the seasons are the ancestors.
For the attainment of the ancestors. // 24 //

(GBr_2,1.25a) Now, in that the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) contain the word "living," he thereby causes the sacrificer himself to live. (GBr_2,1.25b) Now, in that there are three invitatory verses (*yājyā*) for each oblation (*havis*), he summons them with the first and makes them go [to the gods] with the second.
With the third [verse] he indeed restrains [the breath];
moreover, he thereby separates the sacrifice to the gods from the sacrifice to the ancestors;
furthermore, the sacrifice to the ancestors is indeed performed with its conclusion toward the south.
(GBr_2,1.25g) They thus perform that very [offering] with its orientation toward the north.
(GBr_2,1.25h) Now, as for the fact that he finally sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana—this is the Sviṣṭakṛt offering for the fathers.
(GBr_2,1.25i) Therefore, he sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana at the end.
(GBr_2,1.25j) Now, as for the fact that they smell the *iḍā* after inviting it, but do not eat it—the *iḍā* is indeed cattle—and [they do so] lest they should exclude the cattle.

(GBr_2,1.25k) And as for the fact that he recites the blessings for the sacrificer during the *sūktavāka*, [he does so] lest he should exclude the sacrificer. (GBr_2,1.25l) Thus, [it is done] lest they exclude either the cattle or the sacrificer.

(GBr_2,1.25m) Now, as to why they do not perform the *saṃyājana* with the wife: "Lest we should cause the wife to suffer. (GBr_2,1.25n) And as to why they purify themselves with the *pavitra*: water is indeed peace and medicine; thus, this peace and medicine is performed at the conclusion of the sacrifice. (GBr_2,1.25o) Thus, this very peace and medicine is performed at the end of the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,1.25p) Now, when the Adhvaryu makes offerings to the fathers, human fathers follow after those living fathers.
(GBr_2,1.25q) Moreover, they distinguish this sacrifice to the gods from the sacrifice to the fathers.
(GBr_2,1.25r) Furthermore, the sacrifice to the fathers is indeed concluded on the south.
They thus place him facing northward;
then, when they step forward toward the east and worship the sun— the sun being the world of the gods and the fathers being the world of the ancestors— [they do so].
(GBr_2,1.25v) "By this, they are indeed passing over from the world of the fathers to the world of the gods.

(GBr_2,1.25w) Now, when they step out toward the south and worship the fires, they thereby finally offer a portion to the gods out of affection. (GBr_2,1.25x) Then, when they step out toward the north and sacrifice with the *traiyambaka* offerings, they thereby gratify Rudra in his own quarter.
Thus, they distinguish the sacrifice to the gods from the sacrifice to the ancestors.
Furthermore, the sacrifice to the ancestors is performed with a clockwise orientation; they now perform it with a counter-clockwise orientation.
Now, as to why he finally sacrifices with the Aditi offering: Aditi is indeed this [earth].

He thus establishes him finally upon this very [earth]. Then, as to why he subsequently sacrifices with the Full-moon sacrifice: in this way, his sacrifice with the Sākamedha offerings is effectively performed during the waxing fortnight. 25.
He who sacrifices with the Śunāsīrya attains this thirteenth month.

For as great as this thirteenth month is, so great indeed is the year. Now, when they lead forward the fire, it is that very same fire which they churn at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice that they lead forward here.
Regarding that which is churned, its Brāhmaṇa has been explained.
But if it is not churned, the Full Moon sacrifice alone constitutes the ritual procedure;
for the Full Moon sacrifice is indeed a firm foundation.
It is for the sake of stability; furthermore, when he sacrifices to Vāyu, Vāyu is indeed the breath—thereby he gratifies the breath.
Then, when he sacrifices to Śunāsīra, Śunāsīra is indeed the year.
By that, he gratifies the year itself.
Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices to Sūrya: Sūrya is indeed he who shines yonder;
it is him whom he gratifies by that.
Now, when they give a white cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), that is made as a form of this very [soma].
And when they perform a substitute for an expiation, they thereby perform a rite for well-being;
it is for the pacification of the sacrifice and for the healing of the sacrificer.
(GBr_2,1.26p) By means of these Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the gods attained all desires, all offerings, and all immortality.
