(GBr_2,1.26q) This very Prajāpati is the twenty-fourfold year, which consists of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; of him, the Vaiśvadeva is indeed the mouth.
The two arms are the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings;
inhalation, exhalation, and the diffused breath—these three sacrifices are the self; the Great Oblation is the trunk.
The foundation is Śunāsīra.
Indeed, this Cāturmāsya sacrifice is Prajāpati himself,
for Prajāpati is everything.
The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are everything;

he who knows this and he who, knowing thus, performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, obtains everything by means of everything. He performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. Thus ends the first Prapāṭhaka in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, the latter part of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_2,2.1a) Indeed, the fires of one who has established the sacred fires become hungry;
they first long for this very sacrificer.
(GBr_2,2.1b-c) He who offers this animal sacrifice to Indra and Agni every sixth month thereby expiates his self that was swallowed by Indra and Agni. (GBr_2,2.1d) Thus he is freed from it.
One who desires long life should sacrifice [this animal];
Indra and Agni are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath;
verily, he places the out-breath and the in-breath within himself.
(GBr_2,2.1g) He becomes long-lived.
(GBr_2,2.1h) One desiring offspring should sacrifice.
(GBr_2,2.1i) Indra and Agni are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath.
Offspring are born after the out-breath and the in-breath;
he becomes possessed of offspring.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice this [animal].
Indra and Agni are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath;
animals are born after the out-breath and in-breath;
he becomes possessed of cattle.
(GBr_2,2.1p) One who desires, "May I be free from disease in the world of the fathers," should sacrifice a yellowish-green partridge or a white one.
(GBr_2,2.1q) By means of this, indeed, Yama prospered in that world;
he prospers in the world of the fathers.
(GBr_2,2.1s) One desiring offspring should sacrifice a mule dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ.
(GBr_2,2.1t) Prajāpati, indeed, desiring to create offspring, did not find a second pair. [ed. *sisṛksamāṇaḥ*, corrected p. 302; Patyal]
He did not find it; he saw the Vaḍava belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ,
for Tvaṣṭṛ is the progenitor of forms.
By means of it he created offspring;
by means of it he found a mate. He who knows this, and he who, knowing thus, sacrifices this [animal], becomes possessed of offspring and possessed of a mate.

He who offers a desired animal victim without having first sacrificed with the Aindrāgna [offering] seizes the animals according to their wombs; the sacrifice of the desired animal follows after that sacrifice for the sake of success.
(GBr_2,2.2a) The gods indeed went apart in five groups: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, Varuṇa with the Ādityas, and Bṛhaspati with the Viśve Devas.
(GBr_2,2.2b) Those gods said, "We are surely yielding to our rivals, the Asuras, because we are at variance with one another.
(GBr_2,2.2c) Let us gather together those bodies of ours which are dear to us."
They made a compact with one another:

"May he who is the first among us to betray another perish by them. Because they made a compact (*samavādyanta*) regarding their bodies (*tanvaḥ*), that is the essence of the *tānūnaptra* rite; hence its name, *tānūnaptra*.
Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
Therefore, whoever among those who have consecrated themselves with the *tānūnaptra* oath first commits treachery meets with ruin.
In that he portions out the *tānūnaptra* offering, it is for the sake of overcoming his rivals.
He prospers in himself; his hostile rival becomes alienated from him. // 2 //
He cuts off five times;
the sacrifice is fivefold, for they were cut off by them in five ways.
"I take you for the descending one," he says; the descending one is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
by this, he gratifies the vital breath itself.
"For the protector," he says;
for the mind is indeed the protector;
it is the mind that he thereby gratifies.
"To Tanūnapāt," he says;
for they agreed upon those bodies of theirs.
"To Śākvara," he says.
"For by power they indeed pledged those [powers] to you," he says; "for by might, the most powerful," he says,
for by that which is most powerful in themselves they indeed pledged it to you.
"Unassailable," he says;
for this is indeed unassailable.
"Invincible," he says.
"For this is unassailable," he says; "for this is the vital power (*ojas*) of the gods.
For this is indeed the vital power of the gods.
"Protecting from imprecation," he says; for this [sacrifice] protects from imprecation.
"Free from the charge of imprecation," he says.
"For this is not to be falsely accused.

"May the Lord of Consecration favor my consecration; may the Lord of Penance favor my penance; may I straightway attain truth; place me in well-being," he says. This is exactly according to the sacrificial formula. 3.
The gods, having made ghee their thunderbolt, struck at Soma;
the two offering-spoons were their arms.
Therefore, the two offering-spoons do not consume the oblation intended for Soma.
The Soma was withheld from him;
therefore he brought the two offering-spoons and the clarified butter close at hand.
Indeed, they proceed with this [rite] as if it were close at hand for him, in that they proceed with the *tānūnaptra* ceremony.
"O divine Soma, may every stalk of thine swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize," he says.
Whatever of his is lost or wasted, that very thing they cause to swell by this [formula].
"May Indra swell for thee; do thou swell for Indra," he says.
(GBr_2,2.4j) They cause both Indra and Soma to swell.
(GBr_2,2.4k) "Make us, your companions, swell with gain, with wisdom, with offspring, and with wealth," he says;
(GBr_2,2.4l) for the officiating priests are indeed his companions.
With this [verse], they cause those very [Soma shoots] of his to swell.
"May I attain well-being, O divine Soma, at the conclusion of the pressing," he says;
thus he invokes this very blessing.
(GBr_2,2.4p) Indeed, those who cause the *soma* to swell fall away from this world;
for the *soma*, once swollen, has the intermediate region as its deity.
(GBr_2,2.4q–r) "Desired are riches, desired are beautiful things; [I go] forth for fortune."
"Truth to those who speak the truth; homage to heaven, homage to earth!"—by thus paying homage to heaven and earth, he becomes firmly established in this world; he becomes firmly established. 4.
(GBr_2,2.5a) "Makha" is a name for sacrifice, by virtue of its capacity to exclude defects. (GBr_2,2.5b) A defect is said to be a "hole" (*kha*).
(GBr_2,2.5c) Its negation is expressed by the word "ma."
"Lest he should create a flaw," for a flawed sacrifice flows away like a breached ocean; indeed,
that becomes a flaw through the lack of coordination between the officiating priests and the sacrificer.

Furthermore, this [is the expiation] for their failure to employ the mantras, ritual manuals (*kalpa*), and *brāhmaṇas* as required; or for the non-payment of the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); or for deficiency or excess; or for the transgression of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) during portents and wonders.
Indeed, all this is entrusted to the Brahmin.

It is the learned Brahmin—who knows the *Bhṛgu-Aṅgiras*, who studies correctly, who has practiced celibacy (*brahmacarya*), whose limbs are neither deficient nor redundant, and who is vigilant—that protects the sacrifice.

(GBr_2,2.5j) Through negligence or perhaps due to its absence, just as a broken boat on the bottomless great waters becomes the lot of fish, tortoises, porpoises, crocodiles, makaras, purīkayas, jaṣas, rajasas, piśācas,
and others of this kind who live upon destruction; so it is with these and other such beings.

(GBr_2,2.5k) Indeed, when a sacrifice is thus broken, shattered, ruined, full of portents and wonders, and not consecrated by the Atharvans, it becomes the share of the Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, Piśācas, and others of that sort who live upon what is destroyed.
Regarding this, there are also these verses: (GBr_2,2.5l) [Verses follow]
Torn asunder, shattered, and destroyed, the sacrifice, renowned in many ways,
fell down upon the sacrificer, seizing his wealth from both sacrificial offerings and charitable works.
When a sacrifice is ruined, it brings ruin to the officiating priests, to the king, and to the realm; that is a failure lasting for a year.
Sacrifice is traditionally held to incline toward the south, for it has become inclined toward the south.
One who is deficient in a limb is the portion of the Rākṣasas, as is one who has not been consecrated according to the Brāhmaṇa Veda.
The complete sacrifice has four quarters, performed by the fourfold officiating priests;
it is established by means of the four kinds of mantras through the priests who have mastered the Vedas.
"Through expiations, meditations, permissions,
consecrations, and oblations, the Brahman priest shall complete every deficiency in the sacrifice.
Therefore, the sacrificer should appoint one who knows the Bhṛgvaṅgiras hymns as the Brahman priest in that ceremony.
"For he carries the sacrifice across," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Sacrifice indeed rose up from the gods, saying, "I shall not be your food.
The gods said, "No! You shall indeed be our food.
The gods then dismembered it.
When he had been distributed among these [deities], he was not sufficient for them.
Those gods said,
"Truly, being distributed in this manner, he will not be enough for us."
"Come, let us restore him! they said. They restored him. Having restored him, they said, "O Aśvins, heal this man."
The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryus. Therefore, the two Adhvaryus prepare the Gharma.
Having prepared that [mixture], they say: "O Brahman, we shall proceed with the *gharma*; O Hotṛ, recite for the *gharma*; O Udgātṛ, chant the *sāmans*.
He gives permission, saying, "Proceed with the *gharma*," for it is when impelled by the Brahman that they proceed.
Brahman indeed rules over these emanations for the sake of being impelled by Savitṛ;
I heat the Gharma. (PS 5.16.2)
"Born as Brahman" (brahma jajñānam) [PS 5.2.2,
VaitS 14.1]; "May this ancestral, royal [lineage] go forth first" (iyaṃ pitryā rāṣṭry etv agre) [PS 5.2.1].

"One should attend upon the *gharma* while it is being heated with [verses] rich in form, like a *śastra*, verse by half-verse (*ardharcaśas*), excluding the calls (*āhāva*) and responses (*pratigara*).

That which is rich in form is indeed the perfection of the sacrifice. Whatever rite, whether an *ṛc* or a *yajus*, speaks in favor of it, he who knows thus reaches the successful completion of that sacrifice."
This Gharma is indeed a divine couple;
therefore, they proceed with it while keeping [the fire] screened off,
for people engage in sexual union only when they are screened off.
This, they call the divine couple. That which is its *gharma* is its penis;
those which are its two hooves are its testicles.
The two pressing-stones are your two hip-bones;
that which is the milk is the semen;
he places that semen, consisting of the Brahman, into the fire—the womb of the gods—for the sake of procreation.

That Agni is of divine origin, consisting of the *Ṛg*, consisting of the *Yajuṣ*, consisting of the *Sāman*, consisting of the *Brahman*, consisting of immortality, consisting of oblations, endowed with all the senses—the sacrificer ascending to the heavenly world.
Regarding this they say: "One should not perform the *Pravargya* at the first sacrifice; for the subsequent sacrificial rites will indeed not be receptive to him.
However, one may perform it for one who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and a master of the sacred texts (*śrotriya*).
"It is known: 'The self, indeed, is that of the sacrifice.
"He who performs the sacrifice without the *pravargya* performs the sacrifice headless;
for the *pravargya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice."
Therefore, one should cause him to sacrifice only with the Pravargya rite, not without the Pravargya. Regarding this, the following verse has been recited:
"Four are its horns... (RV 4.58.3).
"...as stated [in the *Sakala* and *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa* 1.2.16ff]. // 6 //
The gods and the seers were engaged in conflict with the Asuras.
These cities of the Asuras had been previously conquered: the earth was made of iron, the intermediate space was made of silver, and the sky was made of gold.
In every encounter, those gods were defeated.
They realized, "We are indeed without a dwelling place;
that is why we are being defeated.
They then constructed these fortresses: the oblation-holder from heaven, the *āgnīdhra* from the intermediate space, and the *sadas* from the earth.
Those gods said, "Let us perform the *upasad* ritual;
for by means of the *upasad*, one conquers even a great fortress. They drove [the Asuras] out from these worlds.
With one [day] from yonder world, with one from the intermediate space, and with one from the earth;
therefore they say, "By means of the *upasad* rites, one conquers a great city. Having been driven out from these worlds, they entered the seasons.
They approached those six with the *upasad* rites; by means of the *upasad*s alone, they drove them out from the seasons:
by two from yonder world, by two from the intermediate space, and by two from the earth.
(GBr_2,2.7p) Driven out by the seasons, they entered the year. (GBr_2,2.7q) They approached it twelve times.
(GBr_2,2.7r) By means of the *upasad* rites alone, they drove them out from the year.

With four [verses] from yonder world, with four from the intermediate space, and with four from the earth—these [verses], when extracted for the sake of the year, entered into day and night. Because they approached them in the evening, they drove them out by means of the night; because [they approached them] in the morning, [they drove them out] by means of the day.

Therefore, the cow replenishes the morning [milk] in the evening, and the evening [milk] in the morning. By means of the *upasad* rites alone, they drove them away from these worlds. Then the gods prevailed, and the asuras were defeated.
He who, knowing this, undergoes the Upasad rites, drives away his rival from all these worlds as he approaches them. 7.

(GBr_2,2.8a) There should not be twelve *upasads* for the *agniṣṭoma*; (GBr_2,2.8b) if there were fewer, they would be unappeased and would cause exhaustion; nor should there be three for the *ahīna*.
(GBr_2,2.8c) For the sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) is weightier than that; it would crush him like a heavy burden crushing the neck, and he would meet with ruin.
One should perform twelve for the Ahīna sacrifice, for support and stability; there should be three Upasad days for the Agniṣṭoma, for peace and to avoid exhaustion.
Those gods were not able to enter these worlds after the Asuras;
they entered them with Agni as their mouth.
That Agni is the opening of the Upasads, just as a lord of the field [enters] his field.
They pour it down in this very way; thus, with Agni as their mouth, they go forth leading these worlds along.
He who knows the Sādhyas, the gods, succeeds for him.
These worlds indeed are the Sādhyas, the gods.
He who thus knows these Sādhyas succeeds; he succeeds for this [world], he succeeds for that [world], he succeeds for this world—he who, knowing thus, enters upon the Upasad. 8.

(GBr_2,2.9a) Now, when the Adhvaryu says, "O Āgnīdhra, announce the wives of the gods; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā," then the Āgnīdhra, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire facing eastward and without pausing for breath, announces the wives of the gods:
(GBr_2,2.9b) "The earth is the wife of Agni."
Speech is the consort of Vāta; Senā is the consort of Indra;
Dhenu is the consort of Bṛhaspati.
Pathyā is the wife of Pūṣan;
Gāyatrī is the wife of the cattle;
Triṣṭubh is the wife of the Rudras.
The Jagatī is the wife of the Ādityas;
the Anuṣṭubh is the wife of Mitra;
the Virāj is the wife of Varuṇa.
"The Paṅkti is the wife of Viṣṇu;

Dīkṣā is the wife of King Soma"—he who, knowing this, as the Āgnīdhra priest recites the names of the wives of the gods, ascends beyond his rivals; his rivals do not ascend against him; he ascends above his rivals. // 9 //
[The priests] mount [the chariot]. Just as a chariot moves by resting upon each individual spoke, so does the sacrifice proceed by resting upon each individual body.
Before the [main] performance begins, the offerings must be made in the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
Regarding this, Vāsiṣṭha Sātyahavya indeed said: "When it was said, 'The Soma has been spilled,' he replied, 'Do not be heedless; proceed! Indeed, this morning I completed the Soma sacrifice.
The Soma does not spill for him who, knowing this, drinks the Soma.
He used to sit upon a couch, stirring the Soma with barley meal and drink it.

(GBr_2,2.10f) "I indeed know the sacrifice in its entirety, he who knows these [sacrificial fires]"; (GBr_2,2.10g) "He shall not harm me. (GBr_2,2.10h) The drinking of Soma does not harm him who, knowing this, drinks the Soma.
When they said to him, "Why do you sit here on this seat, drinking Soma stirred with barley meal?

he replied, "I am establishing the sacrifice among the deities themselves. This is the case for one who knows thus; for one who knows thus, if a Brahmin offers an expiation in the sacrifice when the sacrifice has met with misfortune—[this is the expiation for the Brahmin].

(GBr_2,2.10k) He establishes the sacrifice in the deities themselves. (GBr_2,2.10l) He should offer a supplementary oblation for any injury to the sacrifice. (GBr_2,2.10m) This is for the sake of its having a common origin.
"Thirty-three, indeed, are the bodies of the sacrifice":
twenty-nine are the *stomabhāga* verses,
and three are the *savana*s.

The sacrifice is the fourth. By means of the *stomabhāga* formulas, he thus applies the *stomabhāgas*; by means of the pressings, the pressings; by means of the sacrifice, the sacrifice. Verily, all the bodies of this sacrifice become applied, all obtained, and all secured.
"At the impulse of God Savitṛ, for Bṛhaspati, sing the praise!
For whatever the gods impelled Savitṛ to impel, by that they prospered;
thus, impelled by Savitṛ, they indeed sing the praise.
They prosper;
indeed, his chants (*stoma*) succeed in the sacrifice,
the sacrificer prospers, and he prospers through his offspring.
[Corrected p.
302] (GBr_2,2.10z) It prospers for the sacrificial animals;
(GBr_2,2.10aa) it prospers for the Brahman priest—he for whom there is a Brahmā priest who knows thus. // 10 //
The gods and the asuras were indeed contending with one another.
Those gods performed exactly the same rites in the sacrifice; whatever the gods did, the asuras did that as well.
They did not go astray.
Those gods said, "Let us carry this sacrifice beyond the Asuras; we shall spread it above them.
Having covered it with these [formulas], they stepped forth: the sacrificial formulas in the sacrifice, "To the kindling-sticks, svāhā! and so on.
Beyond them, on the other side, they performed the sacrifice for themselves against the Asuras.
The Asuras did not follow that sacrifice of theirs;
consequently, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.

He who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice over the Asuras by passing above them, prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. One should offer these very oblations in a sacrifice performed for the sake of success, reciting four verses at a time;
one should offer them before the Prātaranuvāka.
(GBr_2,2.11m) Indeed, the sacrifice is only as great as this sacrifice; he appropriates that [sacrifice], (GBr_2,2.11n) and he becomes a performer of the sacrifice;
(GBr_2,2.11o) the other is a non-performer of the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,2.11p) One should offer with these very [oblations] prior to the twelve-day sacrifice;
(GBr_2,2.11q) for this indeed is the twelve-day sacrifice manifest before one's eyes.
(GBr_2,2.11r) Having grasped it, one should offer with these very [oblations].
Before the consecration—
this indeed is the direct consecration;
having touched it, he should touch the guest-offering with these [verses].
"By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice" (ŚS 7.5.1, PS 20.2.2, VaitS 16.15). // 11 //
(GBr_2,2.12a) Where he perceives, "O Brahman, the Soma has been spilled," he touches it with this [verse] and consecrates it:
"The god Savitṛ has now become worthy of our praise; at this time of day, he is to be invoked by men.
He who distributes treasures to the descendants of Manu—may he grant us here the most excellent wealth" (ṚV 4.54.1).
With the seven verses beginning, "The fires that are within the waters" (ŚS 3.21.1), he makes an additional offering;
whatever of his has been spilled, that he thereby restores to the fire with the words "go to your own place" (*svagā*).
"For Agni is the foundation of the oblations of those who perform good deeds.
Then, having moved away, he offers the drops-oblations with the mantra:
"The drop has fallen" (RV 10.17.11).
"Thus they offer. Whatever drops of his [the Soma] fall while it is being pressed, or whatever stalks [fall], those he now makes well-disposed (*svagā*) in the Āhavanīya fire;
for the Āhavanīya is the foundation of oblations.
(GBr_2,2.12h) "That drop of thine which falls" (ṚV 10.17.12a, PS 20.13.8a, VaitS 16.17), thus [it is said].
(GBr_2,2.12i) A *stoka* is indeed a *drapsa*.
(GBr_2,2.12j) "That stalk of thine which has fallen from the arms, from the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā*" (ṚV 10.17.12b).
"Thus, the soma-juice,
impelled by the arms, flows over the two pressing-skins;
or that which has fallen from the strainer of the Adhvaryu— that I offer to you with my mind, consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*."
"Thus it becomes, as if it were offered with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* and with the utterance of *svāhā*" (GBr 2.2.12). // 12 //
The seers did not see Indra face to face;
Vasiṣṭha alone saw him face to face. He was afraid that he might reveal [the knowledge] to the other seers.
He said, "I shall tell you, O Brāhmaṇa, how your subjects will be propagated by means of your priests;
but do not speak of this to the other seers. He then spoke these *stomabhāga* formulas to him.

(GBr_2,2.13g) Thereupon, the subjects with Vasiṣṭha as their domestic priest were born. (GBr_2,2.13h) These [bricks] are indeed the Stoma; this is their portion. (GBr_2,2.13i) That is why they are called Stomabhāgās—the "Stoma-portions."
"You are a ray; for dwelling, you!"—the gods are indeed the dwelling;
thus he announces the sacrifice to the gods.
"Thou art the advance for the sake of the sacred law (*dharma*)," he says; "the sacred law is human beings"—
thus he announces the sacrifice to human beings.
"You are the connection; you are the junction; you are the support.
There are indeed three worlds;
verily, he establishes the sacrifice in the worlds.
With "Thou art the support," he secures rain;
with "Thou art the protection, thou art the days," he creates a pair.
"You are the eager one; you are the wise one; you are the good smile.
There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, speech is the thirty-second, the tone is the thirty-third, and there are thirty-three gods.
Thus he has proclaimed the sacrifice to the gods.
"Thou art vigor; for the fathers, thee!"—thus he extends strength to the fathers. "Thou art a thread; for offspring, thee!"—thus [he says].
(GBr_2,2.13bb) He extends progeny along with cattle; (GBr_2,2.13cc) "Rich art thou; for the plants thee! (GBr_2,2.13dd) Thus he establishes the sacrifice in the plants themselves.
"You are the conqueror of armies; for the sake of cattle, you!"—with these words, he extends the offspring toward the cattle. "You are the victorious!"—[he says].
The *ṣoḍaśī* is indeed a thunderbolt;
that thunderbolt is set apart,
and therefore it is set apart from others.
"Thou art not non-existent," he says;
Prajāpati indeed is the seventeenfold;
verily, he wins Prajāpati. 13.
"You are the overlord; you are the supporter; you are the gliding one; you are the bestower of vigor"—thus [he says].
Breath, out-breath, sight, and hearing—these indeed made the person. He approaches the vital breaths for the sake of procreation.
“You are threefold; you are spreading forth; you are self-spreading; you are following along”—thus he creates a pair.
“You are an ascent; you are a forward growth; you are a gathering growth; you are a following growth.”
"Prajāpati himself—
'Thou art Vasuka, thou art Vasyaṣṭi, thou art Veṣaśrī'—
this is indeed stability."
"You are the stepping-stone, you are the crossing, you are the ascent, you are the emergence"—
this is indeed prosperity.
For whatever Savitṛ impelled for the gods, by that they prospered.
Impelled by Savitṛ, they indeed praise;
they prosper; "Praise has been offered to Bṛhaspati."

Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa was the Brahman-priest of the gods; having obtained his consent, [the Hotṛ] says at the morning pressing, "Om bhūr janat," with the Ṛg-verses on both sides, protected by the secret Atharva-Āṅgirasa hymns— thus is the praise performed.
Thus, at the midday pressing, with the words "Oṃ! Let the world of men arise," he is praised by the Yajus-formulas protected on both sides by the Atharvans and Aṅgirases;
thus, at the third pressing, with the words "Oṃ! Let the heavenly world arise."
"Chanted with the Sāmans on both sides, guarded by the Atharvans and Aṅgirases, it is guarded"—thus [he says].
Now, if it should be an Ahīna sacrifice, whether an Ukthya, a Ṣoḍaśin, a Vājapeya, an Atirātra, or an Aptoryāma, he gives permission from that point onward with all the Vyāhṛtis:
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May it increase, may it prosper, may it grow, may it be great—tat śam oṃ! Chant with Indra; chant with Indra!"—thus [he says], "Chant with Indra! and "Chant with Indra! indeed.
He who knows thus, and he who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice with the Stomabhāgas, becomes possessed of the senses, endowed with supernatural power, and self-controlled. 14.

(GBr_2,2.15a) Whoever indeed knows the *stomabhāga* formulas both in their extended form and in their reversed form, he may serve as the *brahman* priest for two parties who are contending over the Soma that has been pressed.

(GBr_2,2.15b) "Praise! For food! Praise! For strength! Praise! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ—Bṛhaspati for you, Prajāpati for you, the Vasu gods for you, the Rudra gods for you, the Āditya gods for you, the Sādhya gods for you, the Āptya gods for you!"
"We invoke all you gods, every one of you gods, from every side;
may he be ours alone among the people;
let him perform his heroic deed from here."
(GBr_2,2.15e) These indeed are the Stomabhāgas, both the forward-going and the backward-going.
(GBr_2,2.15f) Reciting them, the Brahman priest should look down repeatedly upon the others.
(GBr_2,2.15g) Thereupon, their Brahman priest falls headlong.
(GBr_2,2.15h) From that comes the sacrifice; (GBr_2,2.15i) from that, the sacrificer;
(GBr_2,2.15j) when the sacrificer falls headlong, that region where they sacrifice falls headlong.
(GBr_2,2.15k) Once, the gods and the asuras performed sacrifices in which the Soma was pressed simultaneously.
(GBr_2,2.15l) Now, Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa was the Brahman priest of the gods.
(GBr_2,2.15m) Reciting the *stomabhāga* formulas—both those for the advancing and those for the retreating [sacrificial rites]—he looked down from above upon the Brahman priest of the asuras.
Then, with their heads downward, Brahmā fell;
after him, the sacrifice;
after that, the Asuras. // 15 //
The gods lost the sacrifice;
they won it back from the Āgnīdhra fire-altar.
Therefore, that part of the sacrifice which is the Āgnīdhra is invincible.
When he distributes the hearths from the Āgnīdhra fire, he thereby extends this [sacrifice] once again for the sake of victory.
Indeed, those who creep out for the *bahiṣpavamāna* go away from here.
When the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, he says:
"O *agnīdh*, distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes.
Thus, they return while continuing to perform the sacrifice without letting it be defeated.
(GBr_2,2.16j) He distributes coals at two pressings and sticks at the third pressing, so that there may be a residue of the *śukra*.
(GBr_2,2.16k) Moreover, it thus comes into being.
(GBr_2,2.16l) From the south, indeed, the Rakṣases sought to strike down the sacrifice of the gods.
They struck them down with the Āgnīdhra fire-altar;
therefore, standing facing south, the Agnīdh calls for the response.
This is for the conquest of the sacrifice and for the striking away of the Rākṣasas, for the striking away of the Rākṣasas. 16.

Regarding this they say: "Now, why is it that they offer the *pravṛtāhuti* oblations only at the Soma sacrifice, and not at the *haviryajña*? [The answer is: "Incomplete indeed is that worship of the gods which is the *haviryajña*;
but this worship of the gods, which is the Soma sacrifice, is complete."
Therefore, at the Soma sacrifice alone, they offer the *pravṛtāhuti* oblations:
"May I be dear to Speech; may I be dear to the Lord of Speech. O Goddess Speech, place me in that which is the sweetest part of Speech!
Svāhā to Speech! Svāhā to the Lord of Speech! Svāhā to Sarasvatī! Svāhā to Sarasvatī!"
He offers with the utterance *svāhā* in front;
therefore, from that point upward, speech, being released, carries the sacrifice by means of the mind. For the mind is pleased by the mind.

(GBr_2,2.17h) Now some offer seven oblations, saying, "The seven meters have been set in motion, one for each mantra. (GBr_2,2.17i) Just as the girdle is fastened to separate the pure from the impure, even so these [bricks] are laid down to separate the pure from the impure, for the separation of the sacrifice. (GBr_2,2.17j) For the worlds of the gods are to the east of the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), while those of men are to the west.
Therefore, drink the Soma; you must not approach the Dhiṣṇya hearths,
for this is the people,
and they are ascending to the world of the gods.
(GBr_2,2.17n) Of these, this is the abode and the place of departure: namely, the Āgnīdhra and the Sadas.
(GBr_2,2.17o) Whoever moves about there without knowing this incurs misfortune;
(GBr_2,2.17p) but he who moves about knowing this does not incur the misfortune pertaining to the *dhiṣṇya* hearths. // 17 // [ed. vidvant]
The sacrifice, indeed, is Prajāpati;
in it are all desires, all offerings, and all immortality.
These are its guardians, namely the *dhiṣṇya* fires.
(GBr_2,2.18d) When he is about to enter the *sadas*, he pays homage, saying:
(GBr_2,2.18e) "Homage! Homage! (GBr_2,2.18f) For the gods do not disregard homage.
(GBr_2,2.18g) Having paid homage, they release the Creator;
(GBr_2,2.18h) then he enters this Prajāpati, the sacrifice, saying, "Homage! Homage!
(GBr_2,2.18i) For the gods do not transcend homage.
(GBr_2.2.18j) There, as a sacrificer, he attains all desires; he attains all desires. // 18 //
(GBr 2.2.19a) He who knows the Gandharvas of the Sadas does not meet with any affliction in the Sadas. (GBr 2.2.19b) When about to enter the Sadas, he should say: "Homage to the spectator!
(GBr 2.2.19c) Agni indeed is the spectator; to him he thus entrusts himself.
(GBr_2,2.19d) He who knows this reaches a full lifespan; he does not die before old age.
(GBr_2,2.19e) Having entered the sacrificial hall, one should say: "Homage to Upaśrotra!
(GBr_2,2.19f) For Vāyu is indeed Upaśrotra.
Therefore, he indeed entrusts himself to him; he reaches a full lifespan and does not die before old age, who knows thus.
While crawling toward the *sadas* hall, he should say: "Homage to the Anukhyātr!"
The sun, indeed, is the overseer; he entrusts his very self to him. He who knows this reaches a full lifespan and does not die before old age.
Having entered the sacrificial hall, he should say, "Homage to the witness.
For a Brahmin is indeed the witness;
it is to him that he entrusts himself.
(GBr_2,2.19p) He who knows this attains a full lifespan; he does not die before old age.
(GBr_2,2.19q) Those Gandharvas are indeed the members of the sacrificial assembly (*sadasyāḥ*).
(GBr_2,2.19r) Whoever, not knowing these Gandharvas who are the members of the assembly, enters the assembly hall, meets with misfortune within the assembly.
Now, he who moves about as one possessing this knowledge does not meet with any misfortune in the sacrificial assembly (*sadas*).
Indeed, by means of this [knowledge], the Aṅgirasas used to encompass the entire assembly; they did not meet with any misfortune in the sacrificial assembly.

(GBr_2,2.19v) Now, for those whom he might desire, "May they not meet with misfortune in the *sadas*," he should address the entire *sadas* on their behalf with this [formula]. They do not meet with misfortune in the *sadas*.
(GBr_2,2.19w) But him whom he might desire, "May he die," from him he should cut off these [formulas].
It is cognized. 19.

Regarding this they say: "Since the sacrifice belongs to Indra, then why do only two—the Hotṛ and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin—offer at the morning pressing from the directly perceived [verses] dedicated to Indra with two verses addressed to Indra? [The verses are:
"This sweet Soma is for you... (*Ṛgveda* 8.65.8).
"Thus the Hotṛ offers the sacrifice" (GBr 2.2.20c);
"O Indra, we [choose] you, the bull... (RV 3.40.1;
VaitS 19.6)—thus the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
(GBr_2,2.20d) How do those [verses] addressed to various deities (GBr_2,2.20e) become addressed to Indra (GBr_2,2.20f)? [For example:
"We invoke Mitra... (ṚV 1.23.4a).
"Thus the Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites: 'Varuṇa for the drinking of Soma' (RV 1.23.4b).
Whatever has been drunk indeed possesses the form of Indra."
(GBr_2,2.20i) By this, he gratifies Indra.
(GBr_2,2.20j) "O Maruts, in whosever abode..."—
with these words, the Potṛ priest performs the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,2.20k) "That person is the best-protected" (*sa sugopātamo janaḥ*), as stated in *Ṛgveda* 1.86.1c and *Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra* 20.1.2c. [The edition reads *sugopatamo*, corrected on p.
Indra, indeed, is the guardian;
that is the form of Indra. By this, he gratifies Indra.
"O Agni, bring the wives here," with these words the Neṣṭṛ priest sacrifices;
"Tvaṣṭṛ for the drinking of Soma," with these words.
(GBr_2,2.20q) Whatever has indeed been drunk is the form of Indra;
(GBr_2,2.20r) by that he gratifies Indra.
(GBr_2,2.20s) [To him whose food is bulls, whose food is cows... (ṚV 8.43.11a, PS 3.12.6a, ŚS 3.21.6a)
"Thus the Āgnīdhra priest sacrifices" (GBr 2.2.20t).
"To the Ordainer whose back is Soma" (RV 8.43.11b; PS 3.12.6b; ŚS 3.21.6b/20.1.3b)—thus [he says].
Indra, indeed, is the Ordainer.
That is the form of Indra;
by means of it, he gratifies Indra:
"Come hither with the gods who arrive at dawn, O ye of noble wealth, Indra and Agni, for the drinking of the Soma" (RV 8.38.7).
(GBr_2,2.20y) They are self-sufficient for the Acchāvāka.
(GBr_2,2.20z) Thus, these verses belong to Indra;
(GBr_2,2.20aa) in that they have various deities, he thereby gratifies other deities.
Insofar as they are *gāyatrī* verses, they belong to Agni; therefore, by means of these, the threefold [Veda] is attained. // 20 //
(GBr_2,2.21a) Indeed, all of them at the midday pressing sacrifice the *prasthita* cups with verses addressed to Indra (*aindrī*) directly;
(GBr_2,2.21b) some [do so] with verses containing the word "to pierce" (*abhitṛṇavatī*).
(GBr_2,2.21c) "Drink the Soma, O fierce one, for which you are the piercer" (*ṚV* 6.17.1).
"Thus the Hotṛ sacrifices" (GBr 2.2.21d); "O protect him, he who is the consumer of the *ṛjīṣa*, the deliverer" (RV 6.17.2)— thus the Maitrāvaruṇa.
"Thus protect us; as of old, may it exhilarate you"—with these words the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites].
"Come hither; they call you one who desires Soma"—with these words the Potṛ [recites].
"O Soma, this is yours; come hither!"—thus the Neṣṭṛ [recites];
"For Indra, the Somas known from of old"—thus the Acchāvāka.
"Filled is his jar, svāhā!"—
thus says the Āgnīdhra.
In this way, these [verses] become those that overcome.
Indra indeed did not conquer the morning pressing. He pierced through to the midday pressing with these [verses].
Because he pierced through to the midday pressing with these, they are called *abhitṛṇvatī* ("piercing through"). 21.

Regarding this they say: "Since the third pressing belongs to Indra and the Ṛbhus, why then does only one person at the third pressing offer the *prasthita* cups with a verse explicitly addressed to Indra and the Ṛbhus?"—[the answer is:
"The Hotṛ alone [offers], with [the verse]: 'O Indra, [drink] what has been sprinkled together by the Ṛbhus, who possess booty' (*Ṛgveda* 3.60.5)."
(GBr_2,2.22c) The others have various deities;
(GBr_2,2.22d) how do they come to have the *aindrārbhavya* verses?
(GBr_2,2.22e) (*indrāvaruṇā sutapāv imaṃ sutam* [ṚV 6.68.10])...
"Thus the Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the offering prayer. [PS 20.7.5a, ŚS 7.58.1a] (The edition reads *satam*, corrected on p.
"Your chariot comes for the sacrifice, to the feast of the gods"— thus he recites many verses.
"That is the form of the Ṛbhus" and "O Indra and Soma, drink for Bṛhaspati"— with these words, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest performs the sacrifice.
"May the drops, self-sustaining, enter you two"—
thus there are many verses;
that is the form of the Ṛbhus.
"May your swift-gliding coursers carry you hither," with these words the Potṛ priest sacrifices;
"with your swift wings, go forth with your arms."
"Thus, many indeed are the vehicles;
that is the form of the Ṛbhus:
'O you who are easily invoked, come hither to us' (RV 2.36.3)."
"Thus the Neṣṭṛ priest sacrifices," "Go ye!"— these many [calls] are indeed the form of the Ṛbhus.
"O Indra and Viṣṇu, drink of this honeyed [soma]"—
with these words the Acchāvāka offers the sacrifice;
"the intoxicating juices have come to you both."
"Thus there are many utterances;
that is the form of the Ṛbhus:
'This hymn to the worthy Jātavedas' [RV 1.94.1a]."
"Thus the Āgnīdhra priest sacrifices" (GBr 2.2.22); "Like a chariot, let us fashion it with our wisdom" (RV 1.94.1b)— thus he recites many verses.
That is the form of the Ṛbhus;
thus indeed these [verses] belong to Indra and the Ṛbhus.
In that they have various deities, he thereby gratifies other deities.
And as for the *jagatprāsāhā*: the third pressing is indeed connected with the *jagatī* meter; it serves for the complete attainment of the third pressing.
They speak speech that is discerning and pleasing;
they cause the Brāhmaṇa to discern and cause the son of Prajāpati to take pleasure.
"They speak the truth. Indeed, that which is the eye is the truth among humans;
therefore, they say to one who is describing something, "Did you see it?"
When he says, "I saw it," people believe him accordingly;
however, if it were something he himself had seen, he would not believe many people. Therefore, they speak words that are discerning and pleasing.
(GBr_2.2.23j) Indeed, their speech becomes truly superior once it has been uttered. // 23 //
The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed a sacrifice that has come together.
To whose sacrifice do the gods come, and to whose do they not?
This day belongs in common to many sacrificers.
Therefore, on the previous day, one should take possession of the deities.
For indeed, those who take possession of the deities on the previous day—their sacrifice comes to them on the following day.
Therefore, one should mutter the four verses of the Vihavya hymn.
For those who know the sacrifice indeed believe that the sacrifice is completed by the Soma alone; thus the sacrifice is completed by the sacrifice. // 24 //
Thus ends the second chapter in the latter part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_2,3.1a) Om. The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the vessel for the gods. (GBr_2,3.1b) When one utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call, one satisfies the deities with that very vessel of the gods.

(GBr_2,3.1c) Furthermore, when one satisfies them at the conclusion as they are thirsting, it is in this very way that one satisfies the deities when one utters the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭ*).
Just as one there satisfies horses or cattle by repeatedly calling out to them, even so does he satisfy the deities when he performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
"They say that they wait upon these very fires, the *dhiṣṇya*s;
but why then do they offer in the eastern fire alone, and why does he perform the *vaṣaṭ* call in the eastern fire?"
(GBr_2,3.1g) When he pronounces the secondary *vaṣaṭ* with the words, "O Agni, accept the Soma," it is by that very act that he performs the *vaṣaṭ*-call; he thereby gratifies the *dhiṣṇya* hearths.
(GBr_2,3.1h) Now they say: "Those for whom he does not pronounce the secondary *vaṣaṭ*, they consume the completed *soma* offerings.
(GBr_2,3.1i) Regarding this they ask: "What, then, is the portion of the *sviṣṭakṛt* for the *soma*?"
(GBr_2,3.1j) "By the very fact that he performs the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call with the words, 'O Agni, accept the Soma,' they say that they consume the Soma-offerings as completed.
(GBr_2,3.1k) And this which he performs as the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the portion of the *sviṣṭakṛt* for the Soma. // 1 //
The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed a thunderbolt.
If he should hate anyone, he should utter the *vaṣaṭ*-call while meditating upon that person with his mind; thus he hurls that thunderbolt at him.
He utters "vaṣaṭ" six times; for there are six seasons,
[and it is] for the attainment of the seasons.
With "Vauṣaṭ," he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call. Verily, "vau" is the year, and "ṣaṭ" are the six seasons; thus he establishes him within the seasons.
He establishes them in the seasons. Regarding this, Vaida used to say: "By means of this, one indeed establishes these six—the sky established in the intermediate space."
The atmosphere is in the earth;
the earth is in the waters;
the waters are in truth.
"Truth is established in Brahman;
Brahman is established in austerity"—these very deities are the foundations; as they are established, this entire universe is established after them.
He who knows thus becomes established with offspring and cattle. // 2 //
(GBr_2,3.3a) There are indeed three *vaṣaṭ*-calls: (GBr_2,3.3b) the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the one that covers the abode (*dhāmacchad*), and the empty (*rikta*).
(GBr_2,3.3c) That which he utters as the loud *vaṣaṭ*-call with strength—that is the thunderbolt.
He strikes down each [oblation] as a weapon against the hater, the rival, for him whom he is fated to strike down, so that he may be struck down.
Therefore, it should be offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call by one who has a rival.
Now, that which is even and continuous, reaching its own abode, reaches the abode of heaven.
(GBr_2,3.3g) After him, both offspring and cattle follow. (GBr_2,3.3h) Therefore, he who desires offspring or cattle should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call [at this point].
(GBr_2,3.3i) But that by which one fails in the other six [oblations] is empty.
(GBr_2,3.3j) He ruins himself; he ruins the sacrificer.
(GBr_2,3.3k) The one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* becomes worse off, as does the one for whom he utters the *vaṣaṭ*.
(GBr_2,3.3l) Therefore, one should not seek his favor.
"What evil or good of the sacrificer would he care about? he used to say, "he who is his *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.
In this very matter, one should do with him exactly as one desires.

If one should desire of someone, "May he be exactly as he was before he sacrificed, so that he remains the same while sacrificing," then one should utter the *vaṣaṭ* for him in exactly the same way as one recites the *ṛc* for him.
(GBr_2,3.3p) He makes him exactly equal.
(GBr_2,3.3q) If he should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should recite the *ṛc* for him more loudly and utter the *vaṣaṭ* more softly; thus he makes him worse off.
(GBr_2,3.3r) Indeed, he makes him worse off.
(GBr_2,3.3s) If he should desire of someone, "May he become more prosperous," he should recite that person's *ṛc* verse in a lower tone and utter the *vaṣaṭ* call in a higher tone.
He thereby makes him more prosperous; he bestows fortune upon him, indeed, for the sake of fortune. (3)
(GBr_2,3.4a) For whichever deity the oblation has been taken, one should utter the *vaṣaṭ* while meditating on that deity with the mind.
(GBr_2,3.4b) Thus one directly gratifies that deity;
(GBr_2,3.4c) one directly encompasses the deity.
(GBr_2,3.4d) One should offer the *vaṣaṭ* call continuously with the *ṛc*. (GBr_2,3.4e) This is for the sake of continuity. (GBr_2,3.4f) He who knows thus is joined with offspring and cattle. // 4 //
The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed a thunderbolt.
This very [thunderbolt], when hurled, shone forth unappeased; no one at all knew its pacification or its foundation.
Therefore, even now, death is as it were more prevalent.
Of this, indeed, speech is the pacification and this is the foundation.
Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he follows it with the mantra: "Speech! He says:

"O *vaṣaṭ*-call, do not abandon me, nor may I abandon you. I invoke the mind with the *bṛhat* [sāman] and the body with the *vyāna* [breath]. You are the foundation; go to the foundation; lead me to the foundation."
"One should cause it to go," [the edition reads *pratiṣṭhīsi*, corrected on p. 302].
Regarding this, Dīrgha indeed said: "This is truly eternal power, sovereign might, force, force"—with these words one should consecrate it with the mantra.
(GBr_2,3.5h) Vitality (*ojas*) and power (*sahas*) are indeed the two most beloved bodies of the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
(GBr_2,3.5i) He thus brings about fulfillment through those two beloved bodies.
(GBr_2,3.5j) He who knows this prospers with a beloved body. // 5 //
Speech, as well as the out-breath and the in-breath, are the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
At every *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, they depart.
He addresses them with the mantra: "Speech, vigor, force; vigor, out-breath and in-breath—[be] in me."
He establishes speech, as well as the out-breath and the in-breath, within his own self through the Hotṛ;
he attains a full lifespan and does not die before old age, who knows thus.
"Be gracious to our heart when drunk, O Indu; O Soma, be very kind like a father to his son.
Like a friend to a friend, O wise one of wide renown, prolong our life for us to live, O Soma!"—with these words he touches himself.
(GBr_2,3.6h) "This [Soma], if not touched back, is capable of carrying away the life of the sacrificer; let him not consume it without being touched back.
(GBr_2,3.6i) Therefore, when he touches it back with this [formula], he thereby extends his life.
(GBr_2,3.6j) With the two verses, "Swell up" and "May thy milks," they cause the cups to swell, using these appropriate [verses].
(GBr_2,3.6k) Whatever is appropriate in the sacrifice is successful. // 6 //
The seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Therefore, when they perform the seasonal offerings, they place the vital breaths within the sacrificer.
They sacrifice with the formula, "To the season! six times.
(GBr_2,3.7d) They thus place the out-breath (*prāṇa*) in the sacrificer;
(GBr_2,3.7e) "With four [verses] they sacrifice according to the seasons," (GBr_2,3.7f) whereby they place the in-breath (*apāna*) in the sacrificer.
(GBr_2,3.7g) Twice with the words "by the season," they place it above.

(GBr_2,3.7h) Thus, they bestow the diffused breath (*vyāna*) upon the sacrificer. (GBr_2,3.7i) Once gathered together, that breath is distributed threefold as out-breath (*prāṇa*), in-breath (*apāna*), and diffused breath (*vyāna*).

(GBr_2,3.7j) Then, multiplied otherwise, (GBr_2,3.7k) so indeed does the sacrificer attain a full lifespan; he prospers in this world (GBr_2,3.7l) and attains imperishable immortality in the heavenly world.
These seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); therefore, they perform the sacrifice from there without taking a breath,
for the continuity of the vital breaths.
For these vital breaths are, as it were, continuous;
moreover, the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*) are indeed the seasons,
and the concluding *vaṣaṭ* call is the end of the year.
If someone were to pronounce the *anuvaṣaṭ* call here, he would cause the seasons that have not yet concluded to conclude.
If someone were to say of him there, "He has caused the un-concluded seasons to conclude; it will become a time of distress," it would surely come to pass so. (7)

Regarding this they say: "Since [the rule] is 'Let the Hotṛ sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ sacrifice!', why then does the Maitrāvaruṇa direct the Hotṛ with the words 'Let the Hotṛ sacrifice! Let the Hotṛ sacrifice! even though there are other priests present who are chanters of the *hotrā*? Speech indeed is the Hotṛ; speech is all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
"May Vāk sacrifice, may Vāk sacrifice"—thus [it is said].
Now, all these are indeed the seven *hotṛ*s; or rather, it is declared in a *ṛc*: "The seven *hotṛ*s sacrifice in due season.
Then, those which follow are twelve *ṛcs* for the sake of non-repetition (*ajāmitā*).
They indeed become twelve;
for twelve months are a year,
and the year is Prajāpati.
Prajāpati is the sacrifice.

If someone were to eat [the remnant] there, and someone were to say of him, "The consumption is unappeased; it was not accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call; you have swallowed it into yourself and will not live," so indeed would it be. [Ed. reads *anānuvaṣaṭkṛta*; corrected to *ananuvaṣaṭkṛta* by Patyal.]

(GBr_2,3.8k) "He who indeed should eat—the breath is the food, the breath has entered the self"—it is exactly so. (GBr_2,3.8l) "One should, as it were, smear [the lips] and likewise smell; and this also applies in the case of offerings to two deities. (GBr_2,3.8m) That is what they declare there as the instruction.
Now, because the two Adhvaryus, being distinct, do not pass into one another, therefore one season does not pass into another season. // 8 //
When Prajāpati created offspring, he indeed created them exhausted.
He breathed upon them with the *hiṃkāra* alone.
Those offspring clung to the horse; for this sacrifice is indeed bound when the oblations are cooked, when the Soma is pressed, and when the victim animal is immolated.
"By means of the *hiṃ* sound, Prajāpati indeed smells the slain [victim] for the sake of the sacrifice’s being unhurt, for the attainment of the sacrifice, and for the vigor of the sacrifice;
therefore the *hiṃ* is uttered. And therefore, among sons, he who cares for them becomes the most excellent."
For Prajāpati indeed smells him; for when a bird sits upon its egg and it has not yet been hatched, she too utters the *hiṅ* sound.
Moreover, they say that a great seer indeed saw this [song] to be sung at the beginning of the sacrifice.
This *hiṃ* sound is that which is to be sung at the beginning of the sacrifice.
Regarding this, the gods and the seers said, "Let this one be Vasiṣṭha, who has perceived that which is to be sung by us at the beginning of the sacrifice.
This *hiṃ* sound is that which is to be sung at the beginning of the sacrifice.

Thereupon, he indeed became the most excellent among the gods. Because he was the most excellent, he was the most eminent (*vasiṣṭha*). Therefore, one should not exclude from the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that Brahmin who belongs to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, indeed, his *hiṃkāra* becomes pleasing.
Now, when the gods and the seers perceived the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*, they perceived these two.
From the very place where they perceived them, they milked from him this entire yield.
These two, namely the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, are indeed milked out and exhausted;
they are replenished by the *hiṃkāra* alone.
When the *ṛc* and the *sāman* have been replenished by the *hiṃkāra*, they yield their milk for the sacrificer.
Therefore, having uttered the *hiṃ* sound, the Adhvaryus press the Soma; having uttered the *hiṃ* sound, the Udgātṛs chant with the Sāman;
and having uttered the *hiṃ* sound, those who recite the hymns perform their priestly office with the Ṛc.
The Atharvans perform the office of the Brahman priest after uttering the syllable *hiṃ*;
therefore, it is uttered. For Prajāpati indeed smells him [the sacrificer] from there.
Now, moreover, they say: "The cow alone indeed maintains the vow of Prajāpati;
upon her both kinds of animals depend for their livelihood—both those that are domestic and those that are wild. 9.
"The divine clans are to be arranged," they say;
"the metre is to be established in the metre.
At the morning pressing, he calls out with the three-syllable formula, "Śaṃsāvoṃ!"
"Let us two recite for the gods," says the Adhvaryu; he responds with a five-syllable phrase.
That becomes eight syllables, for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
(GBr_2,3.10g) Thus they two fashioned the Gāyatrī itself at the beginning of the morning pressing.
(GBr_2,3.10h) Having recited [the hymn], he says, "The hymn has been recited" (*uktham vāci*), which consists of four syllables.
(GBr_2,3.10i) The Adhvaryu responds, "Om, the hymn-reciter" (*om ukthaśāḥ*), which also consists of four syllables.
That becomes eight syllables;
for the Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables.
Thus, at the morning pressing, they two fashioned the Gāyatrī on both sides.

(GBr_2,3.10m) At the midday pressing, the Adhvaryu calls out with the six-syllable formula, "O Adhvaryu, recite! Let us two recite! (GBr_2,3.10n) The Adhvaryu responds with the five-syllable formula, "Recite for the gods! (GBr_2,3.10o) Thus, it becomes eleven syllables.

The *triṣṭubh* indeed consists of eleven syllables; thus they have fashioned the *triṣṭubh* at the forenoon pressing. Having recited [the hymn], he says, "The hymn has been recited for Indra," which consists of six syllables.
"Om! Recite the offering prayer! replies the Adhvaryu, which consists of five syllables.
That becomes eleven syllables.
The *triṣṭubh* indeed consists of eleven syllables; thus they have fashioned the *triṣṭubh* on both sides at the midday pressing.
At the third pressing, he calls out with the seven-syllable formula: "O Adhvaryu, recite the *śastra*; *Śaṃsāvoṃ*!"
The Adhvaryu responds with "Śaṃsavo daiva," which consists of five syllables;
thus it becomes twelve syllables.
Indeed, the Jagatī meter consists of twelve syllables.
Thus they two fashioned the Jagatī meter at the beginning of the third pressing.
Having recited the hymn, he says, "The hymn has been recited for Indra and for the gods," consisting of nine syllables;
the Adhvaryu responds with "Om, the hymn-reciter! consisting of three syllables.
That becomes twelve syllables;
the Jagatī indeed consists of twelve syllables. Thus, they two fashioned the Jagatī on both sides at the third pressing.
(GBr_2,3.10ee) This, indeed, is that: he establishes the metre upon the metre. (GBr_2,3.10ff) He who knows this arranges the hosts of the gods.
(GBr_2,3.10gg) Concerning this, there is also this verse recited: "That which is the Gāyatra placed upon the Gāyatra... (10)
Now, these various meters are like pits between [the two worlds];
and these two deities are the most massive and most powerful, standing not apart from them.
By means of those two, one proceeds.
That which is the "leaping from the pit" is the form of ascent leading to heaven;
one should transition through it without taking breath.
Indeed, the *praṇava* is immortality.
By means of the immortal itself, one crosses over death.
Just as one might cross a pit by means of a raft or a bamboo pole, even so does one continue on by means of the *praṇava*.
Indeed, the *praṇava* is Brahman.
By means of the Brahman itself, he thus connects him with the Brahman.
The *praṇava* should be pure for those desiring offspring;
it should end in the syllable *m* for those desiring stability.
"Some say that the *praṇava* should end with the letter *m*;
however, it is established as being simply pure (*śuddha*).
Thus has the *praṇava* been investigated."
"Now, therefore, [the rule] that 'here it is pure, here it is full'—
the *praṇava* should be pure in the interval between the *śastra* and the *anuvacana*, so said Kauṣītaki."
Thus it becomes joined; the letter *m* at the end serves for the purpose of a pause (*avasāna*), and the pause is indeed a firm foundation.
It is for the sake of stability;
and also for the attainment of both desires. These two are indeed the flows of the meters; they carry the lower meter beyond to the higher meter.
It does not diminish his lifespan.
If a meter should be over-prolated, one should mentally pierce whomever one hates right there.
[If it is said,] "The cutting edge of the meters is running away or being shattered."
He recites the first verse thrice and the last verse thrice; thereby he ties the sacrificial grass of the sacrifice for stability, strength, and so it may not come loose.
Even if a metre other than the Gāyatrī should be employed at the morning pressing, it should be recited half-verse by half-verse in the form of the Gāyatrī.

(GBr_2,3.11ee) Now, regarding the form of the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana): (GBr_2,3.11ff) it is not the case that the Triṣṭubh and Jagatī [metres] are used at this point when the recitation is by half-verses; rather, whatever metre may be employed at the morning pressing, the recitation for these two [metres] should be by quarters—that is the established rule. (GBr_2,3.12a) Now, therefore, follows the morning pressing of the one-day sacrifice (ekāha).
While Prajāpati was performing the sacrifice, Death indeed assailed him with the noose of death at the very moment of the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.
He [Prajāpati] took refuge in the *ājya* chant by means of a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni.
Seeing him, Death indeed bypassed Prajāpati.
He sat down as the *sāman* at the head;
he reached the *pra-uga* with the verse addressed to Vāyu.
Death, indeed, beholding Prajāpati, moved around him.
He sat down during the midday *pavamāna* chant; with an *aindrī* triṣṭubh verse, he entered upon the *marutvatīya* hymn.
Indeed, Death, beholding him, drew back from Prajāpati.
(GBr_2,3.12k) He sat down upon that very wealth for the first *stotriya* verse of the *niṣkevalya* chant.
(GBr_2,3.12l) He overthrew him.
(GBr_2,3.12m) Therefore, indeed, whoever sits down first, being wise, overthrows that [opponent].
(GBr_2,3.12n) Death fled from the *anavakāśa* [section], while the other [the Hotṛ] praised the *niṣkevalya*.
(GBr_2,3.12o) Therefore, the Hotṛ begins with the Marutvatīya as a single *uktha*, namely the *niṣkevalya* itself.
(GBr_2,3.12p) For it was here that Death abandoned Prajāpati. // 12 //
He said to Mitra and Varuṇa, "You two must restore for us this limb of the sacrifice, [the cup] dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. They said, "So be it.
Having become united and powerful, they overcame death by force.
For those two, Mitrāvaruṇa and Agni, restored this limb of his sacrifice;
therefore, at the morning pressing, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the verses dedicated to Mitrāvaruṇa,
for those two restored this limb of his sacrifice.
And furthermore, as for why he recites the verses addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa:
"At the rising of the sun, O Mitra and Varuṇa, we shall worship you with salutations and oblations" (RV 7.63.5);
"And at the awakening of the dawn, together with the rays of the sun, [we worship] you two" (RV 1.137.2).
Thus it is declared by the *ṛc*:
"Come to us, O Mitra and Varuṇa" (*Ṛgveda* 3.62.16), and "Come to us, O destroyers of enemies" (*Ṛgveda* 5.71.1).
Thus are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.
"Sing forth to Mitra" (*pra vo mitrāya gāyata*,
ṚV 5.68.1) is the opening of the *uktha*.
"Of Mitra and Varuṇa... serves as the *paryāsa*; "Come hither, O Mitra and Varuṇa... he recites for the sacrifice.
These two deities alone he gratifies according to their respective shares;
having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call,
and they touch [the offering] in response.
(GBr_2,3.13o) They do not cause them to swell; (GBr_2,3.13p) for those without the Ārāśaṃsa verses do not sit down. 13.
He said to Indra: "Do you restore for us this limb of the sacrifice, [the office of] the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
"With whom? he asked. "With Sūrya," [he replied].
"So be it," they both replied.
Having become united and strong, they overcame death by force. For these two performed this part of his sacrifice, namely the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* office.
Therefore, at the morning pressing, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites the verses addressed to Indra that pertain to the limbs of Sūrya;
for those two have thereby restored this limb of his sacrifice.
And as to why he recites the verses addressed to Indra that pertain to the limbs of Sūrya—
"O Indra, drink of the pressed juice according to your desire; for the morning pressing is your first draught"—thus it is declared by this *ṛc* (GBr 2.3.14j).
"Come hither, for we have pressed [the juice] for you" (RV 8.17.1).
"Come to us who have pressed the soma" (*ā no yāhi sutāvataḥ*, *ṚV* 8.17.4;
*VaitS* 21.1)—these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
"This one, O you who observe all people... (*ayam u tvā vicarṣaṇe*, *ṚV* 8.17.7).
"Thus is the opening of the *uktha* (*ity ukthamukham*); 'Up indeed, O you who have heard the evil' (*ud ghed abhiśrutāmagham*) is the *paryāsa*."
With the mantra, "O Indra, finder of wisdom" (*indra kratuvidam*), he performs the sacrifice;
he thus gratifies these two deities according to their respective shares.
Having uttered *vaṣaṭ*, he utters the secondary *vaṣaṭ*.
(GBr_2,3.14p) They touch [the cups] facing them (GBr_2,3.14q),
but they do not cause them to swell (GBr_2,3.14r), for those who do not have the *ārāśaṃsa* verses do not sit down. 14.
Indra and Agni said, "The two of you must restore for us this missing limb of the sacrifice, the *acchāvākīyā*.
They replied, "So be it.
Having become united and powerful, they overcame death by force.
For these two indeed restored this limb of his sacrifice, namely the *acchāvākīyā*;
therefore, at the morning pressing, the *acchāvāka* recites the hymns addressed to Indra and Agni,
for these two indeed restored this limb of his sacrifice.

Furthermore, when he recites the verses addressed to Indra and Agni, it is expressed by the verse: "Come hither with the gods who travel at dawn, O ye of noble wealth, Indra and Agni, for the drinking of the Soma" (RV 8.38.7).
(GBr_2,3.15h) "(O Indra and Agni, come hither!
and "I invoke the two bountiful slayers of Vṛtra"—these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses of the *acchāvāka*. [The edition reads *toṣā*.]
(GBr_2,3.15i) "O Indra and Agni, from the work... (*ṚV* 3.12.7)— this is the opening of the *uktha*.
(GBr_2,3.15j) "Here I invoke Indra and Agni" (*ṚV* 1.21.1)—
this is the *paryāsa*.
(GBr_2,3.15k) He performs the sacrifice with "O Indra and Agni, come hither."
These very two deities he gratifies according to their respective portions;
having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call,
and they touch [the offering] in response.
(GBr_2,3.15o) They do not cause [the cups] to swell; (GBr_2,3.15p) for those without the Ārāśaṃsa verses do not sit down. // 15 //
(GBr_2,3.16a) Then, at the calls "Śaṃsāvoṃ," they each call out four times for the *stotriyā*, the *anurūpa*, the *ukthamukha*, and the *paridhānīyā*.
(GBr_2,3.16b) For there are four quarters;
(GBr_2,3.16c) thus they find firm support in the quarters.
Moreover, cattle have four feet;
[this is] for the attainment of cattle.
Furthermore, the *hotraka* priests at the morning pressing have four joints.
Therefore, all recite four *gāyatrī* verses;
for the morning pressing is of the *gāyatrī* nature.
All conclude with verses containing the word "equal" (*samavatī*).
(GBr_2,3.16j) Now, as to why they conclude with the *samavatī* verses: (GBr_2,3.16k) the *paryāsa* is indeed the end,
and the *udarka* is the end.
(GBr_2,3.16m) They conclude with the very same verse with which they began.
(GBr_2,3.16n) All sacrifice with verses containing the word "mad" (intoxicating).
(GBr_2,3.16o) In that they sacrifice with verses containing the word "mad," they all sacrifice with verses containing the words "pressed," "drunk," and "suitable."
(GBr_2,3.16p) That which is appropriate in the sacrifice is successful.
(GBr_2,3.16q) All perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
(GBr_2,3.16r) The *anuvaṣaṭ* call belongs to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
(Let us not exclude the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
This world, indeed, is the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
Of it, there are five directions and five *uktha*s of the morning pressing.
(GBr_2,3.16v) By means of these five hymns, he attains these five directions; he attains these five directions. // 16 //
(GBr_2,3.17a) They indeed kill this Soma when they press it; (GBr_2,3.17b) they indeed kill the sacrifice when the sacrificial gifts are led away;
(GBr_2,3.17c) they indeed strengthen the sacrifice [thereby].
That is the reason for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) being called *dakṣiṇā*. The heavenly world is indeed the midday pressing;
since the sacrificial gifts are led forward at the midday pressing, it is for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(GBr_2,3.17g) Much is to be given.
(GBr_2,3.17h) For the sacrificer thus constructs a bridge for the conquest of the heavenly world and for the conquest of progeny. (GBr_2,3.17i)
(GBr_2,3.17j) He offers two oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire;
(GBr_2,3.17k) the *adhvaryu* causes [the sacrificer] to step forward with the verse addressed to Agni; (GBr_2,3.17l) [he offers] in the *āgnīdhrīya* fire with a verse addressed to Agni.
By that [gift], he wins the intermediate space; by the fact that the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are led forth at the midday pressing, he wins the heavenly world; by this, gold comes into his hand.
(GBr_2,3.17p) Then he leads him away.
(GBr_2,3.17q) Gold is indeed truth;
(GBr_2,3.17r) by means of truth itself he thus leads him away.
In front of the Gārhapatya fire and behind the Sadas, between the Āgnīdhrīya and the Sadas,
they throw those [bricks] northward, leaving a space between the Āgnīdhrīya, the Sadas, and the Cātvāla pit. By this means, it is said, the Aṅgirases went to the heavenly world.
(GBr_2,3.17v) Indeed, these carry one along the path. // 17 //
He gives first to the *agnīdh*;
for the *agnīdh* is the mouth of the sacrifice;
thus, by means of the mouth of the sacrifice, he brings the mouth of the sacrifice to fulfillment.
He gives it to the Brahman priest;
for the Brahman priest belongs to Prajāpati;
verily, by that [offering], he gratifies Prajāpati.
He gives to the officiating priests;
by that he gratifies the *hotṛ*s.
He gives to the members of the assembly (*sadasya*s).
(GBr_2,3.18j) By means of her he ransoms his right to drink the Soma;
(GBr_2,3.18k) for it is not fitting that he should be deprived of the right to drink the Soma—therefore one should ransom it with her.
(GBr_2,3.18l) That which he gives to a learned descendant of seers, by means of her he prospers in the world of the gods.

That which he gives to one who has not heard [the Veda] and who is not of a lineage of seers (*anārṣeya*), with that he prospers in the world of men; that which he gives to one who has not entered [the sacrificial session], with that the trees spread forth;
that which he gives to one who asks for it, with that he overcomes his rival (*bhrātṛvya*).
Out of fear of which the Kṣatra does not overstep the Brahman—
that is the tiger-like Dakṣiṇā whom they push forward.
He who should accept her again, her, having become a tiger, would crush him.
(GBr_2,3.18s) He should receive it together with another;
(GBr_2,3.18t) then indeed it does not dissolve him. 18.
(GBr_2,3.19a) When he gives a cow, the cow belongs to the Viśvedevas;
(GBr_2,3.19b) by that, he attains the dear abode of the Viśvedevas themselves.
(GBr_2,3.19c) When he gives a goat, the goat belongs to Agni.
By that, he attains the beloved abode of Agni himself;
in that he gives a sheep, he conquers through the nature of the sheep; in that he gives prepared food, he ransoms his own flesh.
When he gives a cart or a chariot, he thereby [gives] his body; when he gives a garment, he thereby [gives] Bṛhaspati;
when he gives gold, he thereby makes his life longer.
In that he gives a horse— the horse belongs to Sūrya— he thereby attains the beloved abode of Sūrya.
Finally, it should be given to the Pratihartṛ.
The Pratihartṛ is indeed fierce;
he thus conquers Rudra himself.
If one were to give [the fee] to the Pratihartṛ from the middle, one would thereby offer sacrifice to Rudra from the middle.
Svarbhānu, the son of Asura, pierced the sun with darkness;
Atri dispelled that [darkness],
and Atri beheld it.
In that he gives gold to the descendant of Atri, he thereby strikes away darkness; moreover, he holds light above for the attainment of the heavenly world. 19.
(GBr_2,3.20a) Now, therefore, follows the midday [service] of the one-day sacrifice.
(GBr_2,3.20b) Verily, this world was both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
(GBr_2,3.20c) That which was the *ṛc* was indeed named "she" (*sā*).
The *sāman* is called *ama*.
That *ṛc* and that *sāman* spoke together: "Let us two unite as a couple for the sake of procreation.
"No," said the *sāman*.
"Greater indeed than this is my greatness," [he said].
Having become two, they both spoke;
yet they could not even agree with one another.
Having become three, they spoke.
Because they spoke having become three, he came to be with those three. Because he came to be with those three, therefore they praise with three [verses].
They chant the *udgītha* with three [verses],
for the *sāman* is measured by three;
therefore, one man has many wives.
(GBr_2,3.20p) Indeed, there are not many husbands for one woman.
(GBr_2,3.20q) Now, when she and Ama spoke together, that became the *sāman*.
(GBr_2,3.20r) That is the reason for the name of the *sāman*.
He becomes the *sāman*;
he attains preeminence;
indeed, whoever truly exists becomes the *sāman*.
"They are not common," they say in reproach.

Indeed, having become five different things, and having become five different things, these two fashioned themselves: the *āhāva* and the *hiṃkāra*, the *prastāva* and the first [verse], the *udgītha* and the middle [verse], the *pratīhāra* and the highest [verse], and the *nidhana*.
And the *vaṣaṭ*-call—since these two, having become fivefold and having become fivefold again, were established, therefore they say, "The sacrifice is fivefold; cattle are fivefold.
And since they both attained completion in the ten-syllabled *virāj*, therefore they say, "The sacrifice is established in the ten-syllabled *virāj*."
And as to why he begins with the *bṛhatī*: he who shines yonder is indeed of the *bṛhatī* nature;
thus he endows him with his own form.
He performs two [verses] and three [verses] again, taking them up once more.
The form for procreation:
at first there are as if two;
from that they are born forth. 20.
The self, indeed, is the *stotriya*;
offspring is the *anurūpa*; the wife is the *dhāyyā*.
The *paśu* verses are the *pragātha*;
the house is the *sūkta*;
that which is within the self is the *nivid*.
The concluding verse is the foundation, and the offering verse is food.
He who knows this exists both in this world and in that world; he prospers with offspring, with cattle, and in his home. 21.
He recites the *stotriya*.
The *stotriya* is indeed the self;
it should be recited with a medium tone of voice.
(GBr_2,3.22d) He fashions his very self; he recites what is concordant.
(GBr_2,3.22e) Progeny indeed is the concordant; therefore, they fashion offspring that is a counterpart and concordant.
A truly worthy counterpart is born among his offspring, not an unworthy one;
therefore, they make him a worthy and suitable match. Furthermore, he should be recited as if on a higher pitch.
(GBr_2,3.22j) He thereby makes his offspring more excellent.
(GBr_2,3.22k) He recites the *dhāyyā* verse.
(GBr_2,3.22l) The wife, indeed, is the *dhāyyā*.
That *dhāyyā* verse should be recited as if somewhat lower;
indeed, the wife in his house becomes one who does not speak back against him, where one who knows thus recites the *dhāyyā* somewhat lower.
He recites the *pragātha*.
The *pragātha* is indeed cattle; it should be recited with a voice possessing the *svara* tone,
for the *pragātha* is indeed cattle.
The *paśavaḥ* is the *svara*;
he recites the hymn for the attainment of cattle.
The *sūkta* is indeed the house;
it is enclosed.
Therefore, it should be recited with speech that is most thoroughly enclosed.
Even if he obtains cattle from afar, he desires to bring them back to his home;
for the home is the foundation of cattle. He recites the *nivid*.
That which is within the self is the *nivid*;
he thereby prepares that very thing for him;
he recites the *paridhānīyā* verse.
The concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) is indeed a firm foundation;
thus, he establishes him upon that very foundation.
He sacrifices with the offering verse (*yājyā*).
The *yājyā* verses are indeed food;
he thus provides for him that very food.
The *dhāyyā*s and the *yājyā*s are indeed the root of the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,3.22kk) Therefore, if they were to employ different *dhāyyā*s and *yājyā*s, they would indeed make the sacrifice rootless; therefore, these [verses] should be identical. 22.

Regarding this they ask: "To which deity does the sacrifice belong? One should reply: "To Indra. For when the sacrifice belongs to Indra, the other deities follow according to their respective shares; [they do so] at the morning pressing in the Marutvatīya [śastra], and at the third pressing.
Now, that which follows the Marutvatīya cup belongs exclusively to Indra; therefore, they recite all the Niṣkevalya hymns.
That which is the Niṣkevalyas is the very form of the heavenly world.
Furthermore, regarding the *niṣkevalya* hymns: in the beginning, there was indeed only one pressing, namely the morning pressing.
Then Prajāpati fashioned for his eldest son Indra this pressing which is the midday pressing.
Therefore, at the midday pressing, they recite all the *niṣkevalya* hymns.

(GBr_2,3.23j) That which is the Niṣkevalya hymns is the form of the heavenly world. (GBr_2,3.23k) Furthermore, regarding the Niṣkevalya hymns: whatever deities the Hotṛ recites at the morning pressing, having recited those, the Hotrāśaṃsin priests recite after them; the Hotṛ recites the triplet for Mitra and Varuṇa as the *pra-uga* hymn.
(GBr_2,3.23l) Both of those [verses] the Maitrāvaruṇa recites as the *anuśaṃsa*; (GBr_2,3.23m) the Hotṛ recites the triplet addressed to Indra as the *pra-uga*;
(GBr_2,3.23n) both of those [parts] are addressed to Indra.
The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites the hymn dedicated to Indra;
the Hotṛ recites the triplet dedicated to Indra and Agni as the *pra-uga*;
the Acchāvāka recites both of those as dedicated to Indra and Agni.
Now, that which follows the Marutvatīya belongs exclusively to Indra;
therefore, they recite all the Niṣkevalyas.
That which is the Niṣkevalyas is the form of the heavenly world.
And furthermore, regarding the *niṣkevalya* hymns, it has been declared by the *ṛc*: "When he overcame the godless illusions, then Soma became his own alone" (*ṚV* 7.98.5; *ŚS* 20.87.5).
While the gods were performing the sacrifice, the Asura-Rakṣasas sought to strike them down.
They said to Vāmadeva, "Do you guard this sacrifice for us from the south," and to Vasiṣṭha from the middle.
To the north is Bharadvāja;
following all [of them] is Viśvāmitra.
Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa does not deviate from Vāmadeva, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin from Vasiṣṭha, and the Acchāvāka from Bharadvāja; all [the others] follow Viśvāmitra.
(GBr_2,3.23bb) It is these very Ṛṣis who, day after day, being vigilant, protect the sacrifice for him who knows this—yea, who knows this. // 23 //
Thus ends the third chapter in the latter part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_2,4.1a) Oṃ. "With what [favor] will the wondrous one come to us?
(RV 4.31.1, ŚS 20.124.1); "With what aid of yours...
(RV 8.93.19)—these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
(GBr_2,4.1b) "Who, O Indra, [has attained] you as his helper?
(ṚV 7.32.14)—this is a *pragātha* in the *bṛhatī* meter; (GBr_2,4.1c) its Brāhmaṇa explanation follows immediately after.
(GBr_2,4.1d) "As soon as born, the bull, the youngling" (RV 3.48.1)—this is the beginning of the hymn (GBr_2,4.1e);
"Thus you, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, here... (RV 4.19.1).
Thus is the inversion;
with the words, "Desiring us, well-disposed, come near" (*ṚV* 4.20.4), he performs the sacrifice;
thereby he gratifies that very deity according to its share.
Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call;
they touch [the cups] again,
but they do not cause them to swell.
For those who do not have the Ārāśaṃsa cups do not sit down. // 1 //
"Taṃ vo dasmam ṛtīṣaham" and "Tat tvā yāmi suvīryam" are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
"Up indeed these most honey-sweet songs... (*ud u tye madhumattamā giraḥ*, *ṚV* 8.3.15, *ŚS* 20.59.1)—this is a *pragātha* in the *bṛhatī* meter;
for the *pragātha* is indeed cattle.
The *paśu* verses are the *svara* [chant];
for the attainment of cattle.
Therefore, the *bṛhatī* is indeed the middle among all the meters.
The midday pressing is the middle of the pressings;
by means of that very middle, he brings the middle into fulfillment.
"Indra, the breaker of forts, overthrew the Dāsa with his hymns" (ṚV 3.34.1).
"Thus is the opening of the *uktha* (*ity ukthamukham*); 'The sacred hymns have risen up, seeking glory' (*ud u brahmāṇy airata śravasyā*) is the concluding verse (*paryāsaḥ*)."
He concludes with, “Thus indeed Indra, the bull, whose arm wields the thunderbolt” (RV 7.23.6a;
ŚS 20.12.6a), and [he continues] with, “The Vasiṣṭhas praise him with hymns” (RV 7.26.6b; ŚS 20.12.6b).
Food indeed is the *arka*;
he thus entrusts him with food itself.
"May he, being praised, bestow upon us wealth in heroes and cattle" (RV 7.26.6c; ŚS 20.12.6c).
"Food indeed is the *arka*," he says;
thereby he prays for offspring and cattle for him.
"Do you protect us always with blessings! (*Ṛgveda* 7.26.6d).
"Thus [ŚS 20.12.6d]—this is indeed auspicious and rich in form (GBr 2,4.2s).

That which is rich in form is the perfection of the sacrifice; whatever rite is being performed that is addressed by either an *ṛc* or a *yajus*, its performer reaches the successful completion of that sacrifice, provided he knows this and the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* who, knowing this, concludes with this [verse]."
He sacrifices with the mantra: "The impeller, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull, the subduer of the swift" (RV 5.40.4; ŚS 20.12.7). [Note: The edition reads *ṛjiṣī*, corrected on page 302.]
(GBr 2,4.2v) By this, he gratifies that very deity according to its share.
(GBr 2,4.2w) Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call. (GBr 2,4.2x) They touch [the offering] in response.
They do not cause [the cups] to swell, for those without the *ārāśaṃsa* verses do not sit down. // 2 //

(GBr_2,4.3a) "(With your crossings, [you find] the possessor of wealth" [RV 8.66.1]) and "The crosser indeed desires to win" [RV 7.32.20]— these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the *acchāvāka*.
(GBr_2,4.3b) "Now indeed his [cup] overflows" (*ṚV* 7.32.12;
*ŚS* 20.59.3)—this is a *pragātha* in the *bṛhatī* metre. (GBr_2,4.3c) Its *brāhmaṇa* has been explained.
(GBr_2,4.3d) “He has indeed increased further for heroic power” (RV 6.30.1)— this is the opening of the *uktha*.
(GBr_2,4.3e) “Grant this offering for our gain” (RV 3.36.1).
"Thus [are] the paryāsa verses.
