He extracts the tenth [verse] for Ghora Āṅgirasa; this is his seer-verse so that the recited [hymn] may not consume the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,4.3h) With the words, "Drink! Prosper! For yours indeed are the pressed juices" (ṚV 3.36.3), he performs the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,4.3i) Thus he gratifies this very deity according to its share.
(GBr_2,4.3j) Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
They touch [the cups] facing toward themselves;
they do not cause them to swell, for they do not sit without the *ārāśaṃsa* verses. 3.
(GBr_2,4.4a) Then, "O Adhvaryu, let us recite!"—thus they call five times: for the *stotriya*, for the *anurūpa*, for the *pragātha*, for the *ukthamukha*, and for the *paridhānīyā*.
(GBr_2,4.4b) The *pañkti* consists of five feet; (GBr_2,4.4c) the sacrifice is fivefold.
They recite all [the verses] addressed to Indra in the Triṣṭubh metre;
for the midday pressing belongs to Indra and is in the Triṣṭubh metre.
All [the priests] conclude with verses containing the word "sam".
In that they conclude with verses containing the word "sam" (together), the *paryāsa* is indeed the end and the *udarka* is the end;
thus, by means of the end, they conclude with the end.
All perform the sacrifice with verses containing the word "mad" (intoxicating).
(GBr_2,4.4j) Therefore, when they sacrifice with verses containing the word "mad" (intoxicating), they all sacrifice with verses containing the words "pressed," "drunk," and "congruous.
(GBr_2,4.4k) Whatever is congruous in the sacrifice is successful.
(GBr_2,4.4l) They all perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
(GBr_2,4.4m) There is an *anuvaṣaṭkāra* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (GBr_2,4.4n) [They do this] thinking, "Lest we should exclude the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
(GBr_2,4.4o) The intermediate world is the midday pressing.
(GBr_2,4.4p) Of that [sacrifice], there are five directions;
(GBr_2,4.4q) there are five *uktha* hymns of the midday pressing.
(GBr_2,4.4r) By means of these five *uktha*s, he attains these five directions; he attains these five directions. // 4 //
(GBr 2,4.5a) Now, when they offer at the third pressing in the *aupāsana* fire, he thereby gratifies the ancestors.
(GBr 2,4.5b) The *agnīdhra* priest performs the offering for the *pātnīvata* cup in a whisper.
(GBr 2,4.5c) For the *pātnīvata* is indeed seed.
(GBr_2,4.5d) Indeed, the seed is poured out silently;
(GBr_2,4.5e) therefore he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, thinking, "Lest I should bring to a conclusion the seed that has been poured out.
(GBr_2,4.5f) For the seed that is poured out is truly successful when it remains unconcluded.
This concluding rite is indeed the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call;
therefore, he does not perform the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call.
Sitting either in the lap of the *neṣṭṛ* or at the edge of the *dhiṣṇya* hearth, he consumes [the portion].
The Neṣṭṛ is indeed the distributor of the wives;
the Agnīdh pours seed into the wives,
and from the poured seed, offspring are born.
For the procreation of offspring,
he becomes possessed of offspring and prolific;
it is for the sake of procreation.
He who knows thus is procreated with offspring and cattle. 5.
(GBr_2,4.6a) Then they offer the *śākala* oblations.
(GBr_2,4.6b) Just as a snake sheds its old skin, or as a reed is separated from its sheath, even so those who offer the *śākala* oblations are completely released from all evil.
(GBr_2,4.6c) In the *droṇakalaśa* there are parched grains.
They place them with their hands;
for the parched grains are indeed cattle.
They scatter them on the edge of the ashes of the Āhavanīya fire.
The *āhavanīya* fire is indeed the womb of cattle;
thus they place them in their own stall, from which there is no escape. Then, turning to the left, they cause the Soma draughts to swell in the waters.
They set them down within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*);
for that is the abode of Soma.
To the west of the *cātvāla* pit, the Adhvaryu fills the cups with water, turns them toward the north, and places green grass blades between them.
When indeed the waters and the plants come together, then the Soma becomes complete.
They pour it out with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu;
for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,4.6p) He thus establishes him finally in the sacrifice itself.
(GBr_2,4.6q) Now, when they provide a substitute for the portion to be consumed, they thereby interpose a human consumption between [himself and] the divine consumption. // 6 //
(GBr_2,4.7a) This [Soma], when putrid, carries off both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer in yonder world.

(GBr_2,4.7b) Therefore, if they were to lead him to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) without having poured curds over him, it would be as if they were carrying away a corpse; such indeed would they do to him.
(GBr_2,4.7c) But when they lead him to the purificatory bath after pouring curds over him, they restore him entirely together with his source.
“They bring together prosperity” (GBr_2,4.7e);
with the verse, “Now Savitṛ, the god, has become worthy of our praise” (RV 4.54.1), he makes the offering;
thus he brings him together entirely, including all his joints. (GBr_2,4.7f) [The edition reads *avainaṃ*].
With three verses,
for the sacrifice is threefold;
he offers with verses containing the word "drop" (drapsa).
He gathers him entirely with all his limbs;
he makes offerings over him with verses addressed to Soma;
thus he gathers him entirely together with his vital essence.
He offers with five [verses]; the sacrifice is fivefold;
verily, he wins the sacrifice itself.
The person consists of five elements;
he attains the person himself;
cattle consist of five elements.
He finds support in cattle alone;
he who knows thus finds support through offspring and cattle. // 7 //

Agni indeed is Yama, and this earth is Yamī. It is a loan that the sacrificer takes from Yama when he strews the altar with plants. If he were to depart without burning them up, they would cause him to perish in yonder world.
With the verse, "The debt which I owe to Yama,
that which was borrowed and not yet repaid," he kindles the fire upon the altar.
"Having paid off his debt here on earth by self-restraint and industry, and having become free from debt, he goes to the heavenly world," so says the Hotṛ priest.
"O consumer of all, O burner of all, I offer thee as a libation," thus he says.
For the non-defeat of the sacrificer,
when they move about as if mixed up, he should offer groats with his joined palms into the forest fire;
for this forest fire is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
Thus, he places him in his own womb. 8.
On the Ekāṣṭakā day, which is the middle of the fortnights, one should bake a cake of four śarāvas and burn a thicket with it in the morning.
If it burns, there is an equal amount of merit; if it does not burn, there is an equal amount of evil.
By means of this very knowledge, the Aṅgirasas used in ancient times to undertake long sacrificial sessions (*dīrghasattra*).

Indeed, he who sacrifices knowing the overseer (*upadraṣṭṛ*), the listener (*upaśrotṛ*), and the announcer (*anukhyātṛ*) reaches the world beyond together with his merit from sacrifice and good works (*iṣṭāpūrta*).
Agni, indeed, is the overseer.
The wind, indeed, is the one who overhears;
the sun, indeed, is the one who looks on.
He who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice, goes to that world together with his merit of sacrifice and good works.
"This one is our lord of the sky," he says;
for Agni is indeed the lord of the sky.
(GBr_2,4.9l) He thus says to Agni: "Guard this for us. (GBr_2,4.9m) "You, the lord of the sky," he says.
(GBr_2,4.9n) Vāyu, indeed, is the lord of the sky.
(GBr_2,4.9o) He says this to Vāyu: "Guard this for us.
(GBr_2,4.9p) He says, "O God, the Expander" (deva saṃsphāna).
(GBr_2,4.9q) For the Sun is indeed the god who is the Expander.
(GBr_2,4.9r) He thus says to the Āditya: "Guard this for us.
(GBr_2,4.9s) With the words, "This is your womb," he should consign the fire into the two kindling woods.
Regarding this they say: "If that which has been mounted upon the two kindling woods should be lost, would his fire not perish? Would it have to be established anew?
[To this he says: "O Agni, with that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, mount me; with that enter me."
With the words, "This is your womb," he should internalize the fires within himself;
for this indeed is the womb of Agni;
thus he establishes him in his very own womb. 9.
(GBr 2.4.10a) Verily, he who knows the Agniṣṭoma as the Sāhna attains union with and the same world as the Agniṣṭoma Sāhna—he who knows thus.
(GBr 2.4.10b) Verily, he who shines yonder is this Agniṣṭoma; he is the Sāhna.
They should conclude it together with the day.
This [sacrifice] is indeed called *sāhna* ("of a day").
Therefore, they should proceed without hurrying.
For because they proceed without hurrying during the first two pressings, therefore these eastern communities are settled in great abundance.
Now, because they proceed here in a great hurry at the third pressing, therefore these long forests here become oriented toward the west.
Just as it is at the morning pressing, so it is at the midday pressing, and so it is at the third pressing.
And thus, indeed, the sacrificer becomes free from premature death.
Therefore, they should proceed without hurrying.
When this [sun] rises in the morning, it burns most gently;
therefore, one should recite at the morning libation with the gentlest voice.
(GBr_2,4.10m) Now, when it has come closer, it burns more intensely;
therefore, one should recite at the midday pressing with a stronger voice.
Moreover, when it has come even nearer, it burns most intensely.
Therefore, one should recite at the third pressing with the strongest voice;
one should recite thus if one were master of speech,
for the *śastra* is indeed speech.
But by whichever [recitation] that is more progressive, by which one might be able to complete it, by that one should proceed;
this indeed becomes more highly praised.
Truly, this [sun] never sets nor does it rise.
Therefore, when people think that he has set in the west, he has merely reached the end of the day and then turns himself around;
he makes the day below and the night above. Indeed, he never sets nor does he rise.

When he thinks that it rises in the east, he has actually reached the end of the night and then turns himself around; he makes the night below and the day above. Indeed, this [sun] never sets nor does it rise.
(GBr_2,4.10bb) Indeed, it never sets.
(GBr_2,4.10cc) He who knows this attains union with and residence in the same world as that [sun]. 10.
(GBr_2,4.11a) Now, therefore, follows the third pressing of the one-day sacrifice.
(GBr_2,4.11b) The gods and the Asuras contended for these worlds.
(GBr_2,4.11c) Those gods conquered the Asuras.
Having been defeated, they went toward the junction of day and night.
Indra said, "These Asuras have indeed gone toward the junction of day and night;
who and I shall rise up against these Asuras?"
"I am he," said Agni;
"I am he," said Varuṇa;
"I am he," said Bṛhaspati.
"I am Viṣṇu," he said; they rose up against them and struck them down at the junction of day and night.
Because they rose up and struck them down at the junction of day and night, therefore it is called *utthā*.
(GBr_2,4.11m) He who knows this rises up and utterly destroys his hateful rival.
(GBr_2,4.11n) That Agni, having become a horse, was the first to go forth.
(GBr_2,4.11o) Because Agni, having become a horse, was the first to go forth, they introduce the *uktha* hymns with verses addressed to Agni.
Because Agni, having become a horse, was the first to go forth, therefore the Sākaṃ-aśva [is recited]. Because the five deities rose up together, therefore the five deities are praised in the Uktha.
That which is speech is that Agni.
That which is breath is Varuṇa;
that which is mind is Indra;
that which is sight is Bṛhaspati.

(GBr_2,4.11v) That which is the ear is Viṣṇu. (GBr_2,4.11w) Indeed, these [deities], having stirred them with these five vital breaths, raised them up. (GBr_2,4.11x) Therefore, these five deities are recited in the Uktha. 11.
For Prajāpati created other gods from these five vital breaths; and whatever here is fivefold,
having created that, he caused it to blaze forth.
The gods said, "This father, the source of bliss, has withered away.
Let us fan him back to life and raise him up. Having declared his resolve, he approaches and stands over him.
(GBr_2,4.12g) Even if one performs a sacrifice for a family that has been purified by the sprinkling of water, the essence indeed approaches it according to its reputation.
(GBr_2,4.12h) Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice. (GBr_2,4.12i) He is impelled and raised up by these very five vital breaths.
Indeed, those who by means of the five vital breaths set him in motion and raise him up—
they are these very five deities that are recited in the Uktha.

Regarding this they say: "Since they praise two deities, Indra and Agni, then why are so many more deities recited in the *uktha*? [The answer is: "The *āgnimāruta* is the end; the *ukthas* are the middle; the *āśvina* is the end.
They praise while standing among fewer deities."
(GBr_2,4.13d) Now, why are the deities praised most abundantly in the *uktha*? (GBr_2,4.13e) There are two by two at the openings of the *uktha*; that is why there are two by two. 13.
Now, as for the fact that the Maitrāvaruṇa’s *uktha* is dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa,
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s *uktha* is dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati, and the Acchāvāka’s *uktha* is dedicated to Indra and Viṣṇu— by reciting two [verses] together,
one [hymn] dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa comes into being.

When they recite two [hymns] together, one for Indra and one for Bṛhaspati, there is one for Indra and Bṛhaspati. When they recite two [hymns] together, one for Indra and one for Viṣṇu, there is one for Indra and Viṣṇu.
There are two [hymns] at each opening of the *uktha*.
(GBr_2,4.14e) Therefore, it is two by two. 14.
Now, as for the *aindrāvaruṇa* *uktha* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, it is recited with the verse:
"O Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed juice, drink this pressed Soma, the intoxicating one, O you who uphold the vows" (*indrāvaruṇā sutapāv imaṃ sutaṃ somaṃ pibataṃ madyaṃ dhṛtavratau*).
It is thus recited with the *ṛc*.
(GBr_2,4.15b) For the third pressing is like me; (GBr_2,4.15c) "Come, I will indeed declare it to you" (ṚV 6.16.16),
"Agni, the descendant of Bharata, has come" (ṚV 6.16.19).
Thus are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses of the Maitrāvaruṇa;
"The supporter of the people, the bountiful one, worthy of praise" (*carṣaṇīdhṛtaṃ maghavānam ukthyam*, RV 3.51.1) is the beginning of the *uktha*.
Above that is the Brāhmaṇa:
"The all-knowing Asura propped up the sky" (*astabhnād dyām asuro viśvavedāḥ*, *ṚV* 8.42.1);
this is the Vāruṇa *sāṃśaṃsika*. [Ed.: *astabhnādyām*]
"And I," said Varuṇa, for the purpose of praising both deities together and for the sake of excelling in praise. [Corrected p.
302] (GBr_2,4.15g) (GBr_2,4.15h) "And I. For the purpose of praising both deities together and for the sake of excelling in praise.
(GBr_2,4.15i) "O Indra and Varuṇa, you two for our sacrifice...
(RV 7.82.1)—this is the *paryāsa* addressed to Indra and Varuṇa.
(GBr_2,4.15j) This is his regular *uktha* dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa.
He establishes this very [sacrifice] in its own abode, in its own support.
For these deities, having become pairs, conquered; it is for the sake of victory indeed.
Moreover, it is for the procreation of the pair of duals.
It is one-footed;
with the one-footed [verse], the Hotṛ priest concludes the recitation.
(GBr_2,4.15q) Where they yoke the Hotṛ and the Hotrakas, that is successful.
(GBr_2,4.15r) Indeed, regarding this, [one should recite]:
"O two Kings, may I turn you both toward the sacrifice" (ṚV 7.84.1). [The edition reads *āvāṃ*.]
[Corrected p.
303] In this very way, one should perform a single *paryāsa* and a single *sūkta*;
indeed, for the two following [verses], there is only a single *sūkta*.
With the verse, "O Indra and Varuṇa, of that which is most sweet... he performs the sacrifice;
he thus gratifies these two deities according to their respective portions.
Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call;
they touch [the cups] again, but they do not cause them to swell, for they do not sit down without the *ārāśaṃsa* formulas. 15.
Now, as for the *aindrābārhaspatya* hymn of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin,
it is recited with the verse: "O Indra and Bṛhaspati, drink the Soma, rejoicing at this sacrifice, O you who possess bull-like wealth" (*Ṛgveda* 4.50.10).
For the third pressing belongs to me, as it were.
"O you, the peerless one, we [choose] you... (RV 8.21.1; ŚS 20.14.1/20.62.1) "...who for us has done this and that in the past... (RV 8.21.9; ŚS 20.14.3)
"Thus [are] the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; 'To the most generous, the great one, whose wealth is vast' (RV 1.57.1,
ŚS 20.15.1)— this is the opening of the *uktha*."
(GBr_2,4.16e) It belongs to Indra and the Jagatī; (GBr_2,4.16f) cattle are of the Jagatī nature;
(GBr_2,4.16g) it is for the attainment of cattle.
The third pressing is indeed connected with the Jagatī;
it is the form of the third pressing:
"Like birds swimming in water, guarding [their young]... (RV 10.68.1).
"Thus [is] the *bārhaspatya* *sāṃśaṃsika*.
"And I," said Bṛhaspati,
for the purpose of the mutual recitation and the super-recitation of the two deities.
(GBr_2,4.16m) "Toward Indra our thoughts, finding the light of heaven...
(*ṚV* 10.43.1, *ŚS* 20.17.1)—this is the final verse addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
(GBr_2,4.16n) This is his regular *uktha* dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
He establishes this very thing in its own abode, in its own support.
These deities, having become pairs, conquered; it is for the sake of victory indeed.
And furthermore, for the procreation of the pair itself:
"May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind" (RV 10.42.11a;
[With the verse] "ŚS 7.51.1 / 20.17.11 / 20.89.11 / 20.94.11a," he concludes with a verse addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati;
verily, he establishes the sacrifice upon Indra and Bṛhaspati.
May Indra, our friend, grant wide space for us, his friends—from above, from below, from the evil-doer, from the front, and from the middle. (RV 10.42.11bcd, 10.43.11bcd, 10.44.11bcd;
(GBr_2,4.16v) He invokes a blessing from all directions; he does not fail.
Whatever desire he desires, that desire of his is fulfilled, for one who knows thus, and for one who, knowing thus, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin concludes with this [verse].
With the verse, "O Bṛhaspati and you, O Indra, [bestow] wealth" (*Ṛgveda* 7.97.10), he performs the sacrifice;
he thus gratifies these two deities according to their respective portions.
Having uttered *vaṣaṭ*, he utters the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*.
They touch [the cups] facing toward themselves;
they do not cause them to swell, for those who have no *ārāśaṃsa* verses do not sit down. 16.
Now, as for the fact that the *uktha* of the *acchāvāka* priest belongs to Indra and Viṣṇu, it is recited with the verse:
"O Indra and Viṣṇu, lords of exhilaration, come to the Soma, bestowing wealth" (*Ṛgveda* 6.69.3).
[The edition reads *acchāvākasyoktam*.]
For the third pressing belongs to me, as it were; for thus says the Ṛgveda:
"Now indeed, O Indra, lover of songs," and "This is for thee, O Indra, lover of songs."
These are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the *acchāvāka*.
"The season is the mother; from her works... (*Ṛgveda* 2.13.1)—this is the opening of the *uktha*.
Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa has been stated:
"Now, does a mortal man, seeking to gain, bestow?
This is the *vaiṣṇava* *sāṃśaṃsika* hymn.
"Both 'I' and 'you'," Viṣṇu said, "for the sake of the praise of two deities, so that there may be no excessive praise: 'I impel you both with ritual action and with nourishment' (RV 6.69.1)."
"Thus is the reversal; it belongs to Indra and Viṣṇu.
This is his constant *uktha* for Indra and Viṣṇu.
He thus establishes this very thing in its own abode, in its own foundation.
These deities, having become pairs, conquered; it was for the sake of victory,
and also for the procreation of the pair.
With the verse addressed to Indra and Viṣṇu, "Both have conquered; you two are not defeated" (*ṚV* 6.69.8; *ŚS* 7.44.1), he performs the concluding rite;
thus he establishes the sacrifice in Indra and Viṣṇu alone.
With the verse, "O Indra and Viṣṇu, drink of this honeyed [draught]" (RV 6.69.7), he performs the sacrifice;
thus he gratifies these two deities according to their respective portions.
Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* call, he utters the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call.
They touch [the cups] facing toward themselves;
they do not cause them to swell, for those who have no *ārāśaṃsa* verses do not sit down [for the pressing]. 17.
(GBr_2,4.18a) Then, "O Adhvaryu, recite! Śaṃsāvoṃ!"—thus they call out four times each for the stotriya, the anurūpa, the ukthamukha, and the paridhānīyā.
(GBr_2,4.18b) For there are four quarters;
(GBr_2,4.18c) thus they find firm support in the quarters.
Moreover, cattle have four feet;
[this is] for the attainment of cattle.
Moreover, at the third pressing, the *hotraka* priests consist of four sections.
Therefore, they recite four *triṣṭubh* verses; all [the verses] are *jāgata*, for the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is indeed *jāgata*.
Now, these [verses] are indeed in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
For at the morning pressing, the recitation (*śastra*) of the *hotrakas* in the *marutvatīya* litany is, as it were, lacking in brilliance;
and that which is the third pressing is indeed drained of its essence.

Now, this *śukriya* chant which has been studied is the *triṣṭubh* metre, which is undiminished in its essence; it serves to provide the sacrificial session with sapidity. They all conclude [the recitation] with verses that are equal.

(GBr_2,4.18p) Now, as to why they conclude with verses containing the word "sam" (together): the *paryāsa* is indeed the end, the *udarka* is the end, and the *sajāyā* verses are the end; for it is for the sake of non-separation that they do so.
Thus, by means of the end, they conclude with the end.
All [the priests] sacrifice with verses containing the word "mad" (intoxicated/delighted).

In that they sacrifice with verses containing the word *mad* ("intoxicating"), with all [verses] containing the word *suta* ("pressed") and the word *pīta* ("drunk"), they sacrifice with suitable ones;
whatever is suitable in the sacrifice is successful.
All perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
(GBr_2,4.18v) There is an *anuvaṣaṭkāra* for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. (GBr_2,4.18w) [They say: "Lest we should separate ourselves from the *sviṣṭakṛt*. (GBr_2,4.18x) That world is indeed the third pressing.
Its five directions are the five *uktha*s of the third pressing;
by means of these five *uktha*s, he attains these five directions.
Whatever is the form and whatever is the measure of these worlds, by that form and by that measure he makes these worlds prosper; he makes these worlds prosper. // 18 //
Regarding this, they say: "What is the nature of the *ṣoḍaśin*?
There are sixteen chants (*stotra*) and sixteen recitations (*śastra*). He takes it up with sixteen syllables;
however, two syllables remain over when the *ṣoḍaśin* has been transformed into an *anuṣṭubh*.
These two, indeed, are the breasts of Speech:
truth and untruth.
Truth protects him; untruth does not harm him, who knows this—yea, who knows this. 19.
"He who knows thus"— thus ends the fourth chapter in the second part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
(GBr_2,5.1a) Om. The gods took recourse to the day, and the Asuras to the night.
(GBr_2,5.1b) They were equal in power;
indeed, they did not differ.
Indra said, "Who am I, and who is he? Let us two pursue these Asuras by means of the night.
He did not find a companion among the gods;
they were afraid of the night, of darkness, and of death.
For the night is indeed like darkness, and death is indeed darkness;
therefore, even now, it is as if more prevalent by night. Having retreated even a little distance, one fears.
The meters indeed followed after him. Because the meters followed after him, therefore Indra and the meters carry the night.
No *nivid* is recited, no *puroruk*, no *dhāyyā*, nor any other deity.
For Indra and the meters carry the night; they indeed drove them along by turns. Because they drove them along by turns, they are called *paryāyas*.
(GBr_2,5.1p) That is the reason why they are called "turns" (*paryāya*).
(GBr_2,5.1q) They indeed drove them out from the first watch of the night with the first turns, from the middle watch with the middle ones, and from the last watch with the final ones.
(GBr_2,5.1r) They said, "Even during the night, we have driven them away."
Because they said, "Do not even let us go to the night," that is the reason for the *apiśarvara* meters' name *apiśarvara*. Indeed, these meters of his are called *śarvara*; so it has been said.
These [meters], having rushed toward Indra from the darkness of the night, which is death, held him back.
That indeed is the quality of being "not-night" even for those who are not-night. // 1 //

In the first rounds they chant; they take up again the very first words. Whatever desires these [singers] had, those they obtain by that. In the middle rounds they chant; they take up again the very middle words.

Whatever horses and cattle they possessed, that they recover by means of this; when they chant on the final rounds, they recover their very last steps. Whatever clothing, gold, and gem they possessed as their personal property, that they recover by means of this.
He who knows this takes away the wealth of his enemy and drives him out from all these worlds. // 2 //
"They say that the day possesses the *pavamāna* chant, but the night does not possess the *pavamāna*. How do both become possessed of the *pavamāna*? By what means do they come to have equal shares?"

(GBr_2,5.3d) "This very [Soma] pressed for Indra who delights in the intoxication, O Vasu, this pressed juice; for this has been pressed with power"—thus they praise and recite. By that, the night possesses the *pavamāna* [laud]; by that, both possess the *pavamāna*;
by that, those two become equal sharers.
(GBr_2,5.3g) "The day has fifteen stotras," they say, "but the night does not have fifteen stotras.
How do both become possessed of fifteen stotras? By what means do they both come to have an equal share?"
There are twelve stotras that do not include the night;
with three deities, with the *sandhi*, and with the *rāthaṃtara*, they praise for the *āśvina* [stotra].
By that, the night consists of fifteen stotras.
Therefore, both [the Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa] have fifteen-fold stotras;
thereby they become equal sharers.
They chant the Stotra with a limited number [of verses], while they recite the Śastra with an unlimited number.
"The past is limited, the future is unlimited.
[Thinking,] "May I obtain the unlimited," he chants the *stoma* beyond [the norm]. Indeed, offspring and cattle go beyond the self.
Whatever part of his body is depleted, that they restore for him by means of this.
Now, all this is indeed twofold: moisture and heat.
And that [heat] is obtained from day and night.
(GBr_2,5.3v) For the attainment of moisture and brilliance,
(GBr_2,5.3w) they recite the *gāyatra* *stotriya*s and *anurūpa*s;
(GBr_2,5.3x) for the *gāyatrī* is indeed brilliance.
Darkness is evil, the night; by means of that splendor they cross over darkness and evil.
They recite [the verses] with a repeated taking up.
For thus do the Sāma-singers praise, so that it becomes praised and consecrated;
for that is not truly praised which is not consecrated.
Regarding this they say: "Now, why is it that, having called out from the final *pratīhāra*, they continue the *śastra* with the *sāman*?"
The sacrifice is indeed the person;
its head is the oblation-holder,
and its mouth is the Āhavanīya fire.
The belly is the assembly hall;
food is the *ukthas*;
and the arms are the *mārjālīya* and *āgnīdhrīya* fires.
(GBr_2,5.4g) Those deities which are within the *sadas* are the *dhiṣṇya* hearths;
(GBr_2,5.4h) the two foundations are the *gārhapatya* and the fire for cooking the sacrificial food (*vrataśrapaṇa*). Now, furthermore:
(GBr_2,5.4i) his mind alone is the *brahmán*.
The out-breath is the Udgātṛ;
the in-breath is the Prastotṛ;
the diffused breath is the Pratihartṛ.
Speech is the Hotṛ; the eye is the Adhvaryu;
procreation is the Sadasya.
The limbs are the *hotrāśaṃsin* priests;
the self is the sacrificer.
Now, when the Adhvaryu priest introduces the chant with the words, "Soma purifies himself," he thereby joins the eye with the vital breaths.
(GBr_2,5.4s) Now, when the Prastotṛ addresses the Brahman, saying, "O Brahman, we shall chant; O Praśāstṛ," the mind becomes their leader.
(GBr_2,5.4t) For these vital breaths are impelled by the mind [with the thought], "Let us chant with the Stoma.
(GBr_2,5.4u) Thus, by means of the mind, he unites the vital breaths themselves.
(GBr_2,5.4v) Now, when the Brahman priest gives permission loudly with the words "It is praised," the mind is indeed the Brahman; he thereby unites the mind with the vital breaths.
(GBr_2,5.4w) And when the Prastotṛ priest chants the Prastāva, he thereby unites the out-breath with the vital breaths.
(GBr_2,5.4y) Now, when the Pratihartṛ chants the Pratihāra, he thereby joins the Vyāna with the Apānas.
(GBr_2,5.4z) Then, when the Udgātṛ sings the Udgītha, he thereby joins the Samāna with the Prāṇas.
(GBr_2,5.4aa) Then, when the Hotṛ connects the Śastra with the Sāman—the Hotṛ is indeed speech—he thereby joins speech with the Prāṇas.
(GBr_2,5.4bb) Now, when the *sadasya* priest approaches the *brahman*, the *sadasya* is indeed procreation; he thus obtains procreation.
(GBr_2,5.4cc) Now, when the *hotrāśaṃsin* priests perform the continuity of the *sāman*, the *hotrāśaṃsin*s are indeed the limbs; he thereby joins his limbs together with his vital breaths.
(GBr_2,5.4dd) Now, when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) approaches the hymn (*stotra*), the sacrificer is indeed the self; he thus restores his own self.
Therefore, one should not cause him to hear the *abhi-āśrāvaṇa* call outside the sacrificial altar;
nor should the sun rise while he is present,
nor should it set while he is present.
(GBr_2,5.4hh) One should not warm oneself over the hearth;
(GBr_2,5.4ii) lest one should draw the Self inside from the vital breaths. // 4 //

They chant in the first rounds; they utter the *ninarda* on the first words. Thus, from the very first night, they strike down the Asuras. They chant in the middle rounds; they utter the *ninarda* on the middle words.
Thus, from the very middle night, they strike down the Asuras.
They chant with a loud, repeated note on the highest verses during the final rounds;
they strike down the Asuras from the very last night.
Just as one drives out evil from a house again and again, even so do they strike down the Asuras by means of the day and night through the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* chants.
They recite the *gāyatrī* verses; for the *gāyatrī* is indeed splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Thus they bestow splendor and spiritual luster upon the sacrificer.
Having recited the *gāyatrī* verses, they recite the *jagatī* verses.
The Jagatī is indeed Brahman;
by means of Brahman they thus bestow upon the sacrificer the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
They chant the Gāyatrīs and the Jagatīs alternately.
(GBr_2,5.5m) Thus they make the meters possess distinct powers.
(GBr_2,5.5n) Having recited the *jagatī* verses, they recite the *triṣṭubh* verses.
(GBr_2,5.5o) Cattle, indeed, are the *jagatī*.
(GBr_2,5.5p) Thus they conclude with the Triṣṭubh verses for the sake of the cattle.
(GBr_2,5.5q) The Triṣṭubh is indeed strength and vigor; (GBr_2,5.5r) thus he finally establishes strength in vigor.

The *yājyā* verses should be *triṣṭubh*s containing the words "containing food" (*andhasvatī*), "containing intoxication" (*madvatī*), "containing what is pressed" (*sutavatī*), and "containing what has been drunk" (*pītavatī*); they should be complete and possess auspicious characteristics.
This indeed is the form of the night;
one should remain awake throughout the night.
(GBr_2,5.5v) As long as they neither chant the *stotra* nor recite the *śastra*, so long are the *asuras* and *rakṣases* capable of carrying off the sacrifice.
Therefore, they should say, "Kindle the Āhavanīya fire, the Āgnīdhrīya fire, the Gārhapatya fire, and let the hearths (*dhiṣṇyas*) blaze up! and they should cause them to blaze.
That would be as if they were in the open;
those who begin [the rite] should lie down. Evil does not strike them down, thinking, "He is indeed the best."
They strike away the darkness, the evil; they strike away the darkness, the evil. // 5 //
Indra indeed slew Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Tvaṣṭṛ, his son having been slain, prepared a malevolent soma-rite devoid of Indra. Indra, having caused a disturbance in that sacrifice, forcibly drank the soma.
He spread himself out in all directions;
therefore, Soma must not be drunk by one who has not been invited, for his drinking of Soma becomes fruitless.
From his mouth and from his vital breaths, prosperity and glories went upward;
they entered the animals.
Therefore, animals are glorious.
He who knows this becomes glorious.
Then the Aśvins and Sarasvatī prepared for him this sacrifice, the Sautrāmaṇī, for the sake of healing;
with it they consecrated Indra.
(GBr_2,5.6m) Thereupon, he indeed became the most excellent among the gods.
(GBr_2,5.6n) He who knows this, and he who, knowing thus, is consecrated by the Sautrāmaṇī, becomes the most excellent among his own people and among others. 6.
Then the Brahman priest sings the *sāman*.
The *sāman* is indeed the *kṣatra*; with the *kṣatra* he thus consecrates him.
Moreover, the *sāman* is indeed sovereignty;
by means of sovereignty itself, he thus causes him to attain sovereignty.
Furthermore, the *sāman* is the essence of all the Vedas.
He consecrates him with the essence of all the Vedas;
he sings on the Bṛhatī.
For it is upon the Bṛhatī that yonder sun shines, established in glory and stability.
He sings on a Bṛhatī verse addressed to Indra;
for this Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice belongs to Indra,
and he who sacrifices at this time does so in the very abode of Indra.
(GBr_2,5.7m) He thus gratifies him in his own abode.
(GBr_2,5.7n) Now, why are they called *saṃśānāni*?
(GBr_2,5.7o) By means of these Sāmans, the gods indeed caused Indra to attain equality with power and vigor.

In the same way, the sacrificers, by means of these very *sāmans*, consolidate themselves through power and vigor. There are the *sāmans*: "For hearing," "For wide-hearing," "For true-hearing," and "For fame."
He establishes him in these very worlds. It has four *nidhanas*;
for there are four quarters;
thus he finds firm support in the quarters.
(GBr_2,5.7v) Now, cattle are four-footed;
(GBr_2,5.7w) [this is] for the attainment of cattle.
(GBr_2,5.7x) Regarding this they say: "Now, when this *sāman* is sung, where is the *uktha* of this *sāman*, and what is its foundation?"
"They say, 'The gods are three times eleven'—
this indeed is the *uktha* of this *sāman*, this is its foundation;
he draws the thirty-third cup."
For the stability of the Sāman, for the sake of stability. // 7 //
Prajāpati desired, "May I obtain strength; may I attain the heavenly world.
He beheld this Vājapeya sacrifice. This one who shines yonder is indeed the Vājapeya.
By means of this, the sacrificer attains the world of heaven and gains the prize.
At the morning pressing, the verses contain the word *śukra* and are full of light;
through them, he obtains splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
At the midday pressing, they contain the word "vāja" for the attainment of the heavenly world;
at the third pressing, they contain the words "anna," "gaṇa," and "paśu."
Through them he attains abundance;
everything is seventeenfold,
for Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold.
He attains Prajāpati himself;
the officiating priests wear golden garlands;
thus the form of greatness itself is created.
"This is my light in yonder world; it shall not be non-existent. Gold is indeed light; they thus conceal him with light.
They run the race;
they cause the sacrificer to win;
he ascends the firmament; he ascends to universal splendor; he ascends to all-encompassing splendor; he ascends to total splendor.
(GBr_2,5.8v) They cause him to disappear from the world of men.
(GBr_2,5.8w) "Impelled by the god Savitṛ, may I ascend the heavenly world, the highest firmament," thinking thus, the Brahman priest creeps toward the chariot wheel.
(GBr_2,5.8x) Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he creeps toward it.
Moreover, Prajāpati is indeed Brahmā;
he thus impels him from above by means of Prajāpati,
for the conquest of the firmament.
For the continuity of the swift ones,
he sings the *vājisāman*;
he becomes possessed of swift ones.
The *vāja* is indeed the heavenly world;
he thus ascends to that very heavenly world.
In verses concerning Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, the *bṛhat* [sāman] is the final one.
Having ascended to that very world of heaven, the realm of the sun, he transcends it; he transcends it. 8.
(GBr_2,5.9a) Now, therefore, follows the Aptoryāma.
(GBr_2,5.9b) When Prajāpati created offspring, he indeed created them exhausted.
(GBr_2,5.9c) Once created, they were merely moving away.
They did not return;
he grasped them with a single *stoma*,
and they were left over.
(GBr_2,5.9g) Those [stotras] with two [verses];
(GBr_2,5.9h) those with all [the verses].
Therefore it is called the *sarvastoma* (all-stoma).
He took them up with one back; they were still too many. He took them up with two.
They [are] with all [the *pṛṣṭha* stotras];
therefore it is "all-*pṛṣṭha*.
At the *atiriktoktha*, they warded them off with the *vāravantīya*.
Therefore, this [sacrifice] possesses an additional *uktha*;
therefore it is the *vāravantīya* [sāman]; and because he stopped after reaching those [verses], it is therefore called the *aptoryāma*.
Now, they say that "aptus" means offspring;
it is indeed said to be the restraint of offspring. If he were not to restrain them, then those offspring would perish; therefore, he performs this sacrifice with it.
This very sacrifice consists of eight *pṛṣṭha* chants.
Just as in another sacrifice there is a movement following the *pṛṣṭha* of the Viśvajit, how is it that this is so here?
This is the father of sacrifices.
Just as those who are even hostile would submit to the will of a chief, so too do these submit to the will of the chief for the sake of following after food; they are capable of serving the food. 9.
Just as there, on that day, the hymn for Agni is first among the *ukthas*, even so here too the hymn for Agni is first; indeed,
the two following ones there are for Indra, and these two here are also for Indra.
The *uktha* of the Acchāvāka priest belongs to Indra and Viṣṇu;
there are four calls (*āhāva*) for the additional *ukthas*,
for the *ukthas* are indeed cattle.
(GBr_2,5.10g) Cattle are indeed fourfold;
(GBr_2,5.10h) moreover, cattle have four feet.
(GBr_2,5.10i) It is for the attainment of cattle.
(GBr_2,5.10j) These *stotriya* and *anurūpa* triplets are to be recited half-verse by half-verse.
(GBr_2,5.10k) The half-verse is indeed a foundation;
(GBr_2,5.10l) it is for the sake of stability.
(GBr_2,5.10m) Now, of these very *aśvina* hymns, he recites two together as a pair on each successive day.
(GBr_2,5.10n) The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; (GBr_2,5.10o) therefore, he recites the *aśvina* hymns.
They gave that to the Aśvins, saying, "Heal this!
The verses addressed to Kṣetrapati become the concluding verses (*paridhānīyā*).

Where [the waters] were struck down, there the creatures remained confined, hungry and thirsty; being distressed, he caused them to drink according to their respective fields with these [verses], and he satisfied them.
[Ed. ha tastat, corr.
Patyal] (GBr 2.5.10s) Moreover, this earth is indeed the field;
"In this undepressed [field], we shall finally find our firm foundation," they thought.
The *yājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Where he struck [the earth], there the creatures stood obstructed, hungry and thirsty. With these very verses, he caused them to settle according to their respective abodes.
Therefore these are the *yājyā* verses; therefore these are the *yājyā* verses. // 10 //

(GBr_2,5.11a) Now, therefore, regarding the non-ekāha rites: (GBr_2,5.11b) at the morning pressing, they perform the *śvastotriya* as the *anurūpa* of the *adyastotriya*; (GBr_2,5.11c) thus they maintain the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice.
For the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice:
just as the Ekāha, once pressed, is so the Ahīna is pressed;
just as the pressings of the pressed Ekāha proceed to their completion, so the days of the pressed Ahīna proceed to their completion.
Now, when they perform the *stotriya* of the following day as the *anurūpa* of the *stotriya* of the current day at the morning pressing,
they thus make the day the *anurūpa* of the day;
by means of the preceding day, they thereby take hold of the subsequent day.
Likewise, at the midday pressing,
the *pṛṣṭha* chants— which are indeed prosperity—
remain established in that very place.
By this very same procedure at the third pressing,
they do not make the *stotriya* of the following day the *anurūpa* of the *stotriya* of the current day.
(GBr_2,5.12a) Now, therefore, the introductory offerings themselves:
(GBr_2,5.12b) "With straight guidance, O Varuṇa" (Ṛgveda 1.90.1)—
this is for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
"May Mitra, the wise one, lead us" (RV 1.90.1). Since the Maitrāvaruṇa is the leader of the Hotrakas,
this [verse] contains a reference to a leader.
(GBr_2,5.12e) "Indra we invoke for you from every side" (*indraṃ vo viśvatas pari*),
thus for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
(GBr_2,5.12f) "from among the people" (*havāmahe janebhyaḥ*).
"Thus, day after day, they invoke Indra alone with this [verse].
No other indeed seizes Indra away from their invocation when a Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, knowing thus, recites this day after day:
*yat soma ā sute naraḥ*. (RV 7.94.10a)
"Thus for the Acchāvāka" (GBr 2.5.12i); "Indra and Agni have called out" (RV 7.94.10b)— with this [verse], they invoke Indra and Agni day after day.
(GBr_2,5.12j) Indeed, no other Indra-Agni can deprive them of their invocation when the Acchāvāka, knowing this, recites this [hymn] day after day.
(GBr_2,5.12k) These, indeed, are the ships for crossing over to the world of heaven;
by means of these, they cross over to the world of heaven itself. (GBr_2,5.12l) 12.
Now, therefore, follow the concluding verses (*paridhānīyā*): "(O God Varuṇa,) may we be yours..."— this is for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
"May we meditate upon food and heaven" (*iṣaṃ svaś ca dhīmahi*).
"Food," this world indeed; "heaven," yonder world.
He thus takes hold of both these worlds.
"Having extended across the intermediate space"—
this is for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
(GBr_2,5.13f) A triplet on the theme of "uncovering.
(GBr_2,5.13g) By means of these, he uncovers the heavenly world.
(GBr_2,5.13h) "When Indra, in the light of Soma, split Vala... (*ṚV* 8.14.7bc, *ŚS* 20.28.1bc, 20.39.2bc).
(GBr_2,5.13i) Those who are consecrated are indeed desirous of winning;
therefore, this [chant] becomes powerful:
(GBr_2,5.13j) (GBr_2,5.13k) "He drove forth the cows for the Aṅgirases, making manifest those that were hidden."
"He pushed Vala toward us" (*arvāñcaṃ nunude valaṃ*);
by means of this [verse], he wins the prize for these [beings]. (GBr 2.5.13) [The reading *kṛvan* in the edition is corrected to *kṛvan* by Patyal.]
"By Indra the luminous realms of heaven were made firm and strengthened; they are steadfast and shall not be repelled"— with this [verse],
day after day, he secures for himself the heavenly world.
"(I have drunk of the two who possess Sarasvatī)"— this is for the Acchāvāka [the edition reads *svarasvatīvator*,
corrected on p. 303].
"Of Indra and Agni I choose the aid" (RV 8.38.10b)—this, indeed, is the beloved abode of Indra and Agni, namely speech. Thus he satisfies them with their own beloved abode;
he who knows this prospers through his own beloved abode. 13.
The concluding verses (*paridhānīyā*) for the *hotṛ*-priests consist of both types: those used for the *ahīna* sacrifices and those of the one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifice.
Thereupon, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest concludes with the verses of the one-day sacrifice;
by this means, he does not fall away from this world.
The Acchāvāka [recites] with the āhinīkā verses for the attainment of the heavenly world;
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites] with both [sets of verses].
Thus he goes, grasping both together: this world and that world;
moreover, the *ahīna* and the *ekāha*; moreover, the year and the *agniṣṭoma*; moreover, the office of the *maitrāvaruṇa* and that of the *acchāvāka*.
Thus he goes, grasping both together.
(GBr_2,5.14j) Then, at the third pressing, the *hotrakas* conclude with verses belonging to the one-day (*aikāhika*) soma-sacrifices;
by this means he does not fall away from this world.
(GBr_2,5.14k–l) The *acchāvāka* concludes with verses belonging to the multi-day (*āhinīka*) soma-sacrifices.
For the attainment of the heavenly world,
the Hotṛ may recite at will that which the Hotṛkāḥ would otherwise recite on the preceding day;
for indeed, what the Hotṛ does, that the Hotṛkāḥ do.
The *hotṛ* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the *hotrakas* are the limbs. This vital breath moves along with the limbs;
therefore, the *hotṛ* may, at his will, recite that which the *hotrakas* might have recited on the preceding day.
Whatever belongs to the Hotṛ, that indeed belongs to the Hotrakas.
The Hotṛ is the self, and the Hotrakas are the limbs;
for these ends of the limbs are identical.
Therefore, the Hotṛ may recite at will that which the Hotṛkāḥ would have recited on the previous day;
for what the Hotṛ does, that the Hotṛkāḥ do.
The Hotṛ concludes with the endings of the hymns (*sūktāntaiḥ*).
(GBr_2,5.14y) Now, the concluding verses for the Hotrakas are indeed common to all. // 14 //
(GBr_2,5.15a) That which is the *śvastotriya* they make as the *anurūpa* of the *adyastotriya* at the morning pressing; (GBr_2,5.15b) thus they maintain the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice;
(GBr_2,5.15c) for the sake of the continuity of the *ahīna*.
These *hotṛ*-assistants, having recited the *stotriya* of the six-day rite at the morning pressing, recite the *ahīna-sūktas* at the midday pressing:
"May the true Maghavan, the impeller of the soma-dregs, come hither" (*ā satyo yātu maghavāṃ ṛjīṣī*, *ṚV* 4.16.1)— thus the Maitrāvaruṇa, being truthful (*satyavān*).
(GBr_2,5.15f) "To him, indeed, the very powerful and swift one... (*ṚV* 1.16.1, *ŚS* 20.35.1)—thus the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites].
(GBr_2,5.15g) "The priest, instructing, went to the granddaughter of his daughter... (*ṚV* 3.31.1).
Thus says the Acchāvāka (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.5.15h).

Regarding this, they ask: "Why does the Acchāvāka recite this hymn at both [the morning and midday pressings] as one who carries [the sacrifice], both in verses that look backward and in verses that look forward? (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.5.15i). For the Acchāvāka is indeed a powerful Bahvṛca.

(GBr_2,5.15j) Indeed, the carrier carries the yokes to which he is yoked. (GBr_2,5.15k) Therefore, the Acchāvāka, like a carrier, recites this hymn on both occasions—both on the days that are "far-off" and on those that are "near.
(GBr_2,5.15l) These are recited on five days: at the Caturviṃśa, the Abhijit, the Viṣuvat, the Viśvajit, and the Mahāvrata.
These are called the *ahīna-sūktas* (the hymns from which nothing is lacking),
for in them nothing whatsoever is deficient.
Indeed, these days are directed forward and do not turn back.
Therefore, these [hymns] are recited on these days.
That they recite these is the form of the heavenly world.
Moreover, when they recite these, they summon Indra with them, just as one summons a bull to a cow in heat.
Those gods and seers said, "Let us perform the sacrifice together with what is common.
They perceived this commonality of the sacrifice:
common *pragāthas*, common introductory verses (*pratipads*), and common hymns (*sūktas*).
Indra is either one who moves from his dwelling, or wherever Indra goes first, there indeed the other follows;
this is for the sake of the sacrifice being accompanied by Indra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the latter part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.

By means of these *saṃpāta* verses, these seers indeed ascended to these worlds.

Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa recites these three *saṃpātas* in reverse order, one by one, on each successive day.

Now, these nine and three [hymns] are to be recited day by day; they become twelve. Indeed, there are twelve months in a year.
The year is Prajāpati;
Prajāpati is the sacrifice. Thus, one attains the year, Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
In that year, Prajāpati, they proceed day by day finding firm support in the sacrifice;
they find firm support,
for everything here finds its support in this.

He who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. They should insert those [verses] as the *āvāpa* between [the two sets]. On the fourth day, they should recite the *virāj* verses without the *ūṅkha* interjection; on the fifth day, the *vaimadī* *paṅkti* verses; and on the sixth day, the *pārucchepī* verses.
Now, they may insert other great stotras consisting of eight verses.

in the same way, the sacrificers go to the heavenly world by means of this very hymn.
Therefore, it contains the word "bull" (*ṛṣabha*) and refers to cattle.
For the attainment of cattle;
that [hymn] consists of five verses;
the *paṅkti* is indeed food.
"For the attainment of food" and "May they carry us across by unharmed paths" (RV 6.69.1d)—
