"Up have the sacred words risen, seeking glory" (RV 7.23.1,
ŚS 20.12.1)— with these words the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites; this hymn is rich in *brahman* and is complete.
By means of this hymn, both the gods and the seers went to the heavenly world;
in the very same way, the sacrificers go to the heavenly world by means of this very hymn.
And that [hymn] indeed consists of six verses.
There are six seasons;
it is for the attainment of the seasons that he recites this day after day following the *saṃpāta* verses.
"Like a carpenter, he has fashioned his inspired thought" (RV 3.38.1a)—
with these words the Acchāvāka recites day after day; he addresses [the deity], for this is its form.
"Touching the dear, highest [days]"— those very days which are the highest are the dear ones;
touching those very ones, they proceed, grasping hold of them.
"The world beyond this world is indeed the heavenly world (*svarga*); they touch that very world when they say:
'I, the wise one, desire to see the seers' (*kavīn icchāmi saṃdṛśe sumedhāḥ*, ṚV 3.38.1d)."
(GBr_2,6.2gg) Those who have indeed passed away before by means of this are the seers (*kavayaḥ*); it is to them that he speaks over.
(GBr_2,6.2hh) And as for the fact that there are ten verses, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed ten;
(GBr_2,6.2ii) by means of the vital breath, he thereby attains them.
For the continuity of the vital breaths;
and as for the ten-verse hymn,
there are indeed ten vital breaths in a person.
There are ten heavenly worlds;
he thereby attains both the vital breaths and those heavenly worlds,
and they proceed established in both the vital breaths and the heavenly worlds.
Now, as for that which consists of ten verses:
the Virāj has ten syllables;
this earth, indeed, is the foundation of the heavenly world.
He thus establishes this very [sacrifice] upon this foundation;
he pronounces "Indra" once;
thereby he does not fall away from the form of Indra.
After that, he recites the *sampātas* day after day. // 2 //
(GBr_2,6.3a) (Who, O Indra, [is] that one who has you as his helper? [ṚV 7.32.14]) _(What new thing [is there] among the flaxen plants?
[ṚV 8.3.13]) _(What indeed has not been done by him? [ṚV 8.66.9])
Thus, the *pragāthas* containing the word "kad" are recited day by day;
for Prajāpati is indeed "Ka," and it serves to attain Prajāpati.
That which contains the word *ka* is the form of the heavenly world; and indeed, that which contains *ka*—
for *ka* is food.
Moreover, it is for the attainment of food; and furthermore, because they contain the word *ka*,
and *ka* is indeed happiness.
Moreover, it is for the attainment of food; and furthermore, because they consist of *kad*-verses,
and moreover, because these [priests] proceed day by day employing the peaceful *ahīna* hymns.
They appease them with *pragāthas* containing the word *kad*. Being appeased for them, they become bliss (*ka*). These [verses], being thus appeased, carry them to the heavenly world.
They should recite the *triṣṭubh* verses as the opening stanzas of the hymns. Regarding this, some recite them before the *pragāthas*, calling them *dhāyyās*;
however, one should not do so.
The Hotṛ is indeed the nobility, and the Hotrāśaṃsin priests are the common people;
they would thus make the common people rise up against the nobility,
resulting in an inversion of the proper order.
"One should know that these *triṣṭubh* verses are indeed the openings of the hymns (*sūktapratipad*).
Just as people would cross over the ocean, even so do those who worship the year or the twelve-day rite float across.
Just as those desiring the further shore would board a ship from Sairāvatī, even so do those desiring heaven board these *triṣṭubh* verses."
Indeed, having caused this metre to go forth, one does not return from the heavenly world;
for it is most vigorous.
Therefore, one should not call out to these [metres].
"For the metre is the same;
moreover, [he thinks], 'Lest I should make these into *dhāyyās*.
In that they recite them, that is the form of the heavenly world."
Furthermore, when they recite these [verses], they indeed summon Indra with them, just as one summons a bull to a cow in heat.
"O Indra, Maghavan, drive away the enemies to the east" (PS 19.16.8a, ŚS 20.125.1a)—with this verse, the Maitrāvaruṇa recites daily before the *saṃpātas*.
"Drive away those to the west, O Conqueror; drive them away to the north and away to the south, O Hero, so that we may rejoice in your wide protection" (PS 19.16.8bcd, ŚS 20.125.1bcd). Thus.
The form of fearlessness;
for one seeks that which is indeed like fearlessness.
With the Brahman, joined with the Brahman, I yoke you. [ṚV 3.35.5]
"Thus [ŚS 20.86.1]," the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites this [verse] day after day as one that is "yoked," for the Ahīna sacrifice is,
as it were, yoked.
(GBr_2,6.4h) It is the form of the Ahīna sacrifice.
(GBr_2,6.4i) "Lead us to a wide world" (*uruṃ no lokam anu neṣi*, *ṚV* 6.47.8,
*ŚS* 19.15.4)— thus the Acchāvāka recites day after day.
"Lead him along," he says; for this is indeed the form of the *ahīna* sacrifice.
"Lead him," is the form of the *sattra* sacrifice. Thus, Indra truly becomes one who dwells in their home.
Just as a cow goes to its well-known stall, or as a bull goes to a cow in heat, even so does Indra come to the sacrifice of those [who perform it].
One should not entrust the *śunaṃhūyā* offering to one who has omitted [the ritual];
for such a person, a Kṣatriya falls from his kingdom.
(GBr_2,6.4p) Indeed, one calls out to whoever is superior. // 4 //
(GBr_2,6.5a) Now, therefore, follows the application and the release of the *ahīna* sacrifice.
(GBr_2,6.5b) He extended across the intermediate space... [ṚV 8.14.7a, ŚS 20.28.1a]...
"Thus he yokes the unimpaired one"—
even so [he yokes] Indra. (RV 7.23.6a,
"Longer partīka at 2.4.2"]— thus he releases [GBr_2,6.5d] (surely that is yours [ṚV 2.11.21, 15.10, 16.9, 17.9, 18.9, 19.9])."
With the verse, "He yokes the unimpaired" (*ahīnaṃ yuṅkte*), he yokes;
with the verse, "Now, being praised...
(*nū ṣṭutaḥ*), he unyokes.

(GBr 2.6.5f) "Verily, he alone is worthy of the Ahīna sacrifice who knows how to yoke it and how to unyoke it. This indeed is its yoking, and this is its unyoking. Therefore, if they were to conclude with the one-day rites on the first day—the twenty-fourth day—they would bring the sacrifice to completion on that very first day and would not perform the ritual actions of an Ahīna."

(GBr_2,6.5i) Now, if they were to conclude with the *ahīna-paridhānīyā* verses, it would be as if those who have been harnessed were cut loose without being unharnessed; in the same way, the sacrificers would be cut loose.
They should not perform the *ahīna* ritual in that manner.
(GBr_2,6.5j) But if they were to conclude with both sets of verses, it would be just as one on a long journey might proceed after having unharnessed his team; such is that case.
They should conclude with the *samānī* verses. Regarding this, they say: one should recite the *stoma* in excess by means of one or two [verses], for there are long stretches of forest.

(GBr_2,6.5o) Where the Stoma is chanted with many verses, [it is because he thinks]: "Thus I quickly bestow food upon the gods. (GBr_2,6.5p) With an unlimited number of verses in the two later pressings; for the heavenly world is indeed unlimited. (GBr_2,6.5q) This is for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Just as one would quickly give [water] to one who is gasping for breath or thirsty, so should that [offering] be;
they should conclude with the *samānī* verses.
Thus, their sacrifice remains continuous, undertaken and not fallen apart.
The *vaṣaṭ* should be uttered continuously with the *ṛc*.
He who knows this is joined with continuity through offspring and cattle. 5.
Regarding this, they ask: "How is it that the Hotṛ has two *ukthas* and one *sūkta*, while the other *hotṛ*s have one *uktha* each and two *sūktas*?
That which shines yonder is indeed the Hotṛ;
he is truly one alone.
Therefore, it consists of a single hymn.
When, as it were, it becomes two, that which is pierced is the orb of light itself: one part is white, and the other is black.
Therefore, it has two hymns;
the rays are indeed the *hotṛ*-priests,
and they each [perform] one [hymn].
Therefore they have a single *uktha*;
and because each ray has two colors, they have two *sūktas*.
The year, indeed, is the Hotṛ.
He is indeed one alone;
therefore he has a single hymn (*sūkta*).
Since his days are twofold—some being cool and others warm—therefore he has two chants (*uktha*).
The seasons, indeed, are the *hotṛ*-priests;
they each consist of one [part],
and therefore they are called *ekoktha*.
Since there are two months in each season, therefore they consist of two hymns.
The Hotṛ is indeed man;
he is indeed one alone.
Therefore it consists of a single hymn (*sūkta*).
Because when a man exists, he faces one way and then another, therefore it consists of two recitations (*uktha*).
The *hotṛ*-priests are indeed the limbs.
Indeed, each of those [limbs] is single;
therefore, they are called *ekoktha*.
Since each limb possesses splendor (*dyuti*), they are therefore called *dvisūkta*.

Regarding this they say: "Since the *hotṛ* has two recitations (*uktha*) with one hymn (*sūkta*), while the other *hotṛ*s have one recitation each with two hymns, how is that made equal? One should reply: "Because they sacrifice with [verses] addressed to two deities, and because the *hotṛ*s have two hymns.
Regarding this they say: "Since it is an *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, yet two recitations of the *hotṛ* remain in excess, how is it that the *hotṛ*s are not thereby excluded?"

(GBr_2,6.6ee) "In that they sacrifice with [verses] addressed to two deities, and in that the *hotṛ*-priests' recitations consist of two hymns (*dvisūkta*)," so one should say. (GBr_2,6.6ff) Regarding this, they ask: "Since it is an *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, they cause all the deities and all the meters to swell; then by which meter do they lead forward the *uktha* hymns that have not lost their vigor, and by which deity?"
"One should say: 'With the Gāyatrī metre, with Agni as the deity.
The Asura-Rakṣasas cast spells upon the gods while they were performing the sacrifice, thinking, "We shall destroy their sacrifice at the joints of the sacrifice, at the third pressing.
For at the third pressing, the sacrifice is unimpaired and most powerful.
"We shall lengthen their sacrifice and destroy it," they said; they stationed Varuṇa on the south side and Bṛhaspati in the middle.
To the north was Viṣṇu.
They said, "We are each but one; we are not capable of this."
"Having been praised, [Indra said], 'By whomsoever we two may share this together as a second.
Indra said to them, 'All of you shall have me as your second. Thus, they all had Indra as their second."
Therefore, the offerings to Indra and Varuṇa, Indra and Bṛhaspati, and Indra and Viṣṇu are recited in succession.
Indeed, those who possess a second become their own through this; and those who know thus consider themselves to possess a second. // 6 //
In the verses addressed to Agni, they introduce the *uktha* of the Maitrāvaruṇa;
for Agni is indeed vigor—
by means of vigor, they thus introduce it for him.
The Aindravāruṇa [offering] is recited;
Indra is indeed vigor,
and Varuṇa is sovereignty.
The *ukthas* are cattle;
thus, by means of vigor and dominion, he encompasses cattle on both sides for stability.
For the sake of non-departure,
they introduce the *uktha* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with verses addressed to Indra;
for Indra is indeed vigor.
By means of vigor alone they lead him forward;
the hymn to Indra and Bṛhaspati is recited thereafter,
for Indra is indeed vigor.
Brahman is Bṛhaspati;
the cattle are the *ukthas*.
Thus, by means of virility, by means of the Brahman, and on both sides, he encloses the cattle.
For stability,
for non-departure,
they lead forth the *uktha* of the Acchāvāka among the verses addressed to Indra.
Indra is indeed vigor;
by means of vigor they lead him forward for him.
The hymn dedicated to Indra and Viṣṇu is recited.
Indra is indeed vigor;
Viṣṇu is the sacrifice;
the Ukthas are cattle.
By means of valor alone and by means of sacrifice, having seized the cattle from both sides, he finally establishes them within the *kṣatra*.
Therefore, the *kṣatriya* indeed rules over the greatest number of cattle;
for he is the one who presides over them, the giver, and to whom the Vedas have been bestowed and secured.
They recite these *jāgata* verses dedicated to Indra. Moreover, by means of these very verses, the third pressing becomes accompanied by Indra; by means of these, the pressing becomes *jāgata*.
Indeed, these hymns of his become firm—namely, the *nābhānediṣṭha*, the *vālakhilyas*, the *vṛṣākapi*, and the *evayāmarut*.
Therefore, they should perform these rites together, thinking: "Let us bring this emitted seed to full development and produce it as one.

For if those who do not perform these rites together were to act otherwise, it would be as if someone were to snatch away the emitted seed, or as if one were to dismember a newborn child limb by limb—such is that [result].
Therefore, they should approach them together, thinking, "Together let us produce this emitted seed, made prosperous, in a single form.
He recites the *śilpa* verses; these are the divine crafts.
"Indeed, it is by imitating these crafts that craft is acquired here:
the elephant, the bronze vessel, the garment, gold, and the chariot drawn by mules are the crafts. Craft is truly acquired by him who knows thus."
When he recites the *śilpas*, that is the form of the heavenly world. Moreover, the *śilpas* are indeed the refinement of the self;
thus, they refine his very self. 7.
He recites the Nābhānediṣṭha; the Nābhānediṣṭha is indeed seed;
he thus prepares his seed.
"That becomes mixed with semen" (GBr_2,6.8d), [as in the verse] "Uniting with the earth, he pours forth his semen" (ṚV 10.61.7b); this is for the sake of the successful completion of the semen.
He recites that Nārāśaṃsa;
for *naraḥ* (men) are indeed offspring,
and *śaṃsaḥ* (recitation) is speech.
(GBr_2,6.8j) He places that speech among the offspring; (GBr_2,6.8k) therefore these offspring are born speaking.
(GBr_2,6.8l) Some indeed recite it before the *pragāthas*, saying, "Speech has its abode in the front."
Some say that one should recite it at the end, because speech has its abode above;
however, one should recite it in the middle,
for this speech has its abode in the middle.
(GBr_2,6.8p) As if closer from above,
(GBr_2,6.8q) the Hotṛ, having praised him who has become semen, hands him over to the Maitrāvaruṇa,
saying: (GBr_2,6.8r) "Do you fashion his vital breaths."
He recites the Vālakhilyas;
the Vālakhilyas are indeed the vital breaths;
he thereby prepares his vital breaths.
He recites them as expanded;
for the vital breaths are indeed expanded: by the out-breath [comes] the in-breath.
By means of the *apāna* [breath], the *vyāna* breath distributes [the verses]:
in the first hymn, by the foot;
in the second, by the half-verse.
(GBr_2,6.8bb) Verse by verse in the third [section].
(GBr_2,6.8cc) When he interchanges them in the first hymn, he thereby interchanges speech and mind.
(GBr_2,6.8dd) When [he does so] in the second, he interchanges sight and hearing.
That which [is performed] in the third [round], he thereby distributes both the vital breaths and the self; having attained that, he may dwell according to his desire.
Indeed, the *pragāthas* are suitable for the leader.
One should indeed perform the *atimarśa* [touching];
in this way the *pragāthas* are properly arranged.
That which is the *atimarśa* is the very form of the heavenly world.
Furthermore, regarding the over-reaching: the *bṛhatī* is indeed the self, and the *satobṛhatī* is the vital breaths;
thus he recited the *bṛhatī*.
That is the Self;
then the *satobṛhatī* [is the breath];
these are the vital breaths.
Then the Bṛhatī,
then the Satobṛhatī;
thus he goes forth, encompassing the self with the vital breaths.
Furthermore, as for the *atimarśa*: the *bṛhatī* is indeed the self, and the *satobṛhatī* is offspring; he thus recited the *bṛhatī*.
That is the Self;
then [he recites] the Satobṛhatī;
these are the subjects.
Then the Bṛhatī,
then the Satobṛhatī;
thus he goes about increasing himself through his offspring.
Furthermore, as for the *atimarśa*: the *bṛhatī* is indeed the self, and the *satobṛhatī* is cattle; he thus recited the *bṛhatī*.
That is the Self; now,
the Satobṛhatī—
those are the cattle.
Then the Bṛhatī,
then the Satobṛhatī;
thus he goes, encompassing himself with cattle.
Having fashioned the vital breaths for him, the Maitrāvaruṇa hands him over to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, saying:
"Do you procreate from this.
He then recites the *Sukīrti* hymn.
Sukīrti is indeed a divine womb;
thus, he procreates the sacrificer in that sacrificial, divine womb.
He recites the Vṛṣākapi hymn.
The self, indeed, is Vṛṣākapi;
he thereby fashions the self of this [sacrificer];
he utters the *nyūṅkha* for it.
The *nyūṅkha* is indeed food;
verily, he thereby bestows food upon him, just as one offers the breast to a newborn child. It consists of five parts.
For this person consists of five parts, being divided fivefold:
hair, skin, bone, marrow, and brain.
Having refined the sacrificer to be exactly as large as the person, he hands him over to the Acchāvāka.
"Establish a firm foundation for this," he said;
thus he recites the Evayāmarut hymn,
for the Evayāmarut is indeed a firm foundation.
Verily, he establishes him finally upon a firm foundation;
he sacrifices with the *yājyā* verse. The *yājyā* is indeed food.
Thus, he bestows upon him food and nourishment itself.
Now, these are called the "companions": the Nābhānediṣṭha, the Vālakhilyas, the Vṛṣākapi, and the Evayāmarut. One may recite them together, or one may not recite them together.
If one were to omit any of them, he would omit that from the sacrificer.
If he were to exclude the *Abhānediṣṭha* from it, that would be its seed;
if he were to exclude the *Vālakhilyas*, that would be its vital breaths; if he were to exclude the *Vṛṣākapi*, that would be its self.

If [he recites] the *evayāmarut* verse, since the *evayāmarut* is indeed a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), he should cause him to hear that [verse] from the very foundation—both the divine and the human ones.
He may recite them together, or he may not recite them together.

Now, Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, acting as the *hotṛ* priest at the Viśvajit sacrifice, reflected: "Of these various ritual arts (*śilpa*), there are two *uktha*s for the *hotṛ* during the midday pressing at the Viśvajit which lasts a year."
"Come, let me resolve this very doubt for him," he thought;
so he resolved the doubt for him accordingly.
While it was being resolved in that manner, Gośruti arrived.
He said, "O Hotṛ, why does your *śastra* float about broken?
"What has happened? [he asked].
"This *Evayāmarut* is being recited here on the north," he replied.
He said, "The midday [pressing] belongs to Indra.
Why do you wish to lead Indra away from the midday? He replied, "I do not wish to lead Indra away from the midday. He said:
But this *sāman* of the non-noon pressing is metrical;
it is either *jagatī* or *ati-jagatī*.
And that is the *māruta* [laud].
"Do not wipe it away thus," he said. "O Ārmācchāvāka,
I have authority over this instruction."
He said, "This [Hotṛ] recites the limbs of Indra for Viṣṇu.
Therefore, you must insert [the verses] after the Hotṛ's portion, before the *dhāyyā* addressed to Rudra and before the hymn to the Maruts.
"So be it," he replied.
Even now, that is praised in exactly the same way;

as it was on the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭhya* period, so the sacrifice is made perfect, and the procreation of the sacrificer is made perfect. How is it that here the *nābhānediṣṭha* is not recited, but rather the *vālakhilyas*? Semen indeed comes first, and then the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
In this way, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin has not yet recited the Nābhānediṣṭha; then he recites the Vṛṣākapi.
[The objector asks: "Since semen comes first and then the self, how is there procreation for the sacrificer here? How are the vital breaths secured?"
(GBr_2,6.9hh) By means of this entire sacrificial rite, they consecrate the sacrificer.

(GBr_2,6.9ii) Just as one might deprive a fetus within the womb of its vital breaths, so it would be if one were to deprive him of the Vṛṣākapi hymn as his very self— just as if he were lying there in the process of being born.
Indeed, everything does not come into being all at once at the beginning;
rather, each individual limb comes into being as it is produced.
If all [the rites] were performed on the same day, the sacrifice would indeed be successful, and the procreation of the sacrificer would be successful.
Then, indeed, the Hotṛ should recite the Evayāmarut hymn.
That which is its foundation—in that very foundation he finally establishes him; he establishes him. // 9 //
[The editor notes: *pratiṣṭhāpayati* twice; corrected by Patyal.
(GBr_2,6.10a) The sixth day is indeed the field of the gods.
(GBr_2,6.10b) Those who come to the sixth day truly come to the field of the gods.

"Indeed, the gods do not dwell in one another's houses, nor does a season dwell in the house of another season," they say. Therefore, the officiating priests perform the seasonal sacrifices according to their respective order, without confusion. Thus, when they arrange the seasons, the progenitor [of all] is established in his proper place.

Regarding this they say: "They should not give the *praisha* calls with the *ṛtupraiṣas*, nor should they utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with the *ṛtupraiṣas*; for the *ṛtupraiṣas* are speech, and speech is indeed attained on the sixth day."

(GBr_2,6.10i) If they were to give the directions with the *ṛtupraiṣas*, or if they were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with the *ṛtupraiṣas*, they would encounter speech that has been exhausted, stilled, and rendered barren— speech that has lost its power to carry the sacrifice. (GBr_2,6.10j) They would cause the sacrifice to fall from its unshakable state.
(GBr 2.6.10k) From the sacrifice, from the vital breaths, from offspring, and from cattle, they went astray.

(GBr 2.6.10l) Therefore, one should give the *praisha* call only for those verses containing the word *ṛgmī*; (GBr 2.6.10m) the *vaṣaṭ* call should be made over those verses containing the word *ṛgmī*.
They do not approach speech that is authoritative, peaceful, rich in *ṛks*, and free from devouring; they do not fall away from the unswerving sacrifice,
nor do they turn their faces away from the sacrifice, from the vital breaths, from offspring, or from cattle.
(GBr_2,6.10q) They place verses of Parucchepa before the *prasthitayājyās* of the two pressings.
(GBr_2,6.10r) This metre, namely the Pārucchepa, is indeed called Rohita.
(GBr_2,6.10s) By means of this, Indra indeed ascended to the seven heavenly worlds.
"He who knows this ascends to the seven heavenly worlds.
Regarding this, they say: "Since the fifth day has five feet as its form and the sixth day has six feet, why then are verses of seven feet recited on the sixth day?
By means of six feet alone they attain the sixth day; that which is the seventh day is indeed a severance from that day.
Having ascended by means of that very seventh step, they dwell;
those who, knowing thus, undertake [the sacrifice], proceed with continuous three-day periods, uninterrupted. 10.
The gods and the Asuras contended for these worlds.
By means of the sixth day, the gods indeed drove the Asuras away from these worlds. Taking whatever wealth was in their hands, they cast it into the ocean.
The gods, having followed after them with this very metre, took hold of the treasures within their hands. That indeed is this "step and back-step" (punahpada); that is the hook for drawing [them] in.
(GBr_2,6.11g) He who knows this bestows wealth upon his enemies and drives him away from all these worlds.
(GBr_2,6.11h) The sky, indeed, as a deity, carries the sixth day; the thirty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*) [is its support].
The *Raivata* Sāman, the *Aticchandas* metre—
by this [sacrifice], one who knows thus prospers according to the deity, according to the hymn-form (*stoma*), according to the Sāman, and according to the metre.
That which has a common ending (*samānodarka*) is indeed the form of the sixth day.
For the first day is the same as the last day; that very same word recurs in the sixth day—that which contains "horse" (*aśva*), that which contains "chariot" (*ratha*), and that which is repeated.

Furthermore, that which has ceased, that which is intermediate in form, that world which has arisen, the *nābhānediṣṭha*, the *pārucchepa*, the *nārāśaṃsa*, that which consists of two feet, that which consists of seven feet, the *kṛta*, and the *raivata*— these are the forms of the third day.
These indeed are the forms of the sixth day.
On the sixth day, the essence of the meters that had been consecrated overflowed.
Prajāpati drew it out by means of the Nārāśaṃsī, the Gāyatrī, the Raibhī, the Triṣṭubh, the Parikṣitī, the Jagatī, the Gāthā, and the Anuṣṭubh.
Indeed, these are the meters recited on the sixth day; they are not exhausted in their power.

That is for the sake of the sapidity and the freshness of the meters; his meters become sapid when they are recited on the sixth day. He who knows thus has sacrificed with sapid meters and extends the sacrifice with sapid meters. // 11 //

Now, as for the fact that the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses consist of two-footed lines— namely, "May we now bring these worlds to completion" (*imā nu kaṃ bhuvanā sīṣadhāma*)— the person (*puruṣa*), indeed, has two feet.
The person has two supports;
the sacrifice is indeed the person.
Therefore, the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses consist of two-footed [verses].
(GBr_2,6.12f) Then he recites the *sukīrti* hymn:
"O Indra, Maghavan, drive away our enemies to the east...
"Good report is indeed the womb of the gods" (GBr 2.6.12).
He who thus knows this good report as the womb of the gods establishes his own reputation; he becomes renowned among living beings and is firmly established in the heavenly world.
He who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. Then he recites the *vṛṣākapi* hymn, beginning with:
"For they have set the presser free" (*vi hi sotor asṛkṣata*, ṚV 10.86.1, ŚS 10.126.1).
The sun is indeed Vṛṣākapi.
Because he causes rain to fall while trembling, he is called Vṛṣākapi;
that is the etymological derivation of Vṛṣākapi’s name as Vṛṣākapi.
(GBr_2,6.12n) He who knows this shines like a bull in all the worlds.
(GBr_2,6.12o) In its third quarter, he performs the *nyūṅkha* and the *ninarda* at the beginning and the end.
(GBr_2,6.12p) The *nyūṅkha*, indeed, is food.
(GBr_2,6.12q) The Ninarda is strength;
(GBr_2,6.12r) he thereby places food within his strength for him.
(GBr_2,6.12s) Then he recites the Kuntāpa.
"Ku" indeed signifies that which is contemptible; because it burns (*tapati*), they are called *kuntāpa*s. That is the reason for the name *kuntāpa* of the *kuntāpa*s.
(GBr_2,6.12w) "They torment him for his evil deeds," thus [is he called] *taptakuya*; he becomes firmly established in the heavenly world.
(GBr_2,6.12x) He who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. (GBr_2,6.12y) For him there are fourteen initial [verses], beginning with: "Hearken to this, O people!"
He recites them with a pause, just as he does for the Vṛṣākapi hymn;
for that is the form of the rainy season belonging to Vṛṣākapi, and thus it follows the proper rule.
Then he recites the Raibhī verses: "Sing forth, O Rebha, sing forth" (*vacyasva rebha vacyasva*).
Indeed, it was by singing that the gods and the seers went to the heavenly world.

In the same way, these sacrificers go to the heavenly world while singing praises. Having approached them by grasping them one after another, he then recites the verses concerning Pārikṣita, beginning with "Of the king who belongs to all people."
The year, indeed, is the encircler;
for the year encompasses all this.
Moreover, they say that fire is the encircler.
"For Agni indeed encompasses all this," they say;
moreover, they say that these verses are Gāthās of King Parikṣit. He would do that for us;
these verses are indeed recited as Gāthās.
If it be indeed a *gāthā*, one should say, "It is the *gāthās* of Agni, or of the Year";
if it be indeed a *mantra*, one should say, "It is the *mantra* of Agni, or of the Year. Having approached them, he should grasp them individually.
(GBr_2,6.12rr) Then he recites the Kāravyā verses: "(Indra awakened the poet...
(GBr_2,6.12ss). Whatever auspicious deed the gods performed, they attained it by means of the Kāravyā verses.
In the same way, the sacrificers obtain through the *kāravyā* verses whatever auspicious deed the gods perform;
they [recite] those [verses] by grasping them one after another. Then, having first recited the *diśām kḷptīḥ* (the arrangements of the quarters).
He recites the subsequent *janakalpa* verses beginning with, "He who is fit for the assembly, fit for the sacrificial session" (*ṚVKh* 5.12.1;
*ŚS* 20.128.1), and then, "He whose eyes are unanointed, whose body is unanointed" (*ṚVKh* 5.13.1; *ŚS* 20.128.6).
The seasons are indeed the quarters, the source of procreation. Therefore, having first recited the *kḷpti* verses of the quarters—
[beginning with] "He who is fit for the assembly, fit for the sacrificial session" (*ṚVKh* 5.12.1)— ...
"Thus he recites the subsequent *janakalpa* verses;
thereby he ordains the seasons and establishes them in the seasons. As they find their support, everything here finds its support accordingly."
He who knows thus becomes established with offspring and cattle;
he recites them by half-verses for the sake of stability alone.
Then he recites the *Indragāthās*, beginning with: "O Indra, when you helped in the battle of the ten kings" (*yad indrādo dāśarājñe*).
For by means of the *Indragāthās*, the gods indeed sang themselves to victory over the Asuras and thus surpassed them.
In the same way, the sacrificers, by means of the Indragāthās, sing out against their unpleasant rival and thus overcome him. He recites them verse by half-verse for the sake of stability.
Then he recites the Aitaśapralāpa,
beginning with "These mares leap forward" (*etā aśvā ā plavante*).
For the sage Aitaśa beheld the life-span of the sacrifice.
He said to his sons: "My dear sons, I have discovered the life-span of the sacrifice.
I shall proclaim it; do not think me arrogant. They replied, "So be it."
He cried out.

Then Abhyagni Aitaśāyana, his eldest son, ran toward him and covered his mouth, saying, "Our father is proud. He said, "Shame on you, wretch! I shall make your offspring the most wicked of all. He who—
"If you had not seized my face, you fool, I would have made the cow live for a hundred years and the man live for a thousand years.
Therefore, the Aitaśāyanas, though being noble-born, are the most wicked of others; they offer tribute and give their own father as a gift to their own Prajāpati and their own deity.
That which is the babbling of Aitaśa is the form of the heavenly world.
Furthermore, as for the *aitaśapralāpa*: the *aitaśapralāpa* is indeed unfailing (*ayātayāman*) and inexhaustible (*akṣiti*).
[Thinking,] "May my sacrifice be unfailing; may my sacrifice be inexhaustible," he recites this very *aitaśapralāpa*, taking it word by word.
(GBr_2,6.13n) He chants the *praṇava* for them with the final *pada*, just as for the *nivids*.
(GBr_2,6.13o) Then, having first recited the *pravalhikās*:
"Two rays are stretched out... (*vitatau kiraṇau dvau*, ṚVKh 5.16.1).
"Thus he recites the subsequent *pratirādha* verses;
'Bhuk'—thus [he recites] when [the breath] has arrived" (*bhug ity abhigataḥ*).
[The edition reads: *pratirādhānuttarān*.]

By means of riddles (*pravalhikā*), the gods indeed extracted the vital essences of the Asuras. Because the gods extracted the vital essences of the Asuras by means of these, they are called *pravalhikās*; that is the etymological origin of the name *pravalhikā*.
They indeed prospered through the *pratirādhas*; because they prospered through the *pratirādhas*, they are called *pratirādhas*. That is the reason for the name *pratirādha* of the *pratirādhas*.
(GBr_2,6.13v) By means of *pravalhikā*s alone they extract the vital essences of their enemies and rivals; (GBr_2,6.13w) those *pravalhikā*s indeed they win over by means of *pratirādha*s;
(GBr_2,6.13x) they [win them] by grasping them one by one.
(GBr_2,6.13y) Then he recites the *ajijñāsenya* verses:
"Hither, thither, eastward, westward, northward, southward" (*ihettha prāg apāg udag adharāk*). [The edition reads *udāg*.]
[Corrected p.

303] (GBr_2,6.13z) By means of the *ājijñāsenyā* verses, the gods indeed recognized the Asuras and then overcame them. In the same way, the sacrificers today recognize their unpleasant rival by means of the *ājijñāsenyā* verses and then overcome him.
He recites them half-verse by half-verse for the sake of stability; then he recites the *ativāda* hymn.
"These gods have stepped forth" (*vīme devā akraṃsata*; ṚVKh 5.19.1, ŚS 20.135.4)—thus it is said in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa* (2.6.13ee).
Excellence (*śrī*) indeed is over-excellence (*ativāda*);
he recites that single verse.
The *ekastā* is indeed prosperity (*śrī*); he recites it with the *virebha* [verses],
for by means of the *virebhas*, a person carries prosperity.
He recites it half-verse by half-verse for the sake of stability alone.
(GBr_2,6.14a) Then he recites the hymns to the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases:
"O singer, the Ādityas indeed led away the sacrificial fee from the Aṅgirases" (ṚVKh 5.20.1, ŚS 20.135.6).
(GBr_2,6.14b) This, they call the *devanītha*.
The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases were competing for the heavenly world, saying, "We shall first reach heaven; we shall first reach it.
The Aṅgirases perceived the Soma-pressing of the following day;
they said to Agni, "Go and announce the Soma-pressing of the following day to the Ādityas."
(GBr_2,6.14f) Then the Ādityas saw the sacrifice of that very day.
They said to Agni, "Today is our sacrifice;
you shall be our *hotṛ*. We approach you. (GBr_2,6.14g–h) "We approach you."
He went and Agni said: "Now the Ādityas are looking toward the soma-pressing of today; whom have they chosen as their Hotṛ? They are summoning you, saying, 'We [choose] you.
The Aṅgirases were enraged and said, "Do not go; let us [go] instead. Agni said, "No; for they summon me without reproach."
(GBr_2,6.14l) For it is indeed a sin for one not to go to the call of the blameless;
therefore, whether [the distance be] very far or very short, he should certainly go to the call of the sacrificer.
(GBr_2,6.14m) For it is indeed a sin for one not to go to the call of the blameless.
The Aṅgirases performed a sacrifice for those Ādityas;
they brought this earth as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for them,
but they did not accept it.
This very [cow], having turned back with its head on both sides, pierced by grief and grieving, wandered about in anger, thinking, "They did not accept me.
From her these fissures were torn open, which are found as chasms today.
Therefore, one should not drive up a cow that has turned back from giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), nor should one wipe it down.
"Lest I should crush the sacrificial fee," he thinks;
therefore, if one has a rival born of the same lineage who seeks to harm him, he should give that fee to him. Thus, the sacrificial fee does not turn away from him.
He establishes sorrow in his hateful rival at the very end—that which burns in the fire.
He indeed recites:
"O singer, the Ādityas brought a sacrificial fee to the Aṅgirases; they, O singer, drove it back" (RVKh 5.20.1abc, ŚS 20.135.6abc).
"For they did not return to this earth" (GBr_2,6.14aa)— (referring to the verse) "But they, O singer, did return to it" (ṚVKh 5.20.1d,
ŚS 20.135.6d)— for indeed, they returned to that [other world].
"O singer, they indeed accepted her from us," so it is said;
for they did not accept this earth.
"And O singer, they indeed accepted her from us."
"Thus, having grasped the sun, they did not grasp the other days" (GBr 2.6.14); "the days were not discerning" (RVKh 5.20.2c, ŚS 20.135.7c).
He who shines yonder is indeed the discerning one among the days.
He indeed recites:
"Like leaders of a herd, we have gone before the other sacrifices" (*yajñān itarasaṃ na purogavāsaḥ*).
This sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), indeed, is the leader of the sacrifice.
(GBr_2,6.14hh) "Just as we deserve this, so let him who is the Lord among these be the Unnetṛ-priest.

(GBr_2,6.14ii) "And he is white, possessing swift speed; and he, the youngest, fills the measure with his strides" (*ṚVKh* 5.20.3, *ŚS* 20.135.8). (GBr_2,6.14jj) This very one is the white one; this one possesses swift speed; this one, the youngest, fills the measure with his strides.
"And it quickly fills my measure" (RVKh 5.20.3c, ŚS 20.135.8c).

Thus: "O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, accept this gift with favor, O Aṅgiras! This gift is all-pervading and powerful; this gift is vast and wide. May the gods grant this divine gift; may that be well-disposed toward you."
"May it be yours day by day; grasp it again! (RVKh 5.20.4–5;
ŚS 20.135.9–10). Thus, when he recites the *ādityās* and the *āṅgirasīs*, he recites them day after day for the sake of attaining heaven, just as he recites the *nivid*s.
Then he recites the *bhūtechad* verses,
beginning with "O Indra, grant us protection" (*tvam indra śarma riṇā*).
These worlds, indeed, are the *bhūtechad*.
The gods, indeed, poured out food for the Asuras, desiring to strike them down with that which exists and wishing to overcome them.
These gods then covered them from all beings; because these gods covered them from all beings, it is therefore called *bhūtechad* ("covering from beings").
(GBr_2,6.14ss) That is the "concealer of beings" (*bhūtechad*); (GBr_2,6.14tt) for these worlds indeed conceal one another;
(GBr_2,6.14uu) they struck [the breath] out from all beings.
He who knows thus desires [all things] for all beings. 14.
Then he recites the *āhanasyā* verses, beginning with "That which of this breaker of distress...
(RVKh 5.22.1; ŚS 20.136.1). For indeed, all this has been born from the *āhanasya*.
For from the slayer-like [sacrifice] this indeed is produced;
for the attainment and procreation of all this,
he should recite those six [verses].
There are six seasons;
the seasons are the fathers;
the fathers are Prajāpati.
"Prajāpati [is] the Āhanasyās;
one should recite those ten," such is the statement of Śāmbhavya.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables.
The Virāj is the sacrifice;
embryos subsist upon it;
the Virāj is indeed prosperity.
Fame, food, and prosperity— verily,
he thereby establishes glory, food, and prosperity upon the Virāj;
as these become established, everything here follows after them and becomes established.
He who knows thus becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle.
"One should recite three [verses]," says Vātsya;
for seed, once emitted, develops as a triad: the egg, the membrane, and the placenta.

(GBr_2,6.15u) That which is born from the mother and the father has the *trivṛt* as its basis; that is the third. (GBr_2,6.15v) If one were to recite a fourth [verse], it would be merely a rising from what has not yet come into being. (GBr_2,6.15w) "One should recite all sixteen [verses]," so say some.
One who is afflicted by desire indeed sheds semen;
from that shed semen offspring are born for the procreation of offspring.
One becomes possessed of offspring and capable of procreating for the sake of procreation. He who knows this is born with offspring and cattle. // 15 //
Then he recites the *dādhikrī* verse:
"I have performed praise for Dadhikrāvan" (*dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam*).
After that, he recites the subsequent *pāvamānī* verses.
"Pressed, most rich in honey" (RV 9.101.4;
ŚS 20.137.4)—thus Dadhikrā is indeed food; the *pāvamānī* verses are the means of purification.

Now, some indeed recite the *pāvamānī* verses first and then the subsequent *dādhikrī*, saying, "Speech is this [earth], which purifies as food. But one should not do it in that way; for speech perishes and becomes hungry.
He should therefore recite the *dādhikrī* first and then the subsequent *pāvamānī* verses.
In that he recites the *dādhikrī*, this speech has uttered a voice of slaughter;
thus, by means of the purifier of the gods, he purifies speech.
That [verse] is indeed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
The Anuṣṭubh is indeed speech;
thus he purifies speech by means of its own metre.
He recites it half-verse by half-verse.
It is for the sake of stability indeed;
then he recites the Pāvamānī verses,
for the Pāvamānīs are indeed a means of purification.

(GBr_2,6.16p) This speech has uttered a speech that is destructive; (GBr_2,6.16q) therefore, by means of the *pāvamānī* verses alone, one purifies speech. (GBr_2,6.16r) All of these are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
Speech, indeed, is the *anuṣṭubh*;
thus he purifies speech by means of its own meter;
he recites it half-verse by half-verse.
(GBr_2,6.16v) For the sake of stability indeed—
(GBr_2,6.16w) "The drop descended unto the Aṃśumatī" (ṚV 8.96.13,
ŚS 20.137.7)— he recites this triplet, a hymn dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
Now, this [section] is indeed set aside.
When they recite this final triplet for Indra and Bṛhaspati, and this final triplet for Indra in the Jagatī metre, saying, "This is the support of the pressing;
it is a bulwark," one should not do so.
This speech of these Hotrakas has the *triṣṭubh* as its abode, namely that [verse] addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati at the third pressing.

Therefore, when he recites this final triplet addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati, and the final triplet addressed to Indra in the *jagatī* meter, he gratifies him in his own abode, in his own two deities. He may perform the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) according to his desire, even if it is the regular one.
(GBr_2,6.16dd) At will, [one may recite] with the last verse of the triplet.
(GBr_2,6.16ee) Regarding this, they say: "One should recite it together on the sixth day; one should not recite it together. (GBr_2,6.16ff) How is it that on other days he recites it together?
(GBr_2,6.16gg) "How is it that one does not recite here?
(GBr_2,6.16hh) Now, moreover, they say: "One should certainly not recite;
for the sixth day is indeed the heavenly world. (GBr_2,6.16ii)
"The heavenly world is indeed without a companion.
"Someone indeed pacifies [the gods] in the heavenly world.
Therefore, he does not recite the *saṃśaṃsana*.
That which he does not recite is the form of the heavenly world.

Furthermore, as for why he recites these [hymns]—namely the *Nābhānediṣṭha*, the *Vālakhilyas*, the *Vṛṣākapi*, and the *Evayāmarut*—these indeed constitute the *ukthas* here; therefore, he does not recite them.
The *Vṛṣākapi* belongs to Indra.
All the meters are the Aitaśapralāpa.

That which belongs to Indra and Bṛhaspati at the third pressing has been attained; therefore, he recites this triplet (*ṛc*) as a hymn (*sūkta*) for Indra and Bṛhaspati, and the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) is also for Indra and Bṛhaspati:
"The godless tribes are attacking us."

"The clans are indeed divine, for there is no fear of enemies for him. Where one recites this for one who knows thus, the subjects become peaceful and well-ordered; they endure [all things] where one recites this for one who knows thus—so says the Brāhmaṇa. (GBr_2,6.16ss) 16.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the latter part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
Thus ends the first and second part of the Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda.
